#6198. Atmos Global Concierge: Alaska Airlines’ New Invitation-Only Elite Status

Alaska Airlines is increasingly becoming like the “big three” US carriers when it comes to its route network, as the airline expands globally, following its takeover of Hawaiian Airlines. Now the airline is doing another thing you’ll find at competitors, which is introducing an invitation-only elite status. Let’s take a look at what we know so far about Atmos Global Concierge, which is the name of this new status.

Some Atmos Rewards members on Reddit are reporting receiving an invitation for the carrier’s new status tier that has no published qualification requirements, and it’s above the Titanium tier. Those who have been awarded the status can keep it through December 31, 2027.

So, what are the perks of Atmos Global Concierge status?

We’ll have to of course wait some time to get firsthand reports of the experience, but as you’d expect, this is a lot more about better “soft” treatment, plus having top priority for everything. There’s nothing particularly remarkable about this status otherwise, but that’s not surprising, since that’s typically not the focus on invitation-only elite status.

It’s anyone’s guess what exactly it takes to get an invitation, as it’s a bit of a mystery, much like with American Concierge Key, Delta 360, and United Global Services. It’s possible that criteria differ based on where you mostly fly out of. It does seem like frequent international travel in business class is something that increases odds of eligibility.

Based on the reports so far, it almost seems like this status is being dangled as a “carrot” for those who have maybe taken a few long haul business class trips, in hopes of keeping them flying on Alaska and Hawaiian.

There’s a reason that airlines offer invitation-only elite status, and it’s kind of brilliant. The idea is to keep people on the “hamster wheel,” and keep them booking high yield tickets on an airline over competitors.

Airlines of course have elite tiers with published requirements, and once you qualify for your planned tier for a year, you might consider branching out and booking another airline. But when there’s invitation-only elite status, you don’t know what you actually need to earn it, so you’re more likely to keep flying with the airline. And if you’re spending other people’s money, you’re also more likely to make sure that ticket is expensive as it should be.

At the end of the day, these kinds of status tiers aren’t really about the exact details of the perks. On some level, they’re intended to stroke the egos of travelers, and that works. People get excited when they get to board a flight first, etc., and this whole concept plays into that.

Alaska Airlines has introduced a new invitation-only elite status, named Atmos Global Concierge. The idea is that this is targeted primarily at those flying a lot internationally, and it offers perks like concierge assistance, upgrade priority, some partner elite perks, and more.

With the way Alaska has grown, it’s not surprising to see the airline also copying the “big three” with a status tier like this.

What do you make of Atmos Global Concierge?

#6197. The Legal Origin Story of Wokeness Is a Map to Defeating Woke 2.0

Students walk between classes on the campus of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, Pa., in 2017.

Gail Heriot — a University of San Diego Law School professor who, having spent decades working in civil rights law at a high level, is an exceedingly rare specimen on the right — has brought needed attention to the overlooked story of wokeness’s origins in policy and law. It’s one we need to understand fully if we’re to pursue a solution that actually rolls back the “woke exceptions” to anti-discrimination law that have gutted meritocracy, encouraged bigotry, shut down national conversations, and generally poisoned race relations in our multiethnic republic.

In Why We Walk on Eggshells, a recent release from Encounter Books, Heriot builds a nearly unassailable case that many of these pernicious effects are not “politics downstream from culture,” but rather “culture downstream from law.”

Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.

#6196. Cathay Orders 14 More Airbus Jets As Its A330-900 Commitment Grows To 41

European aircraft manufacturer Airbus today revealed that the Hong Kong-based Cathay Pacific has increased its order for A330-900 and A321 aircraft. The airline confirmed 14 more orders, including 11 A330s, bringing its total commitment for the widebody type to 41 jets. The airline also added orders for three more A321s.

In the aircraft sales war, Airbus and Boeing are constantly competing to announce orders from their airline customers. Both major planemakers have sizeable backlogs for their narrowbody and widebody programmes. Despite this, they are both still keen to add orders to these backlogs.

In a press release issued earlier today, Airbus said the Cathay Group had bolstered its commitment to the A330 family. The group added 11 firm orders to its existing order for the largest member of the A330neo family, the A330-900. The airline already had 30 on order, bringing its total to 41 of the type.

Commenting on the order, Cathay Pacific's Chief Operations and Service Delivery Officer Alex McGowan revealed that the additional aircraft will be used to expand and upgrade the existing fleet, with some replacing older types and others serving as additional new aircraft. This sentiment was echoed by Benoit de Saint-Exupéry, Airbus EVP Sales, Commercial Aircraft.

"Together the A330-900 and A321neo aircraft give the airline the flexibility to match capacity to demand, bringing versatility while benefiting from lower fuel burn and the efficiencies of a streamlined Airbus fleet. We are proud to support the Cathay Group through its exciting next stage of fleet renewal and growth."

According to data from ch-aviation, Cathay Pacific currently has 181 aircraft, of which 14 are inactive. Excluding the new order announced today, the airline has 100 aircraft on order. The airline's order book looks as follows:

The airline currently has 18 A321 aircraft, 17 of which are listed as active. All 30 still on order will then presumably be used to increase the size of the fleet, which has an average age of just 3.6 years. The story is slightly different for the Airbus A330. No A330-900s have been delivered yet, and the airline has 43 older-generation A330-300s, six of which are listed as inactive.

With this in mind, the Airbus A330-900 order is likely more geared towards replacing the A330-300s, which have an average age of 18.2 years. The oldest aircraft type in the fleet is the Boeing 777-300. 14 of these aircraft are listed as active, with an average age of 25.3 years. The incoming Boeing 777-9 will likely help replace this sub-fleet.

The carrier has more than 30 777X jets on order.

Despite being a widebody aircraft, Cathay Pacific typically flies the Airbus A330 on shorter legs. According to schedule data from Cirium, the A330's top route from Hong Kong is to Taipei (TPE). This is a flight that takes less than two hours. Looking at the map above, you'll see that other than a single trip to Perth (PER) and a handful of trips to Cairns (CNS), all of the A330 flights this year have remained within Asia.

The airline is using its larger widebodies for longer-distance flights. For example, when you look at London Heathrow Airport (LHR) and New York JFK Airport (JFK), flights have been operated by the Boeing 777-300ER, the Airbus A350-900 and the Airbus A350-1000. Frankfurt Airport (FRA) and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), meanwhile, have only seen the Boeing 777-300ER this year.

The A330neo has a wing with the highest aspect ratio of about 11:1 of all airliners. The higher the aspect ratio, the lower the induced drag. Induced drag can be up to 70% of the total drag during high AoA operations like take off and ascend. During travel at altitude it can be as lesser than 10% of the total drag during low AoA operations. During travel the slightly higher weight of the A330neo compared to the 787 is leading slightly higher fuel burn of the A330neo. The A330neo burns lesser fuel than the 787 during take off and ascend to travel altitude, but it burns more during travel. The longer the route, the longer the A330neo burns a little more than the 787. After a certain distance the fuel saved during take off and ascend is equal to the extra fuel burned during travel (once it was between 4000 and 5000 miles). Cathey intends to use the A330neo on routes close to or below 4000, what makes the A330neo an attractive choice, since also the acquisition cost is much lower than the 787.

However Delta has used it on many of it's international routes to Europe, South America and Asia.

#6195. Frontier Airlines’ Unique First Class Now On Sale (No Food, Drinks, Or Recline)

Frontier Airlines has just put first class tickets on sale, with the product launching systemwide for flights as of March 2027. This is a major development for the Denver-based airline, as the historically ultra low cost carrier tries to move upmarket, and respond to consumer preferences. This is only one of several initiatives we’re seeing, along with the introduction of Starlink Wi-Fi, plus charging ports at select seats. Let’s cover all the details.

Frontier Airlines has just put first class tickets on sale for flights as of March 5, 2027. For context, Frontier plans to reconfigure its entire fleet to add eight first class seats at the front of the cabin, with two rows of seats in a 2-2 configuration. Specifically, the airline has selected the Geven Comoda seating platform, with seats having up to 37″ of pitch.

Frontier has already started reconfiguring planes with first class cabins, and the idea is that by early March 2027, the entire fleet will have these seats, which is the point at which they’ll be sold as a separate product. So while the seats will already be in service, and some customers will luck out, that’s the formal launch plan.

Obviously this is a fast timeline for retrofitting cabins, but keep in mind most of the cabin will remain unchanged, so it shouldn’t take much time to reconfigure each aircraft. So, what should we expect in terms of the first class product? Here’s how the airline describes it:

First Class seats offer our most spacious seating experience, providing exceptional comfort and additional personal space at the front of the aircraft. These seats are pre-reclined and do not convert into lie-flat beds.

Complimentary food and beverages are not included with the First Class experience. However, a variety of food and beverage options are available for purchase by all passengers.

Frontier’s first class seats will be “pre-reclined” (meaning they won’t recline), and won’t actually offer complimentary snacks and drinks, so it’ll be just like economy in that regard. On the plus side, the seats are expected to feature USB-C charging ports, which will be the first time that the airline offers in-seat power. The carrier is also going from offering no Wi-Fi, to offering Starlink Wi-Fi as of mid-2027, so that’s pretty exciting.

The airline will also be introducing a dedicated extra legroom section in rows three through eight, with seats having up to 34″ of pitch. Not only that, but these seats will also have USB-C charging ports (while the remainder of economy seats won’t offer in-seat power).

With Frontier Airlines first class tickets now on sale, what is pricing like? The airline is increasingly leaning into the concept of bundles, so we’ll see the Basic Fare, Economy Bundle, Premium Bundle, and First Bundle.

The First Bundle includes a carry-on bag and personal item, two checked bags weighing up to 50 pounds each, priority boarding, and no change or cancel fees.

Pulling up a random one-way flight from Denver (DEN) to Los Angeles (LAX), I see the Basic Fare starting at $119, the Economy Bundle starting at $142, the Premium Bundle starting at $172, and the First Bundle starting at $244.

Those are some incredibly attractive prices, especially if you intend to check bags. However, the airline emphasizes how it has promotional pricing at launch, so only time will tell how that pricing evolves.

There’s no single right or wrong way to offer a premium product. However, I feel like Frontier might be taking the wrong strategy here. What Frontier is offering is essentially more along the lines of the initial Spirit “Big Front Seat” — you get more space, and nothing else.

This just strikes me as a missed opportunity, because I feel like psychologically, willingness to pay is going to be substantially higher if you just include free alcoholic drinks and at least some sort of food. It’s not like I was expecting them to install ovens and have hot meals (JetBlue’s new first class will only have cold food).

But I feel like if the airline just invested $10 in drinks & snacks they could charge more, and would also expand the potential customer base. Whether logical or not, there are some number of passengers who would be more likely to even consider a product if it actually had a dedicated soft product, rather than just being a more spacious seat. At least that’s my take.

Obviously at the current pricing, this is an incredibly attractive proposition for customers. However, I also feel like the airline probably wants to be able to charge higher fares in the long run.

Frontier Airlines has started to reconfigure planes with first class seats, with tickets now being on sale for flights as of March 5, 2027 (at which point the entire fleet should be reconfigured). While Frontier first class will have first class-style seats (minus the recline), there won’t be any differentiation in terms of the soft product, as food and drinks will still be available for purchase.

I would’ve liked the airline to actually roll out a differentiated soft product, but it sounds like that’s not happening. Then again, between Starlink Wi-Fi and in-seat power, this will be a much more attractive proposition than flying with Frontier in the past.

What do you make of Frontier’s first class concept?

#6194. American Projects Busiest Thanksgiving Travel Period in Years

American Airlines expects to fly over 8 million people in the days leading up to and following Thanksgiving.

The carrier said Monday that it will operate around 85,000 flights between Nov. 19 and Dec. 1. During that time, an American flight will depart every 13 seconds, officials said.

American said it will operate 7,021 flights on the Sunday after Thanksgiving, Nov. 29, making it the airline’s largest operating day since the COVID-19 pandemic.

At 11 a.m. Central Time on Nov. 20, 29, and 30, the carrier will have 1,130 flights operating simultaneously.

“Our team is ready for one of the busiest travel periods of the year, and we’re focused on delivering a safe, reliable operation so our customers can spend less time thinking about holiday travel and more time enjoying the holiday,” American Chief Operating Officer David Seymour said in a news release.

According to TSA data, the Sunday following Thanksgiving is often the busiest day of the year for air travel. The Tuesday and Wednesday preceding Thanksgiving also rank high, as do certain weekends in June and July.

#6193. Lufthansa’s First Airbus A350-1000 Has Arrived: 299.5 Seats, Four Cabins, Munich Routes

In 2023, Lufthansa Group placed an order for the Airbus A350-1000 — the order was initially for 10 frames, before being increased to 15 frames the following year. The Lufthansa Group is undergoing a massive long haul fleet modernization at the moment, with both Airbus and Boeing planes on the way.

Along those lines, the first Lufthansa A350-1000 has just joined the carrier’s fleet (in a dazzling livery no less), so let’s cover all the details, including the routes the plane will fly, how the plane is configured, etc.

Between late 2026 and 2030, Lufthansa is taking delivery of 15 Airbus A350-1000s. This is only one of several aircraft types the airline is acquiring, as it’s also taking delivery of Airbus A350-900s, Boeing 787-9s, and (eventually) Boeing 777-9s.

The first A350-1000 has just been delivered today, with three more planes expected to be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of the year. This first plane even features the special 100th anniversary livery, as Lufthansa has seven of these flying, with one representing each fleet type.

The first plane has the registration code D-AIFA, and is named “Deutschland” (since Lufthansa names all of its planes). This is a special plane for another reason, as it’s also the 700th aircraft that Airbus has delivered to Lufthansa Group. How gorgeous is this plane?!?

Here’s how Heiko Reitz, Lufthansa’s Hub Manager for Munich, describes this:

“We are proud that the Airbus A350-1000—Airbus’s most modern long-haul aircraft—is coming to Munich. The introduction of the new A350-1000 is part of the largest fleet modernization in the history of the Lufthansa Group and a key driver on the path to more sustainability. Our new flagship features 40 percent more Business and Premium Economy seats. To put it simply: The A350-1000 strengthens our premium hub in Munich.”

On a slight tangent, over the summer I saw the 100th anniversary Boeing 747-8 in Frankfurt (FRA), and I must say, I think it might be the most breathtaking plane in commercial service. Is it just me?

We’ve known that the Airbus A350-1000s will get the new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris first class and Allegris business class. So, what can we expect in terms of the configuration? The A350-1000 features 300 seats, spread across four cabins, as follows:

As a point of comparison, the A350-900 (the non-stretched version of the plane) features 267 seats, as follows:

So the stretched version has 11 more business class seats, 11 more premium economy seats, and 11 more economy seats (11 more seats across three cabins, what a funny coincidence). The airline is still maintaining only one row of first class, which is kind of “bleh.”

You can find the Lufthansa A350-1000 seat map here.

Lufthansa Airbus A350-1000s will all be stationed in Munich (MUC), which is where Lufthansa bases all of its A350s. The first of these planes is entering long haul commercial service as of early December 2026.

Specifically, as of December 3, 2026, the A350-1000 will fly between Munich and Tokyo Haneda (HND), with the next two destinations being Shanghai (PVG) and Singapore (SIN), and those services expected to launch within weeks, though the schedule hasn’t yet been updated to reflect that.

Note that initially the flights won’t be operated by the A350-1000 daily, so there will be alternating service with the A350-900. It’s interesting that the initial route isn’t to North America, where a single plane could do a same day turn, and continuously stay in service. but I guess there’s enough commonality between the A350-900 and A350-1000, so it’s not a big deal.

As far as US destinations go, it’s expected that Chicago (ORD) and Newark (EWR) will be the first two cities to see the new plane, though there’s no exact timeline for that yet.

In 2023, Lufthansa placed an order for the Airbus A350-1000, and the first of these planes has just been delivered, and will enter service in early December 2026. The plane features 300 seats across four cabins, though still only expect one row of first class seats. The Munich-based plane will initially fly to Tokyo, Shanghai, and Singapore. I must say, Lufthansa knocked it out of the park with its centennial livery, and I can’t wait to see this plane flying.

Staying at Walt Disney World on hotel points — within walking distance of two theme parks — might sound like a pixie-dust-fueled dream, but it's actually possible if you stay at the Walt Disney World Swan, Dolphin or Swan Reserve.

These large, highly visible properties are actually three adjacent but distinct hotels that share access to amenities.

The Dolphin is the 27-story pyramid that opened in 1990 and is visible from just about every Disney World theme park.

The Swan opened in 1990 and is home to two 47-foot swan statues, while the Swan Reserve is the newest of the trio, having just opened in 2021.

These three resorts are clustered together and are all bookable with Marriott Bonvoy points. This is possible because while they each have Walt Disney World in their names and in their location, the Dolphin is actually a Sheraton, the Swan is a Westin and the Swan Reserve is in Marriott's Autograph Collection.

Related: These are the best credit cards for earning Marriott Bonvoy points

That means that the current welcome bonus with the (see rates and fees) that awards three free night awards (valued up to 50,000 Marriott points each; certain hotels have resort fees) after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening could cover a three-night stay at one of these properties. And that's especially true if you were willing to top up your awards with up to 25,000 additional Marriott points if the nights you wanted cost a few more points than 50,000. Additionally, new cardholders can receive up to $100 in statement credits (up to $50 biannually) after spending $500 on eligible airline purchases (through June 30, 2027).

Generally speaking, the Walt Disney World Dolphin is a large, busy convention hotel with the most on-site restaurants and amenities. The Walt Disney World Swan is comparatively smaller but still a very large, busy hotel that's closest to the Dolphin, with both connected by a covered walkway.

The Swan Reserve is the smallest, most upscale — and most expensive — of the three properties. But combined, these three properties are positively massive with 2,619 rooms, 23 restaurants and lounges, and a host of amenities and facilities.

Due to some wheeling and dealing in the 1980s, the Swan and Dolphin (and later, Swan Reserve) scored some of the best real estate at Walt Disney World.

These resorts are within walking distance of both Epcot and Disney's Hollywood Studios. Or there's a complimentary water taxi that can take you to either of those parks that leaves from the dock between the Dolphin and the Swan.

Only three of Disney's own operated resorts can claim this same feature: Disney's Yacht Club, Disney's Boardwalk and Disney's Beach Club.

All of those are deluxe Disney resorts that regularly start between $600 - $800 per night, where rooms at this trio of properties can start at half that price if you're paying with cash.

Related: How to save hundreds of dollars on a trip to Disney with the Disney Inspire Visa

There are multiple pools at the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve, with each property having at least one pool located directly on-site.

But the most expansive pools are situated closest to the Dolphin, including the grotto pool with waterfalls and a waterslide.

There is also a lap pool in case you want to get a water-based workout in. A great thing about the pools — and other amenities — is that it doesn't matter which of these three hotels you are staying at; you can use all the amenities at the other hotels, too.

But it's not just pools you can pick from; there is a very long list of amenities in case the Disney parks leave you with some downtime.

At the Dolphin, you'll find a good-sized arcade and even a small bowling alley.

Between the Swan and Dolphin, there is also sand volleyball, an outdoor playground area for little kids and even swan-themed paddle boats that guests can take out on the water at no additional cost, as rentals are included in the hefty $50 nightly resort fee.

If you wanted to have a resort day outside the theme parks during your Disney World vacation, the odds are high that there is plenty to do at the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve to keep you entertained.

Each of the three hotels also has its own fitness area for you to still get your workouts in.

If, after all that activity, you want to rest and enjoy a massage or another treatment, there is a Mandara Spa inside the Dolphin.

Believe it or not, the reason you can enjoy these Marriott hotels, located in the heart of Walt Disney World, dates back to disputes and deals in the 1980s.

The hotels have many Disney perks and an on-property Disney location, but they are not actually Disney-owned and operated hotels. And now they are all hotels where you can earn and use Marriott Bonvoy points to stay in the middle of Mickey's kingdom without paying Mickey's exact price tag.

Guests of the Walt Disney World Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve get to enjoy some really good Disney benefits that are otherwise mostly reserved only for true on-property Disney World guests.

As mentioned, there are complimentary boats to Epcot and Hollywood Studios from these hotels if you don't want to make the 15-20-minute walk.

There are buses that leave from these hotels to Magic Kingdom or Animal Kingdom. The one downside to the buses vs. those at "true" Disney resorts is that the bus to Magic Kingdom takes you to the Ticket and Transportation Center (TTC) instead of to Magic Kingdom itself. From the TTC, you have to take the monorail or ferry boat to the Magic Kingdom.

If that sounds like a hassle to you, it can be a good time to splurge on a Disney-operated Minnie Van you book in the Lyft app to take you directly to the front of the Magic Kingdom with the money you saved by staying at these hotels instead of actual deluxe Disney resorts.

At these hotels, you will find true Disney gift shops, along with Disney park tickets and Disney vacation planning assistance.

If by which hotel is best you mean the nicest, then the answer is likely the Walt Disney World Swan Reserve. It is not only the newest and most expensive of the three hotels, but also the one that falls under the higher-category Marriott Brand, Autograph Collection.

But everyone has different tastes and priorities for their Disney trip, so each of the three hotels has its own fans.

All three of the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve hotels are great choices for families, but if we have to choose, families with young kids may enjoy the Swan and Dolphin a bit more due to more on-site amenities such as the playground and arcade and a slightly shorter walk to the boats or to Epcot and Hollywood Studios.

There are also more on-site food options at the Dolphin and Swan than you'll find at the Swan Reserve.

In part because of conventions and events that do come to these hotels, no single hotel among the three is always the cheapest. The only real way to know for sure on your dates is to run some searches.

However, the Dolphin is the least expensive of the three on average, whether booking on Marriott points or cash, typically followed by the Swan and then the Swan Reserve.

All the rooms at these hotels are nice, especially once the Dolphin finishes its current renovation, but there are differences among them.

Swan Reserve rooms are likely the nicest between the three, with higher-end finishes, two robes available, walk-in showers, a better coffee maker, etc.

The rooms at the Swan are also nice and have been recently renovated. In my experience, they typically offer one robe, and importantly, two queen beds in the rooms with the two bed option.

The rooms at the Dolphin are currently undergoing renovation to make them more similar in appearance to the Swan. However, a significant difference will remain even after the renovations.

The beds at the Dolphin in rooms with two beds are full-sized or double beds, not queen beds. This makes it a tighter fit if you are putting two people in each bed.

There were no robes in our Dolphin room, and the coffee maker is a step down, which makes sense, as this is a Sheraton rather than the higher-tier brands at the other two hotels.

There are more restaurants at the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve than it makes sense for me to put in a big list here, but I will mention a few of my personal favorite options.

First, I'm a fan of Rosa Mexicano, especially for an easy, fun arrival-night dinner with margaritas — especially if I have a resort credit to put to good use, as I did recently by booking via Amex's Hotel Collection with my .

Amare, a Mediterranean restaurant at the Swan Reserve, and Todd English's bluezoo, a seafood restaurant in the Walt Disney World Dolphin, are two additional standouts for me, though there are plenty of other great picks, too.

And believe it or not, if you order an entrée at Todd English’s bluezoo, Amare, or Il Mulino New York Trattoria, Rosa Mexicano, Bourbon Steak or Kimonos, your kids ages 5 - 12 can get two free hours at the on-site Camp Dolphin. This supervised childcare includes a take-home craft and a snack.

I also enjoy the grab-and-go options that are available at each of these three hotels for an easy muffin and coffee sort of breakfast in the morning.

If you have Marriott Platinum elite status or higher — which you can get just by having the — you can choose free breakfast as your benefit for the stay, which will get you a daily voucher to use in these shops.

I've stayed at these hotels over a dozen times and there is no doubt in my mind that the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve can absolutely be worth it when deciding between them and Disney-owned resorts.

And don't get me wrong — I really love a good, true Disney resort stay with all of the elaborate themes and locations — but the prices for deluxe resorts owned by Disney are often more than the prices that these three resorts charge. At these hotels, you're often paying a price that is more in the Disney moderate, mid-tier resort range (and sometimes even a value range), but getting closer to deluxe-tier location and amenities.

And you can even use some of your hotel credits from certain Amex or Chase cards and book via programs that give you free breakfast, resort credits and more, like I just did via American Express with my to get $450 in bonus savings and inclusions on a recent stay.

So there are ways you can really bring down your total cost here that typically don't work at true Disney resorts, which don't participate in most of those programs, including even using the simple $100 annual Chase Travel hotel credit from the (see rates and fees).

And that's assuming you're even paying cash — you can also use your Marriott points or free night awards here and save your cash for other parts of the trip.

So yes, I absolutely think it is sometimes worth potentially spending less to stay in the middle of it all at the Swan, Dolphin or Swan Reserve and still get the overwhelming majority of the perks of being at a true Disney resort.

There are a lot of great places to stay while on a Walt Disney World vacation, but often you have to make trade-offs. You can have a great location, good value, or an upscale stay, but typically not all three at the same time ... except at the Swan, Dolphin or Swan Reserve, which have the potential to give you the best of all worlds.

While the Swan Reserve is my favorite of the three, I've stayed at all of these hotels multiple times over the years on cash, Marriott points, and even using some of the hotel credits from my various credit cards, and I have every intention of many more stays in the future.

#6191. 5 Airlines Offering Premium Economy On Boeing 777-300ER Flights

An aviation writer, pilot, and flight operations professional who sees aviation from both sides of the cockpit door. With a background in aeronautics, safety, and human factors, she brings curiosity, firsthand experience, and a love of the details that turn aircraft and airports into stories worth telling.

Premium economy has become an increasingly important part of long-haul air travel, giving passengers an option between standard economy and business class. The cabin typically offers more personal space, wider seats, greater recline, and upgraded service without the cost of a business-class ticket. However, the product is far from standardized.

Seat dimensions, cabin layouts, entertainment systems, dining, and additional services can differ considerably between airlines, and even between aircraft in the same fleet. The Boeing 777-300ER remains a major aircraft for international operations, and its wide cabin gives airlines room to position premium economy between business class and economy.

American Airlines, United Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Emirates, and Singapore Airlines all offer the cabin on at least some of their 777-300ER aircraft. Their products illustrate how carriers approach the same market in different ways, from a newly redesigned cabin to established long-haul seating and service. The details below refer to the relevant 777-300ER configurations, rather than every aircraft or route operated by each airline.

American Airlines has made premium economy a more prominent part of its Boeing 777-300ER cabin through a major interior redesign. The updated aircraft feature 44 premium economy seats, positioned between Flagship Suite business class and the main economy cabin. The new layout is part of a broader effort to increase the number of premium seating options available on long-haul services.American’s updated 777-300ER has 330 seats overall, including 70 Flagship Suite seats and 30 Main Cabin Extra seats. Main Cabin Extra remains an extra-legroom section within economy, rather than a separate cabin class. The 44-seat section is a clearly defined cabin, rather than a collection of preferred seats scattered through economy.

The redesigned premium economy seats include sculpted headrests, adjustable calf and footrests, and additional personal storage. These details are particularly relevant on overnight flights, when passengers may want to change position or settle in for several hours without moving around the cabin. Wireless charging is also part of the upgraded seating environment, reducing the need to keep a device connected to a cable throughout the flight.

44 seats, wireless charging, adjustable calf and footrests, enhanced storage

24 seats in a dedicated Premium Plus cabin

48 seats, 19-inch width, 40-inch pitch, 15.6-inch 4K screen

Up to 19.5-inch width, 40-inch pitch, calf and footrests

18.5-inch width, 38-inch pitch, 13.3-inch screen

The cabin is intended to create a clearer step up from standard economy, with more space and practical features while retaining a substantially different fare and service proposition from Flagship Suite. Passengers can therefore benefit from a combination of physical support and convenient charging without moving into business class.

The refurbishment also changes the balance of the aircraft, giving American more seats in its premium cabins while retaining a substantial economy section. The airline has said that the updated 777-300ERs are being introduced progressively, so passengers should check the aircraft assigned to a particular flight rather than assume that every 777-300ER has the new interior.

American announced that the first commercial flight with the redesigned aircraft was scheduled from New York John F. Kennedy International Airport to Buenos Aires on September 2, 2026. The program is expected to continue as additional aircraft receive the new cabin. The aircraft assignment can change, and the refreshed cabin should be verified before travel.

United Airlines offers Premium Plus on its Boeing 777-300ER, placing the product between Polaris business class and the economy cabin. In one 350-seat configuration, the aircraft has 60 Polaris seats, 24 Premium Plus seats, and 266 economy seats. The 24-seat Premium Plus section is arranged in a 2-4-2 layout, giving passengers a pair of seats on either side of the cabin and four seats in the center.That arrangement can be appealing to couples and solo travelers who prefer not to sit in a larger block of economy seating. The relatively small section also means that seat selection can be important for passengers traveling together. Premium Plus is designed to provide a more comfortable seat and a more spacious environment than standard economy.

The cabin’s smaller size also creates a more contained atmosphere, with fewer rows and less foot traffic than the main economy section. Passengers receive a wider seat with additional recline and leg support compared with a standard economy seat, alongside upgraded dining and amenities.

The exact onboard service and seat features can depend on the aircraft and route, so travelers should review the details for their specific flight when choosing a fare. The distinction is especially noticeable on overnight services, when the ability to recline and rest becomes more valuable.

United’s seat map also distinguishes Premium Plus from Economy Plus, an extra-legroom seating option within the economy cabin. In the cited 350-seat layout, 62 economy seats are designated as extra-legroom seats, but they do not form a separate cabin class and do not provide the same seat or service as Premium Plus. This distinction matters when comparing ticket options.

Economy Plus primarily provides more space for the legs, while Premium Plus is a separate cabin with a different seat and additional amenities. United’s 777-300ER layouts can vary, making the seat map for the booked flight the most useful reference. Travelers comparing fares should consider the full Premium Plus product rather than treating the seat map as a legroom comparison alone.

Cathay Pacific is Boeing 777-300ER premium economy cabin is part of a wider investment in refreshing the aircraft’s long-haul interior. The airline has been introducing redesigned cabins across its 777-300ER fleet, with updated business class, premium economy, and economy sections. The new premium economy product sits between the Aria Suite business-class cabin and economy.This gives passengers an intermediate option on selected long-haul services. Cathay Pacific has described the work as a major cabin refresh, rather than a change limited to seat covers or small cosmetic details. The cabin refresh is intended to update the passenger experience throughout the aircraft, not just in its premium sections.

These changes are intended to make the cabin feel more comfortable over a long flight, while giving passengers a more modern entertainment experience. The airline has also introduced dedicated premium economy lavatories on the refreshed aircraft. Bluetooth pairing is particularly useful for passengers who already travel with wireless headphones and prefer to avoid an adapter.

Cathay Pacific’s refurbishment program covers 30 Boeing 777-300ER aircraft, with the updated interiors returning to service progressively. As a result, the new premium economy experience is not guaranteed on every 777-300ER flight. Passengers should check the aircraft and seat map attached to their itinerary, particularly when selecting a specific seat or paying more for the refreshed product.

The airline’s newer 777 cabin also has a different upper-end layout from some competing carriers: the announced configuration includes business class, premium economy, and economy, without a separate first-class cabin. That makes premium economy a distinct part of Cathay’s redesigned long-haul offering. This gradual introduction means that the aircraft type alone does not identify which interior a passenger will receive.

Emirates has introduced premium economy on selected Boeing 777-300ER aircraft as part of its wider cabin-refurbishment program. The 777 version has a dedicated 24-seat premium economy cabin arranged in a 2-4-2 layout, located between business class and economy. Its position gives passengers a separate section at the front of the economy area, while the smaller cabin provides a more limited number of seats than the main economy section.The product is available only on aircraft that have received the relevant interior, so it should not be assumed to feature on every Emirates 777-300ER service. The layout creates a separate cabin while retaining a relatively intimate seat count for the aircraft. Emirates' premium economy seat is upholstered in cream-colored leather and is designed with a six-way adjustable headrest, calf rest, and footrest.

The 777 seat has a 38-inch pitch and is 19.5 inches wide, providing more room than a standard economy seat. It also reclines by up to eight inches, while an in-seat charging point helps passengers keep personal devices powered during the journey. A wooden dining table and a separate side cocktail table provide additional usable surfaces, giving passengers more flexibility when eating, working, or using a laptop.

The combination of seat width and pitch is particularly relevant on long sectors, where small differences can affect how easily passengers settle in. Emirates' onboard entertainment system is another part of the product, with a 13.3-inch screen available on premium economy seats. The cabin is designed to provide a more substantial upgrade than simply selecting an extra-legroom economy seat, combining a wider recliner with dedicated foot support and a separate cabin environment.

Emirates has installed the product on selected refurbished aircraft, and the airline’s wider retrofit program means the fleet is changing over time. Travelers should confirm that premium economy is offered on their particular flight before booking around the cabin’s features or paying a higher fare. The screen size and separate table surfaces also give passengers practical space for entertainment and dining.

Emergencies, holding patterns and more. Tap any flight to follow it on the tracker.

Singapore Airlines offers premium economy on its Boeing 777-300ER, with a 28-seat section in the airline’s 264-seat four-class configuration. The cabin is arranged in a 2-4-2 layout, between business class and economy. This gives passengers a choice of paired seats along the windows or seats in the center section, while keeping the cabin separate from the larger economy area.

The 777-300ER configuration also includes four first-class seats and 48 business-class seats, making premium economy one part of a cabin arrangement that serves several different long-haul fare categories. The cabin’s location between business class and economy makes the product easy to distinguish from the standard economy offering.

The smaller premium economy section gives the cabin a more defined atmosphere than the main economy area, while the seat itself is designed to offer additional personal space and recline. Singapore Airlines’ premium economy service also includes benefits beyond the physical seat, with features such as priority check-in and boarding, an increased baggage allowance, and access to its Book the Cook meal-preordering service on eligible flights.

These benefits can make the cabin attractive to passengers who value a smoother airport experience and more choice over their onboard meal, as well as those looking for more room during the flight. Availability of individual benefits can vary by route, so passengers should review the conditions attached to their booking.

As with the other airlines in this list, the exact aircraft configuration is important when booking Singapore Airlines premium economy. The 28-seat layout is specific to the cited 264-seat 777-300ER configuration, and the airline operates different aircraft types and cabin arrangements across its network.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Passengers should use the seat map for their individual flight to confirm that the aircraft includes premium economy and to see the available seat positions. For travelers on a route served by the relevant 777-300ER, Singapore Airlines offers a relatively compact premium economy cabin with a defined set of airport and onboard benefits. This is especially useful when comparing premium economy across airlines, since the fare name alone does not describe every benefit.

#6190. Avelo Brings First Commercial Flights to McKinney

Avelo operated its inaugural flight from McKinney National Airport in McKinney, Texas, on Wednesday.

Avelo Flight 1848, operated with a Boeing 737-800, was the first commercial airliner service from the airport to Fort Myers, Florida.

“We target the secondary airports of very large metropolitan areas where we can offer a different experience to the customers,” Avelo founder and CEO Andrew Levy said in an interview with AirlineGeeks.

McKinney is the third airport in the Dallas/Fort Worth Metroplex to offer commercial service, with Dallas Love Field and Dallas/Forth Worth International Airport being the other two.

“For a lot of folks we’re going to be closer and a more convenient drive. And hopefully they’ll take advantage of that,” said McKinney airport director Ken Carley.

Carley said the airline has been wanting to be in the market since 2018. McKinney is the first new airport in Texas in 20 years to be certified for commercial air service.

“We had to build all this infrastructure because it did not exist. There was nothing on this side of the airport. So it’s not just this building, it’s the ramp and the taxi lane and all of that stuff, the taxiway that connects to the runway system. So it was a building, all the infrastructure, and meeting all those requirements,” Carley said.

McKinney is about 30 miles northeast of Dallas in Collin County. Levy said the area is growing like crazy.

“What we’re going to offer people who live close to this airport is a very different experience than getting on the highways and driving all the way to DFW or going down to Love Field,” he said.

The Texas-based airline will serve 11 destinations from McKinney: Las Vegas, Tampa, Orlando, Fort Myers, Sarasota/Bradenton, Nashville, West Palm Beach, New Orleans, Denver, Atlanta, and Fort Lauderdale.

“I think it’s phenomenal that Avelo has announced additional routes before they’ve even started service. That’s a testament, I think, to what they’re seeing in the response they’re getting from for bookings. So they think it’s a strong market,” Carley said.

Levy said the approach was to offer a lot of selections and get a better sense of the market.

“All the markets we’re serving have massive proven demand from this area. And so of course, the trick for us is just to get people to know we’re here and then give us a try,” Levy said.

McKinney is a crew base for Avelo, its fifth, with pilots, flight attendants, airport operations personnel, and aircraft technicians, about 150 people behind the operation, Levy said.

“The demand will dictate how we grow, if we grow, and how fast we grow. This is going to be based on, do customers like the service? Does it resonate with them? Are we serving a need that exists every other place we’ve been? We don’t have any trouble filling up airplanes. I think this market is just going to do great, but time will tell, and the consumer will let us know,” Levy said.

“Our focus is on building a business that’s sustainable for the long term,” he added. “And that means everything we do has to work. It’s got to work well.”

Avelo currently offers service from DFW to New Haven, Connecticut. Levy said that service will continue but could move to McKinney at some point.

#6189. Midterm Mayhem for the Free and Virtuous Society

The GOP will continue to suffer at the polls until it focuses on building this type of society once again.

President Donald Trump speaks in front of a portrait of Ronald Reagan at the White House in Washington, D.C., March 24, 2026.

There has been some pretty unsurprising but bad analysis of the election results since Tuesday night. There also has been some very good analysis, from National Review’s editors, from our own Jim Geraghty, from our own Dan McLaughlin, from Yuval Levin, from Erick Erickson, and plenty of others on the conservative right. There is no need for a redundant analysis that merely restates what has already been said, even though an amen to all of what they said should be assumed. What I want to suggest, in total alignment with my aforementioned friends and colleagues, is that these election results capture the very essence of the twin deficits in the Trump-era moment: a newfound contempt for both the free and the virtuous society.

The debate over the Iran war’s role in this Republican debacle would be comical if it were not so maddening. With virtually no one operating in good faith or making a serious argument, a whole cabal of people have claimed, all statistical evidence and voter polling to the contrary, that the sole reason for states like Texas, Kansas, and Mississippi flipping is the Iran war. Inversely, no one who disputes that monocausal theory of the case denies that the Iran war is unpopular, and that its unpopularity was a contributor to the decline of approval for President Trump and to the results Republicans suffered all over the country Tuesday night. That voters detest the state of prices, and that they believe (with obvious basis in fact) that tariffs are connected to this, is not disputable by credible people. That the bizarre handling of the Iran war led to a Strait of Hormuz debacle, and to significant problems for fuel prices and a downstream impact from diesel prices, is also obvious. Reasonable people can disagree as to how much of the Iran war contribution was related to opposition to de-nuclearizing Iran versus the way in which it all went (e.g., a failed MOU negotiated by the vice president, repeated claims of victory that were obviously untrue, and a sustained period of time with no clear resolution). But all advocates of a multi-causal explanation of the midterms recognize the significant role Iran played.

David L. Bahnsen is the managing partner of a wealth-management firm and a frequent writer and public commentator on matters of economics, faith and work, and markets.

#6188. All Nippon Airways (ANA) New 777 First & Business Class: Which Routes Get Them?

In 2019, Japanese Star Alliance carrier All Nippon Airways (ANA) launched an all-new first and business class product. In this post, I’d like to take an updated look at ANA’s progress with installing these new cabins, along with which routes currently consistently feature this product.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class and business class products are truly spectacular. ANA has always had incredible service, and now the airline has a hard product to match.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class, known as “The Suite,” is phenomenal. The hard product as such doesn’t look that amazing, but it’s a huge improvement over the old product. First class has eight very comfortable suites, each of which is functionally designed and private. Personally I consider this to be among the world’s best first class products, thanks largely to ANA’s top notch soft product.

All Nippon Airways’ new business class, known as “The Room,” is really what’s most revolutionary. The seats have doors and an unreal amount of personal space. I consider this to be one of the world’s best business class products, along with Qatar Airways’ Qsuites and Japan Airlines’ A350 business class.

While there are certain markets where All Nippon Airways consistently offers the new cabins, we have seen some variance. So let me share the basics of how many ANA 777s have the new cabins, how you can tell if your flight features the new cabins, and finally which routes currently feature the new cabins (though of course that’s subject to change).

All Nippon Airways has 13 Boeing 777-300ERs in its fleet. 10 of the 13 jets currently feature the new cabins, meaning that ~77% of ANA’s 777-300ERs have the new first and business class. Six of these planes have been delivered to the airline since 2019, with the new cabins, while four 777-300ERs have been reconfigured with the new cabins (these planes are 10+ years old).

Unfortunately ANA doesn’t have concrete plans to reconfigure the remaining 777-300ERs, so don’t expect this product’s footprint to grow much for the time being. ANA is expected to eventually take delivery of new 777-9s, which will likely feature this product (or something even better), though that’s still potentially years down the road.

If you want to track registration codes, the following 10 Boeing 777-300ERs feature the new cabins:

And in the interest of being thorough, here are the three Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the old cabins:

It’s obviously frustrating to have a fleet of just 13 planes, and not reconfigure three of them, especially when it has been seven years. What’s the explanation for this? Keep in mind that the 777X has been delayed by around seven years now.

My guess is that ANA had intended to reconfigure 10 planes and retire the other three, and signed contracts based on that. Then with the never-ending 777X delays, the airline decided to keep those jets around, and maybe it just proved too complicated or costly to backtrack on that. At least that’s my best guess.

You can tell whether or not your flight is scheduled to feature All Nippon Airways’ new cabins just by looking at the seat map. The easiest way to tell is to look at the business class seat map:

If you’re on ANA’s website and a flight is scheduled to be operated with the new cabins, you’ll also see the prominent display of “THE SUITE” for first class and “THE ROOM” for business class.

Another method to check without using ANA’s website is to instead go to Google Flights. Just search a business class flight on an ANA 777. When you look at the flight options, if a flight shows as having an “Individual suite,” then that’s the new business class.

Meanwhile if it shows as having a “Lie flat seat,” then that’s the old business class.

Again, it’s only select Boeing 777-300ERs that have these cabins. You won’t find these cabins on other aircraft, including 787s, A380s, etc. However:

Here are the routes that are typically currently operated by the new All Nippon Airways Boeing 777-300ERs:

In other words, as it stands, all flights to London and New York are supposed to feature the new cabins. Meanwhile flights to Chicago and San Francisco all alternate between new and old configurations, so you’ll want to check the seat map. That means there are no routes that are exclusively operated by 777s with the old cabins.

In terms of the rest of the United States route network, Houston (IAH), Los Angeles (LAX), Seattle (SEA), and Washington (IAD), are served by 787s. There’s always the chance for last minute aircraft swaps, and airlines do tweak their schedules over time.

All Nippon Airways introduced a phenomenal new first and business class in 2019, and the airline has rolled this out to ~77% of its 777-300ER fleet (though no additional retrofits have happened in the past several years).

For the current upcoming schedule, you can expect the new cabins to be offered on all flights to London and New York, as well as on select flights to Chicago and San Francisco. While you’ll always want to check the seat map for changes or aircraft swaps, that’s the current plan.

If you’ve flown ANA’s new 777s, what was your experience like?

#6187. Airline Interline, Codeshare, Alliance, And Joint Venture Agreements Explained

Airline partnerships are more complex and advanced than ever before, both for better and worse. About 25 years ago the Star Alliance was formed, which was revolutionary at the time. SkyTeam and oneworld quickly joined the scene.

While they all still exist, the global alliances have definitely been deemphasized a bit in recent years. After all, with these alliances having so many members, how much can loosely affiliated airlines really have in common?

Airlines want to work with other airlines that complement them best, and this can come in many different forms. Just to give a few examples of partnerships outside of the traditional alliances:

Airlines have several different levels of cooperation, ranging from interline agreements, to codeshare agreements, to alliance membership, to joint venture agreements. In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the differences between these agreements. Before I do so, let me add two disclaimers:

With that out of the way, let’s take a look at these four kinds of agreements.

Interline agreements are the most basic kinds of agreements you can have between airlines. An interline agreement is simply a commercial agreement between airlines to handle passengers when they’re traveling on multiple airlines on the same itinerary, and it allows an airline to issue a ticket on another airline (though not necessarily on any sort of favorable commercial terms).

This allows passengers to check their bags through to their final destination, get boarding passes all way to their destination, potentially be rebooked on another airline in the event of irregular operations, etc.

This is a basic level of cooperation, so there are airlines that have interline agreements but don’t otherwise have robust partnerships. For example, Etihad doesn’t belong to a major global alliance, but has an interline agreement with dozens of airlines, ranging from American, to Emirates, to JetBlue, to United, to Qatar Airways.

As you can see, this is a level of cooperation we even see between airlines that don’t partner with one another, and that may not even be fond of one another.

It is worth noting that in some cases airlines specifically pull out of interline agreements. For example, many years ago Delta cut its interline agreement with American. Why? At least in part it’s because Delta found that American was rebooking more passengers on Delta during irregular operations than the other way around, so the carrier no longer thought the arrangement was in its best interest.

A codeshare agreement is the next level of cooperation between airlines. This is when two airlines realize there’s value in working together, and they decide they want to place their “codes” on one another’s flights. Typically the main benefit of this is that it drums up business for the airlines that are in a codeshare agreement with one another.

Just to give an example, Alaska Airlines and Icelandair have a codeshare agreement. Icelandair flies to certain gateways in the United States, and then Alaska Airlines provides some of the “feed” for those flights in the form of codeshares.

For example, if you want to fly from Reykjavik to Los Angeles, Icelandair doesn’t operate that route. However, Icelandair flies to Portland, and then you can book a Portland to Los Angeles flight on Alaska Airlines as an Icelandair codeshare.

When you book a codeshare flight, you’ll notice that the flight number is different. So if you booked through Icelandair, your Portland to Los Angeles flight would also have an Icelandair flight number (in this case FI7696). To be clear:

With these codeshare agreements, generally neither airline is getting a huge cut for booking someone on the other airline. Most of the ticket revenue goes to the operating carrier, and often a small amount goes to the airline that sold the flight. However, the biggest advantage of this arrangement is to boost business for both airlines by increasing the number of flights that passengers have access to.

The “big three” alliances — oneworld, SkyTeam, and Star Alliance — have only developed in the past 25 years, though in the meantime many major global carriers belong to one of them. The basic way that alliances work is as follows:

I’d note that different airlines place different levels of emphasis on these alliances, even if they choose to belong to them. For example, Delta is a founding member of SkyTeam, but the airline is heavily focused on joint ventures and airlines it owns a stake in, and cares very little about the airlines it simply shares an alliance with.

If a codeshare agreement is like dating, then a joint venture is like getting married. A joint venture agreement is a massive business decision that typically requires extensive government approval. When airlines form a joint venture they coordinate pricing and schedules, and have a revenue sharing agreement.

Exactly how the revenue sharing works depends on the specific arrangement, but the idea is that two airlines are essentially acting as one under a joint venture.

Note that typically airlines form joint ventures between specific regions, which is why this is different than an outright merger. For example, American has a transatlantic joint venture with British Airways, Finnair, Iberia, and Aer Lingus, while the airline has two transpacific joint ventures, with both Japan Airlines and Qantas (the two are separate arrangements).

From the perspective of a consumer, a joint venture is both good and bad. The good news is that typically it gives you the most flight options in terms of schedules, since the airlines are operating as one. Airlines also often try to make the experience as consistent across brands as possible. The downside is that it’s like a competitor being eliminated in the market, so it could lead to higher fares as it reduces competition.

There are so many different types of agreements in the airline industry nowadays. While the exact terms vary with every partnership, I think the easiest way to sum it up is that an interline agreement is like a friendship, a codeshare agreement is like an engagement, a joint venture is like a marriage, and an alliance is like having a big family, with everyone sort of doing their own thing.

There’s a lot more to all of this, but hopefully the above provides a pretty fair and basic summary. People often misuse these terms, so I figure it’s worth recapping every so often.

#6186. $7.6 Billion Takeover: easyJet Shareholders Back Apollo Deal That Will Take The Airline Private

Shareholders at British budget airline easyJet have approved a deal worth £5.7 billion ($7.57 billion) for the private equity firm Apollo to take over the carrier. It will make the airline privately owned. Apollo Funds will hold up to 49.9% of the company, while rollover shareholders (choosing shares rather than cash), will hold between 45.1% and 49.9%. The EU Trust will hold up to 5%.

The airline says that the deal will be completed by the end of March, likely requiring regulatory approval. When it comes into effect, 26 years of easyJet's presence on the London stock market will screech to a sudden halt.

97.07% of shareholders voted in favor of the takeover. The price paid was 715p ($9.50) per share. Sir Stelios Haji-Ioannou founded the airline in 1995 and, with his family, owned 15% of the airline. It is understood that he backed the takeover.

It is not surprising that the airline was looking for a buyer given that it had been consulting on proposals to axe approximately 50 roles at head office from its 2,300-strong team. EasyJet had previously been in contact with Castlelake, a US investment firm, about a takeover.

The table below shows the current easyJet fleet, according to Planespotters.net. It represents some of the assets that will come into Apollo's control and is entirely made up of Airbus narrowbody jets. It has also previously flown Boeing 737 and 757, and British Aerospace BAe 146.

EasyJet has commented on the takeover in a statement.

"EasyJet is pleased to announce that, at the Court Meeting and General Meeting held earlier today in connection with the Acquisition, the requisite majority of Scheme Shareholders voted to approve the Scheme at the Court Meeting and the requisite majority of easyJet Shareholders voted to pass the Resolution at the General Meeting."

The deal is being made with Eagle Bidco Ltd, a company that is indirectly owned by Apollo Funds and managed by affiliates of Apollo Capital Management, L.P. Apollo Funds is a US investment company. It is most active in the UK through its company, The Restaurant Group. This firm owns the Asian-style restaurant chain Wagamama.

Apollo began operations in 1990 and is currently headquartered in New York City. It ranked 29th in Private Equity International's 2024 ranking of the world's largest private equity firms.

In 2025, the company managed $840 billion in assets and reported net income of $3.5 billion. $99 billion of these assets were invested in private equity. These figures show that the easyJet purchase does not get close to breaking the bank for Apollo.

Will easyJet continue to exist as we know it today, or will its assets be sold off to the highest bidder?

Reuters has reported that Apollo will maintain the status quo once it acquires easyJet. It will remain a standalone business, with the branding remaining consistent. There should also be comparatively little upheaval for the company's workers. The UK headquarters, along with the UK, Austrian and Swiss Air Operator Certificates, will stay put. Apollo has also pledged to avoid redundancies in the first 12 months of its control over the airline.

Apollo has said it will help the airline by giving it access to additional capital. Becoming privately traded will also mean it can plan for the long term. The strategy is to "do more" with what easyJet already has while ensuring it still offers customers a low-cost product, according to the Financial Times.

However, Apollo has some changes in mind. The first is a far more expansive loyalty program. The second is to introduce some premium elements on select routes.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

A deadly flash flood swept through Grand Canyon National Park in northern Arizona over the weekend. An active search-and-rescue operation is underway along the Colorado River, and parts of the inner canyon and South Rim are closed at this time.

Due to extreme damage and flash flooding in the Grand Canyon this past weekend, the National Park Service announced immediate closures of the following areas until further notice: Phantom Ranch, Phantom Ranch cabins and canteen and Bright Angel Campground. The entire North Kaibab Trail — from the North Kaibab Trailhead to Phantom Ranch — is also closed until further notice. The Silver and Black footbridges crossing the river have been affected as well.

For the latest trail and closure information, visit the park's Key Hiking Messages webpage.

A threat of severe weather still remains, and visitors are urged to exercise caution. Videos posted online by the Associated Press showed the destruction caused by the flooding. This devastating flash flood comes just a year after the Dragon Bravo wildfire forced the evacuation and closure of the North Rim in July 2025.

The closure of the inner canyon will allow the National Park Service and the Arizona Department of Public Safety to continue search-and-rescue operations. There are still visitors unaccounted for, and the NPS Investigative Services Branch is seeking the public’s assistance.

The flash flood significantly affected infrastructure in the canyon, including the Transcanyon Waterline, and, as a result, the visitor facilities at the South Rim are also affected.

Yes, it is safe to travel to portions of Grand Canyon National Park, but there are some restrictions that visitors should be aware of. We suggest bookmarking the park's main page, which lists updates and links to advisories.

The Places To Go page is full of helpful visitor information and maps.

The National Park Service has issued a closure notice for Monday, Aug. 31, at noon local time for the South Rim hotels located within Grand Canyon National Park due to damage to the Transcanyon Waterline. All water at the South Rim is delivered via the waterline, and additional reserves are running low. Only dry camping will be permitted at the South Rim.

It’s important to note that the park will remain open for day use, and food-and-beverage services at the South Rim will remain open (though some may reduce hours of operation).

As we’ve previously reported, the Transcanyon Waterline dates back to the 1960s, and the park has already invested $208 million in a multiyear rehabilitation project that isn't expected to be completed until 2027. The most recent update provided by Grand Canyon Lodges lists the hotels at the South Rim as projected to reopen on November 20, 2026.

Tusayan is the gateway to the South Rim of Grand Canyon National Park at the Route 64 entrance, and its hotels and restaurants remain fully operational and unaffected, as it's located outside the national park.

Until further notice, the Colorado River is closed to river traffic due to metal structures and debris entering the river, according to a notice from the National Park Service. River operations rangers are coordinating with visitors already in the canyon, and the Grand Canyon River Alert system is also sending advisories. If you have an upcoming river trip scheduled, you should contact the commercial outfitter that you booked with or the NPS River Permits office for trip-specific information.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth testifies about the Pentagon’s fiscal year 2027 budget request before the House Armed Services Committee in Washington, D.C., April 29, 2026.

Eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have been proposed in the House by Representative Thomas Massie, a libertarian Republican from Kentucky who lost his seat when the president pushed for his ouster in a primary earlier this year. (The Trump-endorsed candidate, Ed Gallrein, retained the seat for the GOP last week despite the wave that will give Democrats solid majorities in both congressional chambers come January.)

Though still narrowly controlled by Republicans for the next two lame duck months, the House will be forced to consider Massie’s proposal. Impeachment is a privileged motion under House rules; action of some kind must be taken on it within two days after it is filed. Impeachments can stretch beyond a single session of Congress, so if the House impeaches Hegseth, a Senate trial could be postponed until January, when Democrats will have a commanding majority in the upper chamber.

#6183. Plaza Premium Opening Hong Kong Arrivals Lounge… With Live Music?!

Plaza Premium will be opening an arrivals lounge soon at Hong Kong International Airport (HKG). While these facilities are always useful for a shower and breakfast after an overnight flight, it sounds like there might be a bit more planned for this arrivals lounge? I’m certainly intrigued (thanks to Sel_D for flagging this)…

Plaza Premium is expected to open an arrivals lounge at Hong Kong Airport in late November 2026. The lounge will be located on level three of Terminal 2, in the arrivals portion of the terminal, below the Airport Express platform. That means it’ll be landside.

This actually technically represents the reopening of a lounge, as the global lounge operator had such a facility until 2019. At that point it closed due to an expansion project at the airport. Once open, it will be the only arrivals lounge at the airport. Cathay Pacific used to have an arrivals lounge at its hub, but it closed in 2018, and the airline has no plans to reopen such a facility.

The exact entry requirements of the Plaza Premium arrivals lounge in Hong Kong remain to be seen, but like most Plaza Premium lounges, the expectation is that entry will be possible through select credit cards and Priority Pass, and access can also be purchased directly.

Generally we think of an arrivals lounge in terms of its functional purpose, which is to shower, have breakfast, and get some work done, before heading into the city. Many arrivals lounges are only open in the morning, since that’s when there’s the most value. That’s especially true for people who either plan to head to the office, or who are staying at a hotel, where it’s well before the published check-in time.

While it remains to be seen what exactly Plaza Premium’s facility will be like, it sounds like this will be a rather unconventional arrivals lounge, in a good way. The social media post about the new lounge describes it as “Plaza Premium Lounge – Rhythms.” It will offer a “seamless blend of dining, music, wellness, and refreshment.”

In terms of the range of amenities, we’re being promised live music, wellness experiences, refined dining, and private resting spaces. I’m sorry… live music? Like… someone performing music live? In an arrivals lounge? Fascinatingly, the pictures make it look more like an evening-oriented lounge serving cocktails and wine, for lounging around, rather than your typical arrivals lounge.

A post shared by Plaza Premium Lounge (@plazapremiumlounge)

Suffice it to say that I am very interested in what they come up with here. From a monetization standpoint, this seems kind of smart, since it could drum up more business in the afternoons and evenings, when people might not otherwise consider visiting such a facility. Then again, are people really thinking “I just got off a 15 hour flight, what I could really use is a cocktail before heading to my hotel?” Maybe they are, I suppose!

In the coming weeks, Hong Kong Airport will once again have an arrivals lounge, thanks to the opening of a facility by Plaza Premium. Arrivals lounges are usually pretty basic, and are about showers and breakfast. While we’ll see how much of this is fluff rather than actual substance, Plaza Premium is promising what sounds more like a bar vibe, with live music and cocktails. Bring it on, Plaza Premium, I can’t wait to learn more!

What do you make of this Plaza Premium concept?
