#6182. A $1 Aircraft, No Boarding Pass & A Cockpit Seat: Pacific Island Hopping On A Beechcraft Super King Air 200

The Beechcraft Super King Air 200 (B200) twin-engine turboprop is popular as a bush plane and as an island hopper, especially for somewhat longer inter-island routes. The Super King Air 200 I flew with is operated as a scheduled passenger flight between Palau and Yap, offering the only connection between the two culturally and logistically linked Pacific islands.

As the flight bypasses Guam International Airport, it is also the only scheduled passenger flight to Yap (a major island in the Federated States of Micronesia) that bypasses the need to pass through US immigration.

During my tour of the Pacific, I also flew round trip on PMA's second B200 on a mission to the outer Yap island of Ulithi. The aircraft is ideally sized as it is the largest commercial aircraft that Ulithi's little airstrip is able to accommodate. Let's examine life onboard the Beechcraft Super King Air 200 and how it is well suited to some inter-island passenger routes in the Pacific.

In October 2026, I flew from the Pacific Island nation of Palau to Yap (part of the Federated States of Micronesia) on a Beechcraft Super King Air 200. I then flew with the B200 to the outer Yap island of Ulithi on November 2nd. These aircraft are owned and operated by the hybrid charity organization, Pacific Missionary Aviation (PMA).

PMA is a charity company whose aircraft and pilots are supported through donations, and its primary emphasis is providing medical, logistical, and transportation services to the outer Yap islands. To help fund missions to the outer islands, PMA operates a paid passenger airline service between Palau and Yap, as well as sightseeing and charter services, including contracting work like maritime patrol of Palau's waters for the Australian Government.

The airline operates smaller aircraft than the King Air 200 for Palau sightseeing services. PMA operates Beechcraft Queen Air aircraft, but decided to upgrade to Super King Air aircraft to serve the passenger Palau to Yap route after United Airlines dropped the route.

United Airlines ended its direct service between Koror, Palau (ROR) and Yap (YAP) on January 7, 2018. In response, PMA moved to fill part of the void by acquiring a pair of B200s. Today, the only scheduled flight connections for Yap are the weekly PMA flight to Palau and the twice-weekly United flight to Guam.

PMA's pilot, Amos Collins, told me during the flight that the two turboprop Super King Air 200s were donated by the charity organization, Samaritan's Purse, for a dollar each. Since then, Samaritan's Purse has continued to financially assist in maintaining the aircraft and keeping them viable.

They were previously used as charity bush planes in Kenya and received an overhaul, new avionics, and modifications for PMA service in the Pacific as island hoppers. One of the modifications was retrofitting the aircraft with easily removable seats, allowing for passenger and cargo flexibility.

Beechcraft Super King Air Specs (Per Beechcraft)

With two aircraft, PMA can also run the flights if one aircraft is down for maintenance, and two flights if both are operational when demand requires. The day I flew, the aircraft had to carry a large payload of cargo while also having more than normal passengers. As such, PMA removed two seats from my flight.

This reduced the passenger seats from nine to seven, including me in the co-pilot seat, clearing space for the aircraft to carry more cargo. PMA then added a second flight to carry the rest of the passengers and the cargo. The aircraft cabin is pressurized, allowing passengers to enjoy a comfortable, somewhat intimate flight that feels something similar to a flight-seeing tour.

The loyal support base allowed the Bonanza to remain in production for longer than it should have.

To check in for the flight, I went to the Palau International Terminal only to find it was closed. After waiting for a while, a van arrived to pick passengers up and take them to PMA's hangar on the other side of the airport. There, I waited in the PMA waiting room that doubled as a check-in facility. PMA checked in passengers for the morning's scenic tour flight before moving on to the international passenger flight.

PMA checked passengers onto the flight to Yap, although no boarding passes were issued. After checking in, passengers were taken by van to the airport terminal and taken through locked doors to the immigration room (backwards). The immigration staff heard us and shouted "coming" before manning the immigration booth and processing the seven passengers.

Having been stamped out of Palau, we returned to the van and drove back to the PMA waiting room for a while before heading over to the hangar. We walked through their maintenance workshop to reach the Super King 200 parked on the apron. The pilot invited me to sit with him in the co-pilot's seat and wear the headset so that we could chat throughout the flight. Taking off in the turboprop was smooth, with one of the highlights being a de facto scenic tour of the Palau islands.

The Super King Air is an excellent aircraft for short-haul flights where passenger demand is for up to nine passengers. The aircraft is considered more capable than a light aircraft. It is often valued as a maritime patrol and fisheries surveillance aircraft, especially for smaller countries like Palau.

One of its top roles is as an air ambulance/MEDEVAC aircraft, which is one of the roles PMA uses it for. It is an excellent aircraft for general utility transport, being able to move passengers and small amounts of cargo. For small Pacific islands, it can carry substantial baggage, a realistic number of passengers for those destinations, and it is able to operate on relatively short runways.

It has the range to serve long island connections, while also coming with a cruise speed of 260–290 knots. The relatively high speed is one of the distinguishing attributes of the aircraft relative to traditional island-hopper aircraft. An Islander may cruise at around 120 knots, adding significant time on routes measuring in the hundreds of nautical miles.

Another advantage of the Super King Air 200 is a relatively quiet cabin, although for me, it was extra quiet as I was wearing the noise-cancelling headphones. In short, for passengers, the aircraft offers a fast, relatively quiet, and comfortable island-hopping option to remote islands. Its twin engines add a significant layer of safety.

The Beechcraft tale, from audacious beginnings to global successes, is a prime example of general aviation's persistent innovation.

The FAA lists the Super King Air 200 I flew on (registered N875SP) as having been built in 1975 and powered by a pair of Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6A-42 turboprop engines. The aircraft regularly flies between Palau and Yap, as well as to Guam and various outlying islands.

While the aircraft is old, it has been overhauled and comes with modern Garmin avionics and well-maintained engines. The second aircraft owned by PMA is a registered N468SP and was produced in 1998, making it considerably newer than the first. I flew on this aircraft on a short island hop from Yap to the outer island of Ulithi, roughly a 25-minute flight.

Both aircraft have been upgraded with the same Garmin avionics, while their engines have been overhauled and, at times, replaced. Besides the age difference, one of the main differences between the two aircraft is that the first aircraft (N875SP) has been modified with a special underbelly cargo compartment, making its de facto belly close to the ground.

The belly cargo compartment makes the aircraft noticeably slower and increases its weight. This makes it better suited to carrying bulky cargo, while the second aircraft can carry heavier cargo. The second aircraft has a couple of small container compartments installed above the engines on the wings.

The King Air series was initially developed in the 1960s, with production running from 1963 until now, with thousands produced. It outsold all of its turboprop competitors combined. The aircraft PMA operates are Model 200s, which can be easily distinguished from the earlier King Air 90 and King Air 100 series by their distinctive T-tails. This T-Tail was retained for the King Air 300 and 350 series.

The King Air series remains in production, but it has undergone several generations of upgrades with the latest 260, 360, and 360ER models currently in production. These models include the Super King Air 200 in its modernized 260 form. Beechcraft says of this modern variant that:

"The King Air 260 turboprop carries the versatility and reliability that the King Air family is known for, while delivering people where they need to go in unprecedented comfort. This allows for the flexibility to explore new horizons."

These modernized aircraft continue to enjoy a relatively healthy long-term niche supported by substantial military demand. Textron is actively investing in keeping the production line viable and efficient as a mature family with low annual production. Production appears set to extend into the 2030s and possibly beyond.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6181. Delta SkyMiles Gold Card Review: Solid Perks For Occasional Delta Flyers

The Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card is the mid-range personal credit card in the American Express and Delta co-brand card portfolio, which includes seven cards, covering a variety of annual fee levels, across both personal and business products.

This post is my in-depth review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold Amex Card. The card has a reasonable annual fee and is ideal for someone looking for basic benefits that come in handy when flying Delta. However, if you’re a Medallion elite flyer on Delta, another card might be a better option (more on that below).

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card

Before I get into my Delta Gold SkyMiles American Express Card review, here’s a quick look at the card’s main selling points and fees:

Here are my thoughts on the pros and cons of the Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card:

To start, let’s take a look at the Delta Gold Amex welcome bonus and ongoing fees, since these are some of the most important features to consider when opening a new card.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Amex is currently offering new cardholders the following bonus: You may be eligible for as high as 80,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $2,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus is worth up to $880.

This is a solid welcome bonus, though the card recently offered a higher one that included a statement credit along with bonus miles. Everyone has to decide for themselves whether they’d rather wait for a better offer, or apply with this offer so they can take advantage of the perks ASAP.

The welcome offer on the Delta Gold Amex card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available to you if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past.

You’re also not eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had the personal versions of the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (learn more) or the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more). However, you are eligible for this card if you’ve had any version of the business Delta Amex cards before.

One thing worth emphasizing is that if you’re going to apply for multiple personal Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to pick up the Delta Gold Amex first. That’s because if you do, you’d potentially still be eligible for the Delta Platinum Amex and Delta Reserve Amex. Meanwhile if you apply for one of those cards first, you’d no longer be eligible for the “lesser” card.

When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score you need to get approved for the Delta Gold Amex. I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been denied, as it’s only one of many factors that determines card eligibility.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles American Express Card has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150. (Rates & Fees). This is a great opportunity to try the card before you have to “buy” it. The card also has a reasonable annual fee on an ongoing basis, so it’s easy to recoup that fee by taking advantage of the card perks.

You can also add authorized users to the Delta Gold Amex at no extra cost.

If you are going to put spending on the card, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees) with the Delta Gold Amex, so you can use the card abroad without paying those high fees.

When applying for a credit card, the rewards structure is obviously a major consideration for people. With airline credit cards, the question typically comes down to both the miles offered on spending, as well as the ability to qualify for elite status with spending. Unfortunately the Delta Gold Amex isn’t much to get excited about on that front, but let’s still go over the details.

When it comes to the return on spending, the Delta Gold Card offers:

While it’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, I don’t find the bonuses to be particularly compelling. There are still better cards out there for airfare purchases, restaurant purchases, and grocery store purchases.

Nowadays it’s common to see airlines offer elite status qualification through credit card spending. Delta SkyMiles elite status is based on the concept of Medallion Qualifying Dollars (MQDs), and it’s possible to earn elite status with credit card spending.

The catch is that the Delta Gold Card doesn’t earn any MQDs, so if you want to qualify for status, you’ll have to pick up the Delta Platinum Card or Delta Reserve Card. More on that later.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or on Delta’s SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

As I’ll cover below, having the Delta Gold Amex also gives you access to the TakeOff 15 discount on award tickets, and that can also help you stretch your SkyMiles for travel on Delta.

The real reason you’ll want to keep the Delta Gold Card long term is because of the perks and benefits that it offers, which are great for the casual Delta flyer. Truthfully, this is the value proposition of many airline credit cards — it’s largely about the welcome bonus and the perks, so let’s take a closer look at those details for the Delta Gold Amex.

Perhaps one of the biggest incentives to actually spend money on the Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card is the ability to earn a flight credit. Specifically, if you spend $10,000 on the card in a calendar year, you can receive a $200 Delta eCredit to use toward future travel, which will be deposited right in your SkyMiles account. The credit expires one year after it’s issued.

Getting a $200 Delta eCredit in addition to any miles could be a good incentive to spend $10,000 on the card per year. The credit alone is the equivalent of a 2% return on spending, assuming you consider it to be worth face value.

Just for having the Delta Gold Card you receive up to $100 in Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you receive up to $100 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $100, if you wanted to. If used right, the value here is considerable.

Just for having the Delta Gold SkyMiles Amex, you get a first checked bag free. You can also receive a second checked bag free on eligible domestic Delta flights.

This benefit is limited to the primary card member and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for your flight with your Delta Amex, though you do need to have your SkyMiles number in the reservation.

With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up. A first checked bag on domestic flights costs $45, and a second costs $55, so even just checking one bag on two roundtrip flights could effectively cancel out the card’s annual fee.

You receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Gold Amex. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you must ensure the primary card member’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation. This benefit is valid for the primary card member and up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation.

If you have the Delta Gold Amex then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible inflight purchases of food and beverages. The statement credit will post within 8-12 weeks of an eligible purchase.

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card, you can redeem miles for 1.0 cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn miles and MQDs on the portion of the fare they pay in cash.

With the Delta TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta flights booked through delta.com or the Fly Delta app. Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card also comes with a rideshare credit. The way it works is that you get up to $10 back as a statement credits each month when you use the card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers, including Uber and Lyft.

You need to enroll in this benefit in order to get the money back, and it doesn’t kick in until after your first card renewal. So while it’s a useful perk if you already pay for rideshares at least once a month, it doesn’t really make or break the card.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in having as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page. Note that enrollment is required to take advantage of individual offers.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

There are some coverage limits and exclusions to be aware of, so you’ll want to review the full details in the card’s benefits guide before assuming you’re insured.

Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card isn’t a card I’d be using for my everyday spending, since there are many more rewarding cards for that. However:

In other words, for someone who flies Delta occasionally, I think this card could make sense, and the benefits can more than offset the annual fee.

Meanwhile if you’re a more frequent Delta flyer, there could be value to having one of the more premium credit cards, which allow you to spend your way to elite status, and earn Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs).

If the Delta Gold Card sounds interesting to you, but you want a business card instead, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Gold Business American Express Card. Learn more about applying for Amex business cards.

The Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card (learn more) has a $0 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers the following benefits:

Beyond that, though, there are limited perks. If you’d get value out of a first checked bag free or priority boarding, then you’re much better off getting one of Delta’s cards with an annual fee. I can’t really see much upside to getting the Delta Blue Card, over the other options in the market.

The Delta Platinum Amex (learn more) has a higher annual fee of $350 (Rates & Fees) and offers more perks than the Delta Gold:

If you want to earn MQDs toward elite status and enjoy more Delta benefits, like an annual companion certificate, the Delta Platinum Amex is the better option between these two cards.

The Delta Reserve Card (learn more) is the most premium option among personal Delta Amex cards, with the highest annual fee: $650 (Rates & Fees)

It also has the most benefits, so it could be worth it if you frequently fly Delta and want the best perks like lounge access:

Those aren’t even all the Delta Reserve card benefits. It also lets you earn MQDs on spending and gets you upgrade priority over other Delta SkyMiles members with your same Medallion tier, product, and fare experience purchased. The annual fee is high, but it’s absolutely worth a look if you want as many Delta perks as possible.

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. That’s because these points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers:

Furthermore, earning Amex points gives you more flexibility to redeem in other ways, given all the great uses of Membership Rewards points.

The Delta Gold SkyMiles Credit Card is a card that can be worth holding onto for the benefits that it offers, like up to $100 in Delta Stays credit, free checked bags, priority boarding, inflight savings, and more.

For the more frequent Delta flyer, consider the Delta Platinum Card, which can offer a larger bonus and additional perks, but also has a higher annual fee. Meanwhile if you’re a true Delta frequent flyer, consider the Delta Reserve Card, which offers some lounge access perks, helps you qualify for status fastest, etc.

If you want to learn more about the Delta Gold Amex Card, follow this link.

The following links will direct you to the rates and fees for mentioned American Express Cards. These include: Delta SkyMiles® Blue American Express Card (Rates & Fees), Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (Rates & Fees), Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (Rates & Fees), and Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (Rates & Fees).

#6180. United Bans AI Agents From Booking Flights For Customers

In the first such move by a U.S. airline, United will ban third-party AI from parts of its digital platforms and adjust its policies to prevent access via travel agencies and aggregators.

“Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles,” the airline said in a statement.

The carrier also said AI actions could violate FAA and Department of Transportation regulations. As an example, it cited the requirement that passengers confirm in person that their bags do not contain banned items, such as explosives.

“As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access, directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators, to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the statement continued. “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing, and distribution policies.”

United said its stance is in line with companies in the banking and retail sectors. It is now “encourag[ing] others” to consider measures “that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety.”

The airline said it will update its Digital Trust Center to clarify the new restrictions.

#6179. How to fly lie-flat to Europe with Rove for less than the price of a cup of coffee

There is no shortage of ways to redeem your points and miles for travel to Europe. With most flights being overnight, booking a lie-flat seat is an excellent way to ensure you arrive rested and refreshed on the continent.

Points and miles enthusiasts usually need to choose between paying high redemption rates or high surcharges. Programs like Delta SkyMiles charge just $5.60 in taxes and fees for business-class flights to Europe but expect up to 500,000 miles per person for flights as short as seven hours on peak dates.

Many European programs have much lower redemption rates, such as British Airways Club, which charges just 88,000 Avios for a one-way, off-peak flight to London from the Northeast. The trade-off is you will need to stump up almost $500 in taxes, fees and surcharges to BA.

The Scandinavian Airlines EuroBonus program charges just 60,000 EuroBonus points for a one-way, SAS-operated Business Bonus award between North America and Europe. The cherry on top? You'll need to pay just $5.60 in taxes and fees. Although this loyalty currency has traditionally been difficult to earn, thanks to the new Rove transfer option, you can fly to Europe for less than the price of a cup of coffee in taxes and fees by redeeming miles.

Related: Earning 28 miles per dollar: How a 2-night New York City hotel stay earned me enough miles to fly to Europe using Rove

Here's how to do it and what my experience was like.

SAS doesn't add carrier-imposed surcharges to awards on flights it operates, making SAS EuroBonus one of the best-value Rove transfer partners for business-class travel to Europe.

SAS flies nonstop to Copenhagen Airport (CPH) from the following U.S. gateways, although some routes are seasonal:

SAS also flies nonstop from Newark to Oslo Airport (OSL) and Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN).

Related: SAS has brought back European Business class on short-haul flights

Business Bonus seats at the fixed 60,000-point rate were strictly limited and were not available on every route or date I searched. When they were unavailable, SAS displayed regular fares that could be paid with points at a much higher rate, so flexible dates helped a lot.

Rove miles transfer to EuroBonus points at a 1:1 ratio, with a 2,000-mile minimum and transfers in increments of 100 miles. My transfer posted instantly, though Rove says transfers usually complete within one day.

Transfers can't be reversed, so the golden rule applies here: Find award space you're happy with before you move a single mile.

SAS award flights booked on the website must currently be reserved at least three days before departure. The SAS app allows closer-in bookings, but for reservations made within three days of departure, the EuroBonus member must be traveling.

Taxes and fees were higher on the way back. When I checked, a SAS business-class award from Copenhagen to the U.S. required about $95 one-way.

Related: A game of thrones: Flying business class on Scandinavian Airlines' A321LR from Copenhagen to Washington

EuroBonus isn't the only option to redeem your Rove miles to fly to Europe. Other transfer partners can be used, but the combination of redemption rates plus taxes, fees and surcharges is not as attractive as EuroBonus:

Related: How to avoid paying fuel surcharges when redeeming points and miles

My journey to Europe began by purchasing a tall latte from Starbucks at ATL for $6.16, including Georgia sales tax, more than the taxes and fees I paid for my business-class flight.

I then used the Sky Priority check-in for my flight to Copenhagen, which allowed me to check two bags, each up to 70 pounds.

SAS business-class tickets to Europe include access to Delta Sky Club lounges. SAS departs from Concourse F, one of the two international concourses at Atlanta Airport, so I headed to the Sky Club in this concourse.

Related: A posh Delta One lounge is coming to Atlanta

It featured an outdoor terrace, which was a great place for planespotting and soaking up the Georgia sunshine.

A kindly staff member who noticed my photo-taking gave me a tip that there was a newer and more luxurious Sky Club in Concourse D I could access on the same ticket. Since I still had several hours before my flight, I headed over there.

It was a big, bright room with floor-to-ceiling windows on both sides looking out over the airfield, and the green and teal decor was a nod to Atlanta's "City in a Forest" nickname.

Based on my visit, I would recommend heading to Concourse D if you have time; I preferred its newer, larger space.

Related: Inside Delta's brand-new Sky Club in Atlanta, its nicest one yet

There were plenty of hot and cold food options available, which is ideal for anyone heading to Europe and wanting to maximize their rest on their flight.

Despite being busy during the late afternoon and early evening, the bartenders happily served up sparkling wine, beers and soft drinks and well as whipping up cocktails and chatting to guests about their travel plans.

After taking advantage of priority boarding for business passengers, I boarded the SAS Airbus A350-900, which had 40 business-class seats in a 1-2-1 layout, so every passenger had direct aisle access.

The cabin had a calm, understated palette of charcoal gray seat shells with brushed silver trim and blue-flecked gray fabric, with a tan, leather-look panel lining each side console to warm it up.

The bedding was already at my seat when I boarded, wrapped in plastic. It came from Dux, the Swedish bedmaker that was SAS's official comfort partner at the time, and included a gray and white pinstriped duvet and two pillows.

The amenity kit was a limited-edition one for SAS’s 80th anniversary. It came in a navy zip pouch with the airline’s 80 logo on the front. Inside was a matching navy eye mask, earplugs and a dental kit, plus lip balm and hand cream from Swedish skincare brand Muro Scents.

A pair of SAS-branded over-ear headphones hung on a hook in the side console. There was a universal power outlet and a USB port right next to it, and the seat itself was controlled from a touchscreen panel, including lumbar support.

I was more interested in sleep than cinema on my flight to Denmark, but the 18.5-inch touchscreen had a solid selection of recent releases, including "The Devil Wears Prada 2."

The drinks list was where SAS leans hardest into its Scandinavian roots.

Alongside Charles Heidsieck Brut Reserve Champagne, there was a hazy IPA brewed by Danish brewery Mikkeller in collaboration with SAS; two SAS-exclusive spirits, Herno Old Tom Gin and High Coast whisky from Sweden; and a cocktail menu that included the SASmopolitan.

For my Atlanta departure, the menu had a definite Georgia flavor. The starter options were grilled peaches wrapped in prosciutto with mozzarella and balsamic pearls or seared ahi tuna. Main courses included smoked beef short rib with stone-ground grits from Georgia's Riverview Farms, a hot honey-glazed chicken thigh and goat cheese and apple ravioli.

I chose the ahi tuna, which was a light and fresh start to the meal, with a hearty slice of sourdough bread on the side.

For the main course, I went for the beef short rib, an indulgent and delicious option with super-tender beef and creamy grits.

With a fairly short flight time and a full stomach, I skipped dessert, reclined my seat fully flat and settled in for the night.

The crew set up a snack bar for business-class passengers who got hungry during the flight, but most focused on getting a good night's rest.

I slept right through breakfast (the crew had asked at dinner whether I wanted to be woken) and arrived refreshed and ready to explore the charming city of Copenhagen.

After years of having to choose between high redemption rates and high surcharges, booking through SAS EuroBonus could be the ultimate sweet spot to Europe.

I've flown plenty of business-class products across the Atlantic, and SAS offered a very respectable experience on the A350 with friendly staff, direct aisle access, comfortable bedding and some fun Scandic touches.

Joining Rove costs nothing, and you can earn 1,500 bonus miles when you sign up through TPG's link. As an added bonus, new users can earn an additional 5,000 miles after making their first hotel booking of $500 or more with code "BRIANKELLY500".

I'd much rather pay $5.60 for a lie-flat seat to Europe than a cup of coffee. How about you?

#6178. ATMA: Aman’s New Brand, Debuting With A 1,049-Foot Miami Tower

Aman is known for being one of the world’s top luxury hotel groups. Currently Aman Group consists of Aman (the original hotel group) and Janu (intended to be more of a “lifestyle” version of Aman). Aman is now launching a third brand, and it’s yet another departure from the origins of Aman.

Aman Group has announced the launch of ATMA, described as a “new ultra-luxury brand pioneering performance living.” ATMA means “the spirit” or “the true self” in Sanskrit, and the intent is for the brand to combine wellness, sport, nutrition-led dining, design, and experiential entertainment.

ATMA will “focus on advanced wellness programming and world-class sport facilities, which have been developed exclusively by ATMA Global Partner Novak Djokovic.”

The first location will be ATMA Miami, and it will include a hotel, branded residence, and a private members club. Specifically, the property will be in the Brickell neighborhood and will have a private marina, with an anticipated opening in 2031.

ATMA Miami is expected to be a standalone 1,049-foot tower, which is as tall as buildings can get in Miami. In terms of height, it’ll be match the new 100-story Waldorf Astoria Miami that’s currently under construction, which will be the tallest building in Florida, once complete.

Details about ATMA Miami are still fairly limited, but we know there will be 480 residential units, in addition to the hotel. Residential units will be between one and six bedrooms, and will be “supported by Aman Group’s service standards.”

There will also be a 120,000 square foot spa and wellness area, set to be the largest of its kind in Miami. Developed in partnership with Djokovic, it will offer performance and recovery experiences alongside indoor padel, tennis and squash courts, a fitness center, group and private training studios, mobility and conditioning labs, a medical wellness center, and dedicated recovery spaces.

So far we’ve only learned about the Miami location, but the claim is that the brand will span urban and remote destinations.

Look, I’ve made my opinions about the Aman brand pretty clear, so I don’t want to sound like some old dude just ranting about the “good old days.” When Aman was founded by hospitality legend Adrian Zecha, it was truly among the most innovative and passion driven hospitality projects we’ve ever seen.

In 2014, Zecha sold the brand to Vladislav Doronin, and since then, the entire philosophy has changed. It’s hard to fault someone for purchasing a brand and trying to cash in and maximize profitability — I mean, that’s kind of how the business world is supposed to work, right?

But of course that doesn’t mean we have to be happy about the evolution. It started with Aman ditching its approach of largely opening hotels in the middle of nowhere, where that was part of the charm. Instead, we saw Aman focus on city hotels. Then Aman became all about opening members clubs. Then we saw the launch of the Janu brand, essentially a higher room count version of Aman, with a more lively spirit.

And now we’re seeing Aman getting into building full-on skyscrapers. Well, or at least partnering on them in terms of branding. Of course some Aman properties already have a residences component, so that’s nothing new, as such. However, the scale of this project couldn’t be more opposite of what Aman initially was. We’re talking about a 100-story building that will have nearly 500 residences, and who knows how many hotel rooms (it hasn’t yet been announced).

Of course in Miami, one of the biggest trends is branded residences, with brands just selling out their name. But if Aman were to just slap its name on a residential project, you’d think it would be something smaller scale than this. This is among the highest unit count developments we’ve ever seen in Miami, at least for a project spanning just one building.

Aman Group has just announced its third brand, and it will be named ATMA. It’s described as a “new ultra-luxury brand pioneering performance living.” The first location will open in Miami in 2031, and it’ll be a roughly 100-story building with 480 residences, a hotel, and a members club.

Aman as a brand has become unrecognizable compared to what it was 15 years ago. But that’s fair enough, and it’s also what happens when you sell a company to someone looking to maximize their ROI. You can hardly fault someone for that, as much as I don’t personally like it.

#6177. 5 Boeing 737 MAX 10 Customers With The Largest Orders

An aviation writer, pilot, and flight operations professional who sees aviation from both sides of the cockpit door. With a background in aeronautics, safety, and human factors, she brings curiosity, firsthand experience, and a love of the details that turn aircraft and airports into stories worth telling.

TheBoeing 737 MAX 10 has attracted significant interest from airlines seeking additional passenger capacity while retaining the operational familiarity of the 737 family. On October 20, 2026, the aircraft received FAA type certification, marking a major milestone after years of development and regulatory review.

Boeing reports that more than 30 customers have ordered a total of 1,555 MAX 10s, making the aircraft an important part of the manufacturer's narrowbody backlog. Several major airlines have committed to the largest member of the 737 MAX family, with firm orders ranging from 100 to 167 aircraft among the carriers featured here.

This ranking compares confirmed firm orders rather than combining them with additional purchase options, which may not be exercised. Delta Air Lines and Pegasus Airlines share fifth place with 100 aircraft each, meaning the five ranking positions include six airlines. The distinction between firm orders and options is particularly important when comparing the airlines' actual commitments.

Delta Air Linesordered 100 Boeing 737-10 aircraft in July 2022, with options for another 30. Announced at the Farnborough International Airshow, the agreement formed part of Delta's plan to modernize its single-aisle fleet and respond to passenger demand. The order gives the carrier a substantial commitment to the largest MAX variant.

Meanwhile, the additional options provide flexibility for future fleet requirements without increasing its current firm order total. The aircraft will be an important addition to Delta's narrowbody operations, offering greater passenger capacity than the smaller members of the MAX family.

Delta has said the 737-10 will be 20% to 30% more fuel-efficient than the retiring aircraft it is intended to replace. Its order also reflects the airline's continued investment in newer aircraft as it works to improve operating efficiency and the onboard experience. Although Delta has options for another 30 jets, only the original 100 firm aircraft are counted in this ranking.

Pegasus Airlines also has 100 firm Boeing 737-10s on order, following an agreement announced by Boeing on December 19, 2024. The Turkish low-cost carrier's purchase consists of 100 firm aircraft and options for another 100, potentially bringing the total commitment to 200.

Pegasus said the aircraft would support its fleet modernization and network expansion plans, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2028. Its firm order therefore matches Delta's, although the two airlines have different fleet strategies and delivery schedules. The additional purchase options remain separate from the confirmed 100-aircraft commitment.

Alaska Airlines announced an order for 105 Boeing 737 MAX 10 aircraft on January 7, 2026, as part of the largest aircraft order in its history. The agreement also included five Boeing 787 widebody aircraft, while Alaska secured rights to purchase another 35 MAX 10s. The order extends the airline's aircraft delivery stream through 2035, providing a longer-term framework for fleet growth and modernization.

Its 105 firm MAX 10s place Alaska Airlines ahead of Delta and Pegasus in this ranking, while the additional purchase rights are not included in the total. The MAX 10 is the largest member of Boeing's 737 MAX family, typically accommodating between 185 and 210 passengers in a two-class configuration.

Its maximum seating capacity is 230 passengers, while its range reaches approximately 3,100 nautical miles. For Alaska Airlines, the aircraft offers an opportunity to add capacity while maintaining commonality with its existing 737 fleet. The airline's agreement also provides flexibility to adjust its future aircraft requirements, with the additional 35 purchase rights giving it the option to increase its commitment if needed.

Alaska Airlines' January announcement is particularly notable because it combines a large narrowbody order with additional widebody aircraft for its expanding international ambitions. The five Boeing 787s included in the agreement are intended to support the airline's long-haul network, while the MAX 10s will serve its single-aisle requirements. With 105 firm MAX 10s and rights for 35 more, the airline has secured a significant position in Boeing's order book.

American Airlines announced its first order for the Boeing 737 MAX 10 on March 4, 2024, committing to 115 aircraft. The agreement combined 85 newly ordered MAX 10s with the conversion of 30 previously ordered 737 MAX 8s to the larger variant. This distinction is important when comparing airline order totals, as the 30 converted aircraft were already part of American's Boeing order book before the change.

The resulting 115-aircraft firm commitment places American third in this ranking. Boeing's announcement also confirmed that American secured options to purchase another 75 MAX 10s in the future. Those options provide the airline with the ability to increase its commitment, but they are not firm orders and are therefore excluded from the ranking.

American described the agreement as part of its wider fleet modernization program, intended to add newer and more efficient aircraft across its network. The MAX 10 gives the carrier another capacity option within the 737 family without introducing an entirely different aircraft type. American's 115 firm aircraft orders place it ahead of Alaska Airlines and behind Ryanair in this comparison.

If the carrier eventually exercises all 75 options, its potential MAX 10 commitment would increase to 190 aircraft, although that remains a possible future purchase rather than a confirmed order. The distinction also demonstrates why options should not be added to firm-order rankings. For American, the agreement provides a way to secure additional capacity while adjusting an existing commitment to Boeing's narrowbody family.

Ryanair announced an agreement for 300 Boeing 737 MAX 10 aircraft on May 9, 2023. Its commitment comprised 150 firm orders and options for another 150, making it one of the largest orders placed for the variant. The agreement was the largest aircraft order in the airline's history at the time and represented a major investment in its future fleet.

Deliveries are scheduled to take place between 2027 and 2033, giving Ryanair a multi-year schedule for introducing the aircraft. The airline plans to configure its MAX 10s with 228 seats, according to the original order announcement. This high-density layout is consistent with Ryanair's low-cost operating model and its focus on carrying large numbers of passengers across short- and medium-haul routes.

The carrier has also said that approximately half of the aircraft will replace older 737NGs, while the remaining deliveries will support traffic growth. Ryanair linked the order to its longer-term ambition of carrying 300 million passengers annually by March 2034. Ryanair's 150 firm orders place it second among the airline customers in this ranking, behind United Airlines.

The additional 150 options could eventually double its MAX 10 commitment if exercised, but they remain separate from the aircraft already ordered on a firm basis. Its planned 228-seat configuration also gives the airline a high-capacity version of the 737 for its extensive European network. With deliveries scheduled to begin in 2027, Ryanair is preparing for a substantial fleet transition over the following years.

Emergencies, holding patterns and more. Tap any flight to follow it on the tracker.

United Airlines leads the ranking with 167 Boeing 737 MAX 10 aircraft on firm order, according to its June 2026 regulatory filing. That figure places the carrier ahead of Ryanair, American Airlines, Alaska Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and Pegasus Airlines. United's commitment makes it the largest identified airline customer for the aircraft, although Boeing's overall order book also includes other airlines and leasing companies.

The 167-aircraft figure represents United's firm commitments rather than additional options or purchase rights. United's relationship with the MAX 10 dates back to June 2017, when it became the launch customer by converting 100 existing 737 MAX orders to the larger variant.

The agreement was announced at the Paris Air Show, where Boeing confirmed that United would become the largest single customer for the aircraft. At the time, the airline said the MAX 10 would allow it to use larger and more efficient aircraft across its domestic network. Its original commitment established a prominent place in the program, and its current 167-aircraft order keeps United at the top of the customer ranking.​​​​​​​

The FAA's certification of the 737 MAX 10 on October 20, 2026, brought the aircraft closer to commercial service after a lengthy development and approval process. Boeing's certification campaign included nearly 1,000 test flights and more than 2,000 flight hours, alongside extensive ground testing and regulatory reviews.

With 167 firm aircraft on order, United has the largest identified airline commitment waiting for the type to enter service. Nearly a decade after the carrier first committed to the MAX 10, the certification milestone brings the aircraft closer to fulfilling the role United originally envisioned for it.

#6176. The Don Jr. Wedding May Be the Emblem of a Corrupt Age

‘Hogs get slaughtered,’ as the old saying goes — people will tolerate graft only up to a point.

Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Anderson, disembark from Air Force One at Dublin Airport in Dublin, Ireland, September 12, 2026.

On May 31, 1871, William Marcy Tweed threw a spectacularly lavish wedding for his daughter, Mary Amelia, in New York City. “Boss” Tweed was then at the height of his power as the political master of New York City, its ruling Democratic Party, and its Tammany Hall machine. Elected to the U.S. House at 29 in 1852, he sacrificed his career in Washington to vote for the Kansas–Nebraska Act, which was massively unpopular in the North. This was not a stance on principle: The vote was a test of party loyalty, and the Pierce administration paid off Tweed by appointing a friend to a job as postmaster. Returning home to New York, Tweed was running Tammany Hall by 1858.

The corruption he oversaw was immense. It at least doubled the cost of building anything that the city could touch. The Tweed Courthouse cost some $13-14 million to build, twice the cost of the Alaska Purchase during the same period. David McCullough argued in The Great Bridge that the Brooklyn Bridge would never have been completed had the Tweed Ring not fallen early in its construction. Tweed and his cronies were convicted of stealing tens of millions of dollars — some modern estimates place the real amount in the hundreds of millions — which would be worth billions today. Alfred Ely Beach, who published Scientific American, decided to build a pioneering subway line between 1868 and 1870, powered by an immense pneumatic tube, and to avoid paying off Tweed, he built it like a bank heist, removing the dirt at night and not telling the city what he was building until it was ready for passengers.

#6175. Will Credit Card Interest Rates Be Capped At 10%? Democrats Want To Work With Trump

With the recent midterm elections, the balance of power in Washington is very quickly changing. Given the extent to which things shifted left, Democrats certainly want to be able to show that they can accomplish something in the next two years, to make life better for average Americans.

Along those lines, we’re once again seeing a proposal floated regarding capping credit card interest rates. There’s a lot more support for this than in the past, given the majority that Democrats have, plus the fact that President Trump has also been in support of this concept (or at least claimed to be). Will it actually pass, though?

Senate Democrats are renewing a proposal to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, with Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts specifically bringing this up in a “Face The Nation” interview. Warren is likely to chair the Senate Banking Committee, and could use her position to help advance the proposal.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) says she wants to work with President Trump to cap credit card interest rates at 10% and Democrats “have the bills ready to go” to work with the president. “We got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price… pic.twitter.com/0r17PwXPQT

Now, before anyone gets political, keep in mind that this is a concept that Trump actually proposed earlier this year. He claimed that Americans were being ripped off by credit card companies, and that as of January 20, 2026, credit card interest rates should be capped at 10%. However, this just came in the form of a social media post, rather than any actual legislation:

Please be informed that we will no longer let the American Public be “ripped off” by Credit Card Companies that are charging Interest Rates of 20 to 30%, and even more, which festered unimpeded during the Sleepy Joe Biden Administration. AFFORDABILITY! Effective January 20, 2026, I, as President of the United States, am calling for a one year cap on Credit Card Interest Rates of 10%. Coincidentally, the January 20th date will coincide with the one year anniversary of the historic and very successful Trump Administration. Thank you for your attention to this matter. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP

Donald J. Trump Truth Social Post 08:10 PM EST 01.09.26 pic.twitter.com/47SQ03yMeo

Unsurprisingly, there was no enforcement mechanism, and this never happened, especially since he got pushback from other Republicans. If he really believed in that proposal, then it sounds like this will be his chance to actually turn it into some sort of a law, with support from Democrats. We’ll have to mark this as “developing” for now.

Just for some context, credit card issuers make money in three primary ways — through interchange fees, through interest charges, and through annual fees. When it comes to interest rates, credit card companies are known for having very high rates, an average of over 20%. These are the charges that apply if you don’t pay your full balance before the payment due date. You don’t pay interest charges if you simply charge your purchase to a credit card, and then pay your balance in full.

On the surface, capping credit card interest rates of course sounds great — some of the rates are really high, and many people view banks as greedy, and think they can afford to give up some of their margins. Obviously for those who are currently financing charges, a cap on interest rates would be positive.

The thing is, a policy change like this wouldn’t come without some other changes. There’s no denying that if interest rates were capped at 10%, lots of consumers with not-great credit would be locked out of getting credit cards, and might even have their accounts closed, because card issuers would find it too risky to loan them money at that rate.

After all, there’s a huge risk to people not making payments, and the economics of that work differently with 10% interest rates rather than 25% interest rates. I would imagine that tens of millions of Americans would have their accounts closed, that we’d see fewer no annual fee cards, etc.

Beyond that, if we did see a long term cap on credit card interest rates, it would likely change the credit card landscape in terms of how rewarding cards are, with everything ranging from welcome bonuses, to rewards on spending, to perks.

Right or wrong, credit card economics are heavily reliant on a cross-subsidized system. That’s the whole reason some of us are able to get such outsized value. Credit card rewards structures nowadays largely more or less rebate back interchange fees to consumers, as it’s easy to earn 2% cash back with cards, or even to earn huge multipliers on spending.

The reality is that the revenue that subsidizes a lot of rewards is the interest charges, since that’s the highest margin revenue stream from many card issuers. So we’re partly earning huge welcome bonuses and 5x points on some transactions because someone else is paying close to 30% interest.

I’m not saying that’s a good system, but I’m just being realistic about how it works. If interest rates are forced to be slashed by more than half in the long run, it will have major implications for rewards. Maybe that’s objectively not a bad thing, but it will happen.

For that matter, it would even have a major impact on airlines — they’re so reliant on credit card revenue nowadays to turn profits, and this would greatly hurt their margins in that area as well.

With Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, there’s a renewed push to cap credit card interest rates at 10%. This is a proposal that Trump made earlier this year, but it didn’t get support from Republicans.

While I totally appreciate that credit card interest rates are often incredibly high, it’s not without reason, given the rate of default on some cards. Approval standards for cards would change, many consumers would have their cards shut down, etc. It would also likely change the economics of the credit card industry, which could even impact airlines.

However, I’m not some lobbyist or apologist for the credit card industry. If the change happens, many people will benefit, and I’m sure the industry will adapt. However, unarguably many people will go from paying 25% interest on their credit card, to potentially paying even higher rates for payday loans, doing business with loan sharks, etc.

What do you make of this proposal to cap credit card interest rates?

‘Tis the season … when frequent flyers scramble for eleventh-hour ways to qualify for airline elite status they haven’t quite reached yet.

If Southwest is your airline of choice, the end of 2026 is particularly important to hit status milestones, as Southwest’s Rapid Rewards program is about to change in major ways in early 2027.

With fewer international flight options and no premium cabins for upgrades, chasing Southwest status might not seem as necessary as it does with larger competitors like United Airlines or Delta Air Lines.

But if you fly Southwest a lot and are close to hitting a status goal, it’s wise to explore easy and inexpensive ways to get over that hump.

What you need to do to earn status depends on what part of Southwest’s program you are targeting. Southwest technically has two official status tiers in 2026. Plus, members who fly (or spend) the most can unlock its popular Companion Pass.

Coming next year: Commonly asked questions about Southwest's recent Rapid Rewards reboot and Companion Pass changes

You can check how close you are to status by logging into your Rapid Rewards account where there are easy-to-read status bars for each goal.

There are very different methods for earning the Companion Pass than there are for earning A-List and A-List Preferred status. If the Companion Pass is your only goal, you need to act quickly. The “easy” way to do that with credit card bonuses effectively ends forever no later than Dec. 2, 2026.

This year also marks the last that many partner points count towards Companion Pass, from credit card refer-a-friend bonuses to completing hotel stays booked on the Southwest Hotels portal.

More: Last chance to earn a Southwest Companion Pass the easy way with card bonuses as high as 90,000 points

If traditional A-List or A-List Preferred status is your goal, however, here are 5 ways you can get the flights or points you might still need.

Note that beginning in 2027, Southwest will rename those tiers as part of a broader overhaul (more on that below), but that will not affect how you qualify in 2026 for 2027.

If you are only a few flights away from qualifying for Southwest status, one of the easiest ways to get to the finish line is by taking a trip or two before year’s end.

The amount of money spent doesn’t matter at all if you qualify purely by counting up the number of one-way flights flown, so book and fly the cheapest nonstop Basic fares you can find.

Use Southwest’s Low Fare Calendar to search quickly for the least expensive days to fly to various destinations. The best deals are usually midweek. Early and mid-December (between peak Thanksgiving and Christmas holiday travel) will likely offer lower prices and reduced chances of travel disruptions.

If you can’t hit a status goal by counting one-way flights and need to earn status via tier qualifying points instead, you should take the opposite approach. Instead of booking inexpensive Basic fares, book and fly Southwest’s most expensive fare option: Choice Extra.

This fare earns a whopping 14 TQPs per dollar spent in 2026. If you spend $500 on Choice Extra fares for a November or December mileage run, for example, you will add a quick 7000 TQPs to your Rapid Rewards account balance—one fifth of the way to A-List status.

Those same points are also worth about $90 when redeemed for award travel, so consider the rebate in your cost-benefit calculation.

If actually flying the airline before the year is up isn’t a realistic option, another way to earn tier qualifying points is by spending on a Southwest credit card.

The different cobranded cards earn TQPs differently in 2026. Holders of the lower annual fee (see rates and fees) are out of luck; that card doesn’t earn TQPs at all.

The higher fee cards each earn incrementally higher TQPs, as follows:

(Note, however, that all cards earn Companion Pass qualifying points at a different rate—1 point per $1 spent.)

One critical detail: TQPs earned from credit card spending only count towards 2026 status if the points post to your account before year’s end. That means it is essential to complete all spending before the closing date of your December credit card statement, meaning many travelers may only have a few weeks left.

A reminder, though: Credit card spending will count differently beginning next year for customers trying to qualify for status for 2028.

*The information for the Southwest Rapid Rewards Premier Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

If you have a card (see rates and fees) and already spend heavily on it, there is a quick and easy shortcut to Southwest A-List status (but not A-List Preferred). If you spend $75,000 on that card annually, you'll be rewarded with complimentary A-List status for the remainder of the year and the following year (activation required).

You'll also earn a $500 annual credit towards booking Southwest flights in the Chase Ultimate Rewards portal. That same spending level unlocks other perks from a variety of travel brands like Hyatt and IHG, so there are more benefits than just the Southwest ones to consider.

This method doesn’t require fussing with flight counts or TQPs or even hopping on an airplane before 2026 is up, but it’s only a viable option for a smaller subset of Southwest customers who carry the card and are capable of meeting a significant spending minimum.

Like many airlines, Southwest offers a status match promotion and challenge where you can leverage your elite status on another airline into temporary status on Southwest. If you hold status elsewhere, consider taking advantage.

The current promotion is open for registration through Dec. 30, 2026. As soon as you register, Southwest confers automatic status for a 120-day trial period. You can extend this status for another 12 months if you complete additional flights or earn additional TQPs in the promotion period.

If you plan to fly several trips on Southwest at the end of 2026 or in early 2027, this promotion might make sense. The requirements to meet the status challenge extension are substantially lower than the ones for achieving status the standard way.

Just be aware that only flights booked after registering for the status match count. If you have future Southwest travel already booked, you’ll need to cancel and rebook, potentially at higher prices.

Before committing to any of these strategies, be certain that you understand how Southwest counts Rapid Rewards points in 2026.

Southwest currently counts points three different ways. There are points redeemable only for award travel, and there are two other types that count towards status. Only tier qualifying points, earned primarily through flying or credit card spending, count towards A-List and A-List Preferred Status.

A broader collection of companion pass qualifying points (including credit card welcome bonuses) still count towards earning the Companion Pass for 2026 only.

A lot will soon change when the calendar page turns to 2027.

A-List members will become Silver, and A-List Preferred members will become Gold. Members who have earned a Companion Pass due to points activity in 2026 will continue to be able to use those benefits until the end of 2027.

If you want to earn a Companion Pass anew in 2027 or later, however, you’ll have to aim for a new status tier: Platinum. And if you want to achieve Silver or Gold in subsequent years, be aware that that benchmarks will change. The way TQPs are calculated for several Southwest fare types and for credit card spending will be different as well.

#6173. American First Class Will Get Mini-Meals On Shorter Flights (700-899 Miles)

American Airlines is making a very nice change to first class service on some short haul flights that didn’t previously qualify for a meal service, and it’s something I’m sure passengers will be happy to see.

As things currently stand, American serves meals in first class on flights of at least 900 miles during meal times (900 miles roughly correlates to a little over two hours of flying, on average). In the US, this is basically the industry standard, as Delta and United have the same cutoff of 900 miles for serving meals. On flights shorter than that, airlines only offer drinks and a snack basket in first class.

It looks like American will soon be leading the industry when it comes to service in first class on shorter flights, as it brings back a program it used to offer. JonNYC was first to report that American will be bringing back the “light bites” concept on flights of 700 to 899 miles (700 miles correlates to a little over 90 minutes of flying, on average).

AA:"Light bites”/mini-meals coming back to short haul domestic first class flights 700-899 milesStarting on NYC/ORD.

As now confirmed by American, this is launching this month on flights between Chicago (ORD) and New York, including Kennedy (JFK) and LaGuardia (LGA). It remains to be seen when it expands to other routes. It must be a decade at this point since American offered this concept.

The expectation is that there will be a rotating selection of options, with two available on each flight, and they won’t be available via pre-order.

Breakfast selections may include smoked salmon, tropical chia overnight oats, prosciutto and melon, fruit and cheese plates, prosciutto and brie, or apple cinnamon chia pudding. Lunch and dinner options may include curry chicken salads, Thai noodle salads, turkey and gouda sandwiches, whipped burrata, poached shrimp with noodle salads, mezze plates, blackened chicken, or grilled vegetable wraps.

It goes without saying that expectations of premium cabin travelers differ massively around the globe. In the Middle East, it’s common to have a 30-minute business class flight with a lie flat bed, cappuccinos, champagne, and a substantial, tasty snack.

In Europe, you’re typically stuck with a pretty underwhelming hard product on short haul flights (just economy with a blocked middle), but regardless of the length of the flight, you’re almost always served something fresh, even if the flight time is well under an hour.

In the United States, we have the benefit of actually having a dedicated first class cabin with larger seats, but the soft product just isn’t great. You can be on a flight of nearly two hours and just be served packaged snacks.

We do have to give credit to Alaska for this, as it’s the only US carrier to serve some sort of fresh food on flights of under 900 miles. On most Alaska flights you’ll get a snack on shorter services, so kudos to the airline for that.

American Airlines will once again serve fresh food in first class on flights of 700-899 miles. This concept will debut on flights between Chicago and New York, and passengers will have the choice of two rotating options. This is really a resumption of something that American offered many years back.

Among the “big three” US carriers, American will be the only one to serve fresh food in first class on flights of under 900 miles, so kudos to the airline for that.

What do you make of American serving mini-meals on shorter first class flights?

#6171. Breeze Airways Launches 15 New Routes From This Airport: See Full List Now

Breeze Airways first flew to Raleigh-Durham in February 2023, with the North Carolina airport quickly becoming a critical part of the fast-growing airline's network. This is influenced by the so-called Research Triangle region being among the fastest-growing areas of the US.

For all of 2026, Cirium Diio data shows that Raleigh-Durham is Breeze's most-served airport for flights. However, from January 2027, Tampa will gain the throne, relegating the North Carolina airport to the second spot. While subject to change, the latest information shows that Raleigh-Durham is due to rank first again next July and August.

Comparing the carrier's Raleigh-Durham network in 2025 with what's scheduled for 2026 shows that the following routes have all taken off, one in the past few days. To qualify for inclusion, all the markets must still be scheduled for 2027. This article simply summarizes Breeze's development at the North Carolina airport while providing additional context.

The list includes one international market: the ever-popular Dominican Republic tourist destination of Punta Cana. Until 2018, no nonstop flights existed. Frontier operated in 2018 and 2019, followed by American and Avelo in 2025. While American continues to run, Avelo pulled out in January 2026, which spurred Breeze's entry two months later.

Raleigh-Durham has not previously had nonstop flights to several of the places. Breeze is renowned for beginning brand-new routes, with its relatively low-capacity, 137-seat Airbus A220-300s helping. Atlantic City, Bangor, Madison, Orange County, Provo, Tallahassee, and Vero Beach are all new to the airport's map.

Some of the other destinations were served by other airlines in the past. For example, Stewart was part of American Airlines' network (when the carrier had a hub at Raleigh-Durham) until 1995 and later by Midway Airlines (which also had a hub). San Antonio was served by Frontier in 2018, while others (like Expressjet and Southwest) flew in the past. Midway served Dayton until 2001, while Expressjet flew to Birmingham until 2008.

While it is inevitable that more routes will be announced in due course for next year, the following list summarizes what is known as of November 11. Only one of them, Las Vegas, has previously been served by Breeze. The long transcontinental market to Sin City, which covers 1,761 nautical miles (3,261 km), had flights by the airline between September 2023 and January 2024.

US Department of Transportation data shows that the airline transported 10,284 passengers to/from Las Vegas and filled 78.2% of seats. As the load factor was similar to Breeze's average across its whole network at that time, the reason for the very short existence was to do with fares.

The same source shows that the distance-adjusted total revenue per available seat mile was overwhelmingly the airline's lowest across its Raleigh-Durham routes at the time. It was also 31% lower than to Los Angeles, with that route pulled in January 2026. Breeze's return to Nevada will benefit somewhat from the exit of Frontier last August. However, it'll still face Delta and Southwest.

The carrier will now fly to six international destinations. Find out more here!

While subject to change, the airline has scheduled 44 routes from Raleigh-Durham between January and June next year. It'll have well over double the number of routes of any other carrier. However, because most of its links will only have two to three weekly flights, all on 137-seat aircraft, it'll only be the North Carolina airport's fourth-largest operator for both departures and capacity.

Recall that Breeze began flying to Raleigh-Durham in February 2023. Now that flights to Las Vegas are returning, the airline has ended only one route in nearly four years. This was to Los Angeles, with flights available between May 2023 and January 2026. While California's busiest airport is no longer served, Breeze started flying to Orange County, for the enormous LA Basin, in May this year.

#6170. Amex Business Gold Card Bonus: As High As 200K Points Welcome Offer

The American Express® Business Gold Card is one of the most rewarding business cards if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

We’re currently seeing an excellent Amex Business Gold Card welcome offer, which is the biggest bonus we’ve ever seen on the card, making it the ideal time to apply. If you’re eligible for this card and the highest possible bonus, it’s absolutely worth taking advantage of, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Business Gold Card

The Amex Business Gold Card currently has a massive welcome offer that’s as high as 200,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $15,000 on eligible purchases within the first three months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Find out your offer.

Amex uses a variety of factors when it comes to deciding what offer people are eligible for, including history of opening and closing cards with Amex, spending history with Amex, how many welcome offers people have earned, etc. So, how does this Amex Business Gold Card bonus actually work?

You should find the highest possible offer through the above link. However, if you don’t, it can always be worth checking refer-a-friend links, opting in to targeted emails from Amex, or even using the CardMatch tool to see what you’re eligible for there. That being said, don’t expect to get a higher offer through any of those sources, since offers are typically targeted based on the person, rather than the application method.

It goes without saying that the Amex Business Gold bonus spending requirement is potentially significant, as it averages out to $5,000 per month. However, there are lots of ways to be creative with reaching minimum spending, and to make a plan. You could time your application around some large upcoming business expenses (whether that’s an ad campaign or buying inventory), prepay for some items, and maybe even put some expenses on credit cards that you might otherwise pay for with cash. Of course make sure you pay off everything in full by the payment due date, so that you don’t get stuck paying high interest charges.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, 200,000 points are worth $3,400, which is an incredible offer, assuming you’re eligible. This is the biggest publicly available bonus that we’ve seen on this card, and in the past, we’ve often only seen offers of 70,000 to 100,000 points, so this is much better. I’d consider the Amex Business Gold Card bonus to be among the best welcome offers out there.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners, ranging from Air France-KLM Flying Blue, to Emirates Skywards, to Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. Just to give a couple of examples of Amex points redemption opportunities:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the Amex Business Gold Card bonus isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply.

There are a few additional things to note when it comes to apply for Amex business cards:

Anecdotally, I find this to be a pretty easy card to get approved for, and you can read about my experience applying here.

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the Amex Business Gold, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that impacts card approval.

The Amex Business Gold Card has a $375 annual fee (Rates & Fees). There are many reasons to consider picking up this card.

I’d say the single biggest reason to get the Amex Business Gold is because of the rewards structure. Each billing cycle, the card earns 4x points in the two categories in which your business spends the most. There are a total of six eligible categories to choose from. Note that you earn 4x points on the first $150,000 in combined purchases from these categories each calendar year, and then 1x points thereafter.

Categories eligible for 4x points on the Amex Business Gold include the following:

The Amex Business Gold also offers 3x points per dollar spent on flights and prepaid hotels booked through Amex Travel (either on amextravel.com or the Amex Travel app), and 1x points on all other eligible purchases, with no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees).

On top of that, the Amex Business Gold offers up to $845 in annual credits, potentially more than offsetting the annual fee. The Amex Business Gold credits include the following:

There’s currently an excellent Amex Business Gold Card bonus, as the welcome offer is as high as 200,000 Membership Rewards points upon completing minimum spending. While the spending requirement is significant, so is the number of points you can earn, so this is worth it if you can swing it… assuming you’re eligible!

The main reason to consider picking up this card (beyond the great welcome offer) is because it offers 4x points in valuable categories. On top of that, though, the card offers some credits that can help offset the annual fee.
