#6169. ENDING SOON: 100,000 Points Plus A Companion Award—Why Alaska’s Best Credit Card Beats Those From Bigger Airlines

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card is probably the best airline cobrand credit card, and it has a limited-time offer – 100,000 bonus points. Get 100,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award with this offer. To qualify, spend $6,000 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account. The annual fee is $395.

The offer gives you two different things. The 100,000 bonus points and the 25,000 point Global Companion Award that reduces the points needed for a second passenger’s award ticket.

I think the strongest reasons to consider it are the annual companion award and earning 3 points per dollar on eligible foreign purchases. Alaska has also put a substantial reward at $60,000 in annual spending.

Each account anniversary brings another 25,000-point Global Companion Award, with no annual spending requirement. Spending $60,000 in your card anniversary year earns a separate 100,000 point Global Companion Award. You can earn both. These work on eligible Alaska, Hawaiian and partner awards available through Alaska’s website, in any cabin. Suppose an award costs 35,000 points per passenger. Two tickets would normally require 70,000 points. Applying a 25,000-point certificate brings that down to 45,000 points, plus applicable taxes and fees. If each ticket costs 100,000 points apiece, the larger certificate brings the combined price down from 200,000 to 100,000 points, plus taxes and fees. Things to know: Book both travelers together on the same itinerary. The certificate applies to a new booking, not an existing reservation. You can use it for one-way or roundtrip travel. Multi-city and open-jaw itineraries are excluded. If the companion’s ticket costs more than the certificate covers, pay the difference in points. If it costs less, you lose the unused value. Book within one year of issuance. Travel can take place later, but changes after certificate expiration forfeit the discount. Partially used tickets can’t be changed. Only one certificate can be applied per reservation, and it can’t be combined with another discount. Pay taxes, fees and surcharges with the Summit card. The cardholder doesn’t need to travel – you can book for any two travelers. You still need award space for two. Using all 25,000 points of the anniversary certificate would cover the $395 fee if those saved points are worth 1.58 cents each to you. At 1.5 cents, it’s $375. That’s close enough that using another benefit can put you ahead. But don’t give the certificate full value if you’d otherwise let it expire or use it to save only 10,000 points. Foreign Purchases Are The Standout Earning Category The card earns: 3 points per dollar on eligible dining, foreign transactions, and Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases. 1 point per dollar on other purchases. A 10% relationship bonus on purchase points when you have a qualifying Bank of America or Merrill account. That makes the rates 3.3 and 1.1 points per dollar. Dining and airline bonuses are something offered by numerous cards. Getting a bonus on eligible shopping and other purchases abroad that wouldn’t ordinarily fall into a bonus category is much more interesting. (Generally Chase buys points at a discount from its cobrand partners on foreign transactions, effectively subsidized by the program, making it uneconomic to offer something like this.) The relationship bonus triggers with qualifying checking accounts, consumer savings and certificates of deposit, as well as Merrill investment accounts. A new account can take up to 60 days to trigger the bonus. The Card Can Save Money On American Award Tickets Atmos charges a $20 partner award booking fee per person, each way. Summit waives it when you redeem points from the primary cardholder’s account and pay the award’s taxes and fees with that card. The primary cardholder doesn’t have to be traveling. That saves $80 on a roundtrip partner award for two. Five such bookings would save $400, more than the annual fee, without assigning any value to the companion award or lounge passes. This is a fee Alaska imposes and then lets its premium cardholders avoid. I’d prefer they didn’t charge it in the first place. But if you’re booking these awards anyway, the savings are great. Free points sharing helps, too. The primary cardholder can establish a network with up to ten other Atmos members and move redeemable points between linked accounts without a transfer fee. Each member can belong to only one network, and the primary cardholder can change each linked account only once every 12 months. Status points can’t be transferred. Being able to combine balances is useful when several family members have points but no one has enough for the award you want. Lounge Access, Bags And Travel Benefits The card’s travel benefits include: Eight Alaska Lounge passes annually, issued two per calendar quarter. They expire at the end of that quarter. Each covers one adult and up to two accompanying children under 21, with access to Alaska Lounges for the travel day. You need an eligible same-day boarding pass, and access is subject to capacity. These don’t admit you to Hawaiian’s lounges or partner lounges. Eight Alaska Wi-Fi passes annually, also two per quarter. Each is for one flight, and unused passes expire at quarter-end. A first checked bag free and preferred boarding for the cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights, when airfare is purchased with the card. Include the primary cardholder’s Atmos number. 20% back on eligible onboard purchases. This is for Alaska food, beverages and Wi-Fi, and Hawaiian food and beverages, when paid with the card. Up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fees every four years when charged to the card. Complimentary upgrade waitlist priority for eligible elite members. A same-day confirmed change fee waiver. Alaska’s benefits page includes eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights. Saver fares are excluded, and routing and same day travel restrictions apply. For a family of two adults and two children under 21, two lounge passes can cover everyone for a travel day. There’s also a $50 delay voucher. For an eligible Alaska booking purchased directly with the Summit card, a departure delay of at least two hours or a cancellation within 24 hours of departure can qualify. It’s for the primary cardholder, limited to one per calendar day, and expires 48 hours after issuance. Activation instructions arrive by email, and eligible spending is reimbursed as a statement credit. There’s also trip and baggage delay coverage, trip cancellation and interruption protection, and lost luggage reimbursement. along with primary rental car collision coverage. The $60,000 Spend Strategy Summit earns one status point per $2 in purchases, plus 10,000 status points each account anniversary beginning with your first anniversary. Atmos Gold requires 40,000 status points and comes with oneworld Sapphire. So $60,000 of spending produces 30,000 status points. An anniversary deposit of 10,000 in the same qualification year gets you to Gold which is oneworld sapphire. Status qualification runs by calendar year. The $60,000 companion award threshold runs by card anniversary year. Spending split between two calendar years can earn the certificate without producing Gold in either year. And a new cardholder doesn’t receive the anniversary status points immediately upon opening the account. Suppose you put $60,000 of purchases that earn the base rate on Summit. With the relationship bonus, you’d earn 66,000 redeemable points and the 100,000-point companion certificate. A card earning 2 points per dollar would generate 120,000 points on that same spending. You’re giving up 54,000 points in the alternative program in exchange for the certificate and the status credit. That can definitely be worth it even aside from the status. Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card Topics on this pageAlaska AirlinesCredit cardHawaiian AirlinesLoyalty programAlaskaAtmos EnergyBank of AmericaChaseGlobal EntryMerrillTransportation Security AdministrationTSA PreCheckWi-Fi+9 more More From View from the Wing

Each account anniversary brings another 25,000-point Global Companion Award, with no annual spending requirement. Spending $60,000 in your card anniversary year earns a separate 100,000 point Global Companion Award. You can earn both.

These work on eligible Alaska, Hawaiian and partner awards available through Alaska’s website, in any cabin.

Suppose an award costs 35,000 points per passenger. Two tickets would normally require 70,000 points. Applying a 25,000-point certificate brings that down to 45,000 points, plus applicable taxes and fees.

If each ticket costs 100,000 points apiece, the larger certificate brings the combined price down from 200,000 to 100,000 points, plus taxes and fees. Things to know: Book both travelers together on the same itinerary. The certificate applies to a new booking, not an existing reservation. You can use it for one-way or roundtrip travel. Multi-city and open-jaw itineraries are excluded. If the companion’s ticket costs more than the certificate covers, pay the difference in points. If it costs less, you lose the unused value. Book within one year of issuance. Travel can take place later, but changes after certificate expiration forfeit the discount. Partially used tickets can’t be changed. Only one certificate can be applied per reservation, and it can’t be combined with another discount. Pay taxes, fees and surcharges with the Summit card. The cardholder doesn’t need to travel – you can book for any two travelers. You still need award space for two. Using all 25,000 points of the anniversary certificate would cover the $395 fee if those saved points are worth 1.58 cents each to you. At 1.5 cents, it’s $375. That’s close enough that using another benefit can put you ahead. But don’t give the certificate full value if you’d otherwise let it expire or use it to save only 10,000 points. Foreign Purchases Are The Standout Earning Category The card earns: 3 points per dollar on eligible dining, foreign transactions, and Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases. 1 point per dollar on other purchases. A 10% relationship bonus on purchase points when you have a qualifying Bank of America or Merrill account. That makes the rates 3.3 and 1.1 points per dollar. Dining and airline bonuses are something offered by numerous cards. Getting a bonus on eligible shopping and other purchases abroad that wouldn’t ordinarily fall into a bonus category is much more interesting. (Generally Chase buys points at a discount from its cobrand partners on foreign transactions, effectively subsidized by the program, making it uneconomic to offer something like this.) The relationship bonus triggers with qualifying checking accounts, consumer savings and certificates of deposit, as well as Merrill investment accounts. A new account can take up to 60 days to trigger the bonus. The Card Can Save Money On American Award Tickets Atmos charges a $20 partner award booking fee per person, each way. Summit waives it when you redeem points from the primary cardholder’s account and pay the award’s taxes and fees with that card. The primary cardholder doesn’t have to be traveling. That saves $80 on a roundtrip partner award for two. Five such bookings would save $400, more than the annual fee, without assigning any value to the companion award or lounge passes. This is a fee Alaska imposes and then lets its premium cardholders avoid. I’d prefer they didn’t charge it in the first place. But if you’re booking these awards anyway, the savings are great. Free points sharing helps, too. The primary cardholder can establish a network with up to ten other Atmos members and move redeemable points between linked accounts without a transfer fee. Each member can belong to only one network, and the primary cardholder can change each linked account only once every 12 months. Status points can’t be transferred. Being able to combine balances is useful when several family members have points but no one has enough for the award you want. Lounge Access, Bags And Travel Benefits The card’s travel benefits include: Eight Alaska Lounge passes annually, issued two per calendar quarter. They expire at the end of that quarter. Each covers one adult and up to two accompanying children under 21, with access to Alaska Lounges for the travel day. You need an eligible same-day boarding pass, and access is subject to capacity. These don’t admit you to Hawaiian’s lounges or partner lounges. Eight Alaska Wi-Fi passes annually, also two per quarter. Each is for one flight, and unused passes expire at quarter-end. A first checked bag free and preferred boarding for the cardholder and up to six guests on the same reservation on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights, when airfare is purchased with the card. Include the primary cardholder’s Atmos number. 20% back on eligible onboard purchases. This is for Alaska food, beverages and Wi-Fi, and Hawaiian food and beverages, when paid with the card. Up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fees every four years when charged to the card. Complimentary upgrade waitlist priority for eligible elite members. A same-day confirmed change fee waiver. Alaska’s benefits page includes eligible Alaska and Hawaiian flights. Saver fares are excluded, and routing and same day travel restrictions apply. For a family of two adults and two children under 21, two lounge passes can cover everyone for a travel day. There’s also a $50 delay voucher. For an eligible Alaska booking purchased directly with the Summit card, a departure delay of at least two hours or a cancellation within 24 hours of departure can qualify. It’s for the primary cardholder, limited to one per calendar day, and expires 48 hours after issuance. Activation instructions arrive by email, and eligible spending is reimbursed as a statement credit. There’s also trip and baggage delay coverage, trip cancellation and interruption protection, and lost luggage reimbursement. along with primary rental car collision coverage. The $60,000 Spend Strategy Summit earns one status point per $2 in purchases, plus 10,000 status points each account anniversary beginning with your first anniversary. 100K SUB is better than 70-80K. Great ‘keeper’ card, actually.

This card is too much value. I have too many points and certificates to the point that I can barely use them all. I haven’t paid for a flight in a year. Please stop signing up for this card so I can find more Saver J awards

I love this card. Easily worth the annual fee – after the SUB.

There’s one other benefit for high status AS flyers. Having the Summit card is a tiebreaker for upgrade priority. AS still has (for now) a higher number of seats available for upgrade than say Delta, so it can matter.

I avoided going for airline status in the past; the Summit card changed the calculus for me, because the opportunity cost (3x Dining and Foreign purchases) of earnings is so much lower, and because of the consumer friendliness of the Atmos program (distance-based earnings, status points earnings on award flights). Now I’m an Atmos Platinum and I’m looking forward to visiting some First Class lounges in the near future.

Also echo EasyMoney, it’s been too easy for me to find opportunities to use my points in the past 18 months; including a Starlux J flight and booking AA Flagship Suites for my brother and sister-in-law (not the best use of the 100K companion cert, but it was their first time ever flying J so it was worth it). Hope AS doesn’t start nerfing those opportunities anytime soon.

@Samar — Between Alaska and Bilt, you’ve really been knocking-it-out-of-the-park this year. Your recent SE Asia tour reports on OMAAT are the proof!

@EasyMoney — I thoroughly enjoyed your sales-pitch, above… “This card is too good!! I’m getting crushed by all this excess value!! AHH!!”

Great card, use VFTW links, but most importantly, welcome to late October, may the increased year-end SUBs descend upon all of us.

@Peter — Move over Toyotathon, it’s a SUB-Festivus for the rest of us! Time for the Airing of Grievances against C1—torching all 3 bureaus for a single rejection is the Feat of Strength nobody asked for. May the Q4 approval odds be in your favor!

primary auto rental collision damage waiver coverage WITHOUT excluding New York residents as Chase does.

I got the regular Atmos card ($99/yr) at the beginning of the year. Now, it will anniversary in January… does anyone know if I’m entitled to these bonus points if I upgrade? I made the mistake last year with Capitol 1 Venture/Venture X… and I paid the price of not reading the fine print/asking enough questions.

@Jack. I would not count on a product change to get you a signup bonus. You can have both the Ascent and Summit at the same time. I have 2 grandfathered Ascents and the Summit so I know it’s possible.

@LK — I don’t get why there’s still confusion with this. In NY, if you don’t have a primary auto insurance policy, because, let’s say, you don’t have a car (many people in NYC don’t), then Chase Sapphire Reserve (and Preferred) are effectively primary, if you decline CDW, etc. (follow all their other rules.) Like, I’ve had nominal claims covered since that update occurred, using CSR, and I’m based in NY, so it wasn’t an issue.

Just checked, one way on Alaska Air’s Hawaiian airlines direct in lie flat JFK-HNL December 15, 2026, is 200K miles. On recliner (which this blog just complained about in “Ugh: Alaska Airlines Will Fly 8 Hours From Anchorage To Tokyo on A 737 MAX”) via Seattle is 150K miles. Somehow that 100k bonus doesn’t seem like such a good deal.

Alaska has inflated the value of miles dramatically (can I say exponentially) in the last couple of years. The trajectory is horrible and I am still waiting for the other shoe to drop.

I am sure Alaska will do the hustle: (1)The other airlines are worse or (2) If you look at it the right way it is a good deal.

@Other Just Saying — Using Alaska points on Alaska/Hawaiian has rarely been best use; it’s all about partner J and F, though availability can be an issue. Just have to time it right. Think, JL, JX, even AA.

Convince me, as a solo leisure traveler, this card is worth it. Other than the SUB, which doesn’t really get ypu much aspirational these days. I already have Hiltom Amex Aspire and AA Citi Exec. The primary benefit touted, the companion passes, sort of makes me feel spit on, as a solo traveler. I’m open to being convinced. But with the other cards I carry, aren’t seeing it.

I have the card. The 3 x points on foreign transactions is makes it a convenient card to use when I travel internationally.

However, partner airlines tickets prices have doubled, tripled, and so forth. Actually, when partner tickets that used to cost 80K two years ago are now 200K or 300K, it is hard to take a value proposition too seriously. Now, it may be that is the partner increasing prices, but the same inflation is in the Alaska Tickets.

Also I also cannot find much availability (if any) on routes that Alaska covers, for example, JFK-TYO, outside of Alaska’s own metal.

All USA airlines are doing this in tandem. Of course, just following market trends is also a hustle. In the long run, consumers are not too stupid to notice.

If you fly United Airlines regularly, the (see rates and fees) can be a powerful way to earn more miles and reduce your out-of-pocket travel costs.

As someone who frequently flies United, I've found that the Quest hits a practical middle ground. It offers meaningful airline perks, including a $200 annual United TravelBank credit, two free checked bags and discounts on award flights, without the hefty annual fee of a premium airline card.

But with a $350 annual fee, the Quest isn't necessarily right for everyone.

Here's who I think can get the most value from the card and who might be better off with another option.

Related: I just changed my airline loyalty — here's how the United Quest Card sealed the switch

New United Quest cardholders can currently earn 500 PQP after their first purchase and 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, you can earn another 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, which peg United miles at 1.2 cents apiece, the full 90,000-mile bonus is worth $1,080. That's not including the additional value of the 500 PQP, which can help you get closer to United Premier status.

While not the strongest offer we've seen in the card's history, it's still a great time to apply if you've already been considering the Quest, particularly if you have upcoming United travel planned.

There's a lot to love about the . Here's who will benefit most from having the card.

If you fly United several times per year, you'll want to take a closer look at the Quest.

That’s because many of the card’s most valuable perks are tied directly to flying United. Cardholders receive:

One of the card's strongest perks is its earning structure. The United Quest earns a strong 10 total miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights as a United MileagePlus member — that's a whopping 12% return, according to TPG's valuations (mileage earning may differ for basic economy and base option tickets).

As someone who holds Premier Silver status, I can earn a total of 12 miles per dollar spent on eligible United flights when using my Quest, which is an even better return.

But what I find especially valuable are the discounts United cardholders now receive when booking award flights. Eligible United cardholders without Premier status save at least 10% on qualifying United-operated award flights, while cardholders with Premier status save at least 15%.

I take advantage of these discounts pretty regularly. Recently, I booked two tickets from Washington, D.C.'s Dulles International Airport (IAD) to London's Heathrow Airport (LHR) for a mother-daughter trip to Europe. Thanks to my cardholder discount, each ticket cost just 34,000 miles plus $11.20 in taxes and fees, rather than 45,000 miles plus taxes and fees.

That's a savings of 11,000 miles per ticket, or 22,000 miles total, worth $264 according to TPG's valuations.

The Quest also offers two additional award flight discounts: 10,000 miles beginning with your first card anniversary and another 10,000 miles after spending $20,000 on purchases in a calendar year.

I recently used my 10,000-mile award flight discount toward a transatlantic flight from Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS) to IAD. The flight would have cost 34,000 miles, but the credit brought it down to just 24,000 miles plus $112.83 in taxes and fees.

That's another $120 worth of miles saved, based on TPG's valuations.

Between the cardholder award pricing discounts and the annual award flight credits, the Quest gives me several ways to stretch my United miles further, which is why it's a card I plan to keep in my wallet long-term.

Related: United unveils huge MileagePlus shake-up, rewarding cardholders with higher earn rates

This is one of the most underrated — and potentially most valuable — perks of the United Quest Card.

The card includes two free checked bags for you and a companion on the same reservation. On domestic economy flights, United typically charges $50 ($45 if prepaid) for the first checked bag and $60 ($55 if prepaid) for the second bag.

That means you could pay up to $110 per person each way if you check two bags without a card benefit.

If you and a companion each check two bags round-trip on just one domestic flight, that could cost up to $440 total. That alone covers the Quest Card’s $350 annual fee.

Personally, I frequently fly United and regularly check two bags free thanks to my Quest Card. For travelers who often travel with a companion, don’t pack light, take longer trips or occasionally travel with bulkier items like skis or golf clubs, this benefit alone can justify holding the card year after year.

Related: These 27 credit cards can get you free checked bags on your next flight

Each account anniversary, the Quest Card provides $200 in United TravelBank cash. This credit can be used toward United-operated flights and is automatically deposited into your TravelBank account.

I recently used my $200 TravelBank credit to offset the cost of a round-trip flight from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to IAD to visit family. The ticket originally cost $560, but my TravelBank credit brought my out-of-pocket cost down to $360.

And the TravelBank credit isn't the only statement credit available with the Quest.

Cardholders can also receive other statement credits, including:

I wouldn't go out of my way to use a credit just to justify the card's annual fee, but if you're already spending money with these merchants, they can provide some additional savings.

For me, the TravelBank credit is the easiest to use. When you subtract its $200 value from the Quest's $350 annual fee, that leaves an effective cost of $150 — assuming you can use the credit in full — before factoring in free checked bags, award flight discounts and other benefits.

If you're working toward United Premier status, the Quest Card can also help you get there.

Cardholders can earn 1 PQP for every $20 spent on purchases with the card, up to 18,000 PQP per calendar year.

Those PQP count toward United Premier status qualification, potentially helping you close the gap to your next status tier.

Plus, beginning in 2027, eligible United cardholders will receive a head start on status qualification. United will deposit PQP equivalent to 5% of the amount required for their current Premier status tier into their accounts at the start of the year. That means Premier Silver members, for example, will receive a 300-PQP boost.

I earned United Premier Silver status for the first time last year, and I've already secured it again for next year, thanks in part to the PQP boost I received at the beginning of the year and the PQP I've earned through flying and spending on my Quest.

I generally don't put much spending on the card outside of United purchases, since I have other cards that earn more flexible rewards on everyday expenses. However, I did intentionally increase my Quest spending over the past few months to earn the additional PQP I needed to secure Silver for another year.

For me, that was worth it because I regularly fly United and appreciate the benefits that come with Premier status.

Of course, I wouldn't recommend putting unnecessary purchases on a card just to earn PQP. But if you're already close to qualifying for status, the Quest can give you another way to get there.

The United Quest Card is a strong step up from the (see rates and fees) — especially for travelers who fly United more than once or twice per year.

The Explorer is a great entry-level option, with a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year (then $150) and useful perks like a free checked bag and two one-time United Club passes each year. For occasional United flyers, that may be all you need.

But if you’re booking multiple United flights annually and check bags or redeem miles, the Quest’s incremental perks can quickly outweigh the difference in annual fees and deliver stronger long-term value.

In short, the Explorer fits the occasional flyer. The Quest is designed for frequent United travelers who can maximize its recurring value.

While the is packed with benefits for United fans and frequent travelers, there are a few reasons why the card might not be the right fit. Let's take a deeper look at who the card isn't the right fit for.

While the United Quest Card has many travel-related benefits, it does not come with any lounge privileges, and you don’t get any guest passes.

If lounge access is a priority, the (see rates and fees) may be a better fit. It includes a United Club membership as part of its annual fee, which grants access for the primary cardholder and eligible guests.

And for those who don't want to pay the United Club's steep $695 annual fee, remember that the offers two guest passes annually for a much more approachable fee ($0 introductory; $150 after the first year).

That said, not everyone needs airline-specific lounge access. For example, I personally get lounge access through the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, so I don’t need the Quest Card to provide that benefit.

While the number of Capital One lounges is limited, the Venture X also includes a Priority Pass lounge membership (at participating lounges), so I rarely feel short on options.

If you also already have lounge access through another premium travel card, the lack of United Club access here may not matter.

Related: Is the United Club Card annual fee worth it?

The United Quest Card is subject to Chase’s 5/24 rule. If you’ve opened five or more personal credit cards across all issuers in the past 24 months, you’re unlikely to be approved.

If you’re currently over 5/24, you may need to wait — or consider a card from another issuer.

Related: Chase's 5/24 rule: Everything you need to know

The United Quest Card earns United MileagePlus miles. If you don’t regularly fly United — or you prefer more flexibility in how you redeem your rewards — a transferable points or miles card could be a better option.

Flexible points and miles can typically be transferred to multiple airline and hotel partners or redeemed in other ways, giving you more options.

Two strong alternatives with significantly lower annual fees include:

If you value flexibility over airline-specific perks, one of those cards may be a better long-term fit.

If you fly United multiple times per year, check bags regularly and can easily use the $200 annual TravelBank credit, the United Quest Card’s ongoing perks can quickly offset much of its $350 annual fee.

However, if you prioritize lounge access, prefer flexible points or miles over airline-specific miles or only fly United occasionally, another card — either within United’s lineup or outside of it — may be a better fit.

Ultimately, the Quest Card shines for travelers who are loyal enough to United to benefit from its airline perks but don’t need the full premium treatment of a club membership.

#6167. Aer Lingus Pilots Threatened With Criminal Charges Over Bomb Threat Diversion

Last week, I covered how dozens of flights across Europe were faced with bomb threats. It was clearly a hoax, but these have to be taken seriously, and we saw all kinds of diversions, flight cancelations, and more.

Europe’s largest union representing pilots is now sharing the details of an incident that happened with one of these diversions, whereby an Aer Lingus flight was forced by fighter jets to divert to a French military base. When the pilots weren’t comfortable doing so, they were reportedly threatened with criminal charges.

This incident happened on Thursday, November 5, 2026, and involves Aer Lingus flight EI402, scheduled to operate from Dublin (DUB) to Rome (FCO). The Airbus A320 with the registration code EI-DEH took off at 6:40AM local time, and made its way southeast toward Rome.

The A320 flew for around an hour, and made it just past Paris, when the plane changed heading and prepared to divert. French fighter jets had been deployed to escort the aircraft, and demanded that it divert to a French military base. Specifically, the plane diverted to Évreux-Fauville Air Base (EVX), located in Normandy.

The plane touched down there at 10:05AM local time, 2hr25min after it first departed (there was a one hour time change). Coincidentally, that’s basically the same flight time as it would’ve been to Rome, as the aircraft had to hold for an extended period of time.

The plane ended up returning to Dublin later in the day, departing at 4:59PM local time, and landing in Dublin at 5:20PM local time, after a flight time of 1hr21min. So passengers spent nearly 12 hours on the plane, only to end up back where they started. Man, that’s rough, especially when you consider these A320s don’t have power ports, Wi-Fi, etc.

Here’s where the story gets really interesting, as explained by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), which represents over 44,000 pilots across Europe, including pilots at Aer Lingus. The union is expressing serious concerns about how this incident was handled.

What happened is that the Aer Lingus pilots didn’t want to divert to Évreux-Fauville Air Base, because they didn’t have the necessary operational information and aeronautical charts to land there. They requested a landing at another airport, but were rejected. According to the pilots, they were even threatened with criminal charges if they didn’t divert to the airport as requested.

That’s the point on which the union is sounding the alarm. Let me just quote the union on this:

As representatives of the pilot profession, ECA, IALPA and SNPL fully recognise and appreciate the assistance provided by authorities in responding to these threats and supporting flight crews in bringing their passengers and aircraft to safety.

However, reports indicate that, in certain circumstances, military aircraft have intercepted civilian airliners and directed aircraft commanders to land at specific airports without adequately considering aircrafts’ operational and safety requirements.

According to information received by IALPA, in one recent incident involving an Aer Lingus aircraft, military fighter aircraft directed the flight crew to divert to a military airfield for which they did not have the necessary aeronautical charts and operational information to safely conduct a landing. Despite the flight crew seeking an alternative and more suitable diversion airport, their request was refused.

ECA, IALPA and SNPL are also alarmed by subsequent reports that the pilots were apparently faced by the prospect of possible criminal prosecution for actions that were, at all times, aimed at protecting their passengers, crew and aircraft.

The union emphasizes that the captain of a flight should have the ultimate responsibility for the safety of passengers, crew, and the aircraft, and that the captain is uniquely positioned to assess the operational circumstances and determine the safest course of action, taking account of all relevant factors, including aircraft performance, available aeronautical information, airport suitability, operational limitations, and the availability of emergency assistance on the ground.

The union points out how the prospect of criminal prosecution against pilots exercising their professional judgment in such circumstances risks undermining aviation safety, and the effective cooperation between flight crews and authorities.

An Aer Lingus A320 was recently forced to divert to a military base in France, after the aircraft faced a bomb threat (which also impacted dozens of other flights). Fighter jets reportedly demanded the plane divert to this airport despite objections from the pilots, who felt they didn’t have sufficient operational information and aeronautical charts to land there.

The union representing pilots claims that the pilots were threatened with criminal charges if they didn’t divert there, which the union believes undermines the responsibility that pilots should have over the safety of their aircraft.

I fully side with the pilots and union here. It’s silly to me that a bomb threat that’s an obvious hoax puts pilots in a situation where they don’t feel comfortable landing at, with no alternatives offered.

What do you make of this Aer Lingus pilot situation?

#6166. America Needs an Arsenal of Democracies

We must combine American and allied innovation and manufacturing to take on the threats we share.

A worker along the assembly line handles large caliber 155mm metal projectiles at the Scranton Army Ammunition Plant in Scranton, Pa., April 16, 2024.

An Israeli-developed missile is now rolling off an American production line. On October 9, Raytheon-Rafael Protection Systems, an American Israeli joint venture, announced the first Tamir interceptors manufactured in Camden, Ark. They are intended for Israel’s Iron Dome missile-defense system, with plans to produce a U.S. variant for the Marine Corps.

The Camden facility builds on decades of allied weapons production, including the AIM-9 Sidewinder air-to-air missile with West Germany as well as the F-16 with multiple partners. But today’s conflicts require an industrial network that produces weapons at scale, maintains deliveries during disruptions, and replenishes forces across theaters. Co-production alone does not deliver that. It changes where a weapon is built; resilience depends on whether production can continue when something breaks.

#6165. Elizabeth Warren May Team Up With Trump On A 10% Credit Card Interest Cap—Putting Your Credit And Rewards At Risk

Both Elizabeth Warren and President Trump want to cap credit card interest rates, even as AI pushes long-term interest rates higher. And Warren is making a full court press to work with the President to make this happen. Donald Trump and J.D. Vance, and Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, actually agree on a lot of economics. They share the same distrust of markets, dislike of market outcomes, and generally lean into the same government interventions. “Horseshoe theory” suggests the political spectrum bends into a U, with supposedly opposing ends becoming closer to each other than their labels would suggest. National conservatives and progressive populists both argue that powerful interests have rigged the economy, that international competition has harmed American workers, and that government should dictate outcomes. Their constituencies are different and who they want to benefit are different but their economics are often the same. Here’s Warren saying she wants to work with the President on their shared goals. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) says she wants to work with President Trump to cap credit card interest rates at 10% and Democrats “have the bills ready to go” to work with the president. “We got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price gouging, on protecting our rural hospitals, on making sure people have access to healthcare,” she says. “…We got a lot of ways to deliver for the American people, whether Donald Trump wants to be a part of it or not.” — Face The Nation (@FaceTheNation) November 8, 2026 The economic illiteracy here is downright dangerous. Limits credit availability. Unsecured credit is expensive for a reason. Default risk, fraud, and card servicing mean that rates actually need to be higher to offer the product to most people. You’ll have fewer credit applications approved, reduced credit lines, and closed accounts – focusing on the riskiest borrowers. It’s only better-credit borrowers who might still get credit. Forces people into worse products. The need for credit doesn’t go away, just the best options people have been choosing for credit. So they get pushed into payday loans, overdrawing checking accounts, pawn shops, etc. Drives up card fees. If issuers can’t charge current rates, they have to generate revenue in fees – annual fees, balance transfer fees, etc. Bad for the economy. Unsecured credit makes transactions easy and frictionless. Less credit means fewer transactions, less economy activity. Destroys rewards programs. When products aren’t profitable there’s little reason to incentivize transactions. Better rewards cards often rebate the full value of merchant swipe fees to the consumer, spending on rewards in search of consumers who will revolve balances. When that’s not profitable anymore, the card programs no longer make sense. And that also hurts airlines, makes flights less profitable, and there’ll be fewer flights and at higher cost. Increases market concentration. Thin-margin card issuers and smaller players get pushed out, while larger issuers can cross-sell products and operate more efficiently surviving longer. Credit cards are a very competitive space (and if they could make money at 10% APR, they’d do it to win business). But this competition will erode under an APR cap. Hurts credit scores. As credit limits get cut, credit utilization spikes which drives down credit scores. That also makes other borrowing (auto, mortgage, even insurance pricing in some states) more expensive. In the most simplistic thinking, ‘stuff is unaffordable’ so we’ll ‘pass a law that says it should be more affordable.’ But that’s not how policy works. You don’t get to dictate outcomes, just the rules of the game, and that leads to outcomes including unintended consequences. Here, it’s almost as though those outcomes are intended because they’re so obvious. Donald Trump and J.D. Vance, and Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, actually agree on a lot of economics. They share the same distrust of markets, dislike of market outcomes, and generally lean into the same government interventions.

“Horseshoe theory” suggests the political spectrum bends into a U, with supposedly opposing ends becoming closer to each other than their labels would suggest. National conservatives and progressive populists both argue that powerful interests have rigged the economy, that international competition has harmed American workers, and that government should dictate outcomes. Their constituencies are different and who they want to benefit are different but their economics are often the same.

Here’s Warren saying she wants to work with the President on their shared goals.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) says she wants to work with President Trump to cap credit card interest rates at 10% and Democrats “have the bills ready to go” to work with the president.

“We got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price gouging, on protecting our rural hospitals, on making sure people have access to healthcare,” she says. “…We got a lot of ways to deliver for the American people, whether Donald Trump wants to be a part of it or not.”

— Face The Nation (@FaceTheNation) November 8, 2026

The economic illiteracy here is downright dangerous.

Limits credit availability. Unsecured credit is expensive for a reason. Default risk, fraud, and card servicing mean that rates actually need to be higher to offer the product to most people. You’ll have fewer credit applications approved, reduced credit lines, and closed accounts – focusing on the riskiest borrowers. It’s only better-credit borrowers who might still get credit.

Forces people into worse products. The need for credit doesn’t go away, just the best options people have been choosing for credit. So they get pushed into payday loans, overdrawing checking accounts, pawn shops, etc.

Drives up card fees. If issuers can’t charge current rates, they have to generate revenue in fees – annual fees, balance transfer fees, etc.

Bad for the economy. Unsecured credit makes transactions easy and frictionless. Less credit means fewer transactions, less economy activity.

Destroys rewards programs. When products aren’t profitable there’s little reason to incentivize transactions. Better rewards cards often rebate the full value of merchant swipe fees to the consumer, spending on rewards in search of consumers who will revolve balances. When that’s not profitable anymore, the card programs no longer make sense. And that also hurts airlines, makes flights less profitable, and there’ll be fewer flights and at higher cost.

Increases market concentration. Thin-margin card issuers and smaller players get pushed out, while larger issuers can cross-sell products and operate more efficiently surviving longer. Credit cards are a very competitive space (and if they could make money at 10% APR, they’d do it to win business). But this competition will erode under an APR cap.

Hurts credit scores. As credit limits get cut, credit utilization spikes which drives down credit scores. That also makes other borrowing (auto, mortgage, even insurance pricing in some states) more expensive. In the most simplistic thinking, ‘stuff is unaffordable’ so we’ll ‘pass a law that says it should be more affordable.’ But that’s not how policy works. You don’t get to dictate outcomes, just the rules of the game, and that leads to outcomes including unintended consequences. Here, it’s almost as though those outcomes are intended because they’re so obvious. #6164. United Airlines To Finally Bring NEXT Cabin Retrofits To Its 21 Boeing 757-300s

United Airlines plans to modify its Boeing 757-300 fleet to the United Next cabin standard, bringing seatback entertainment, larger overhead bins, and refreshed interiors to 21 aircraft that average roughly 24 years old. The plan surfaced in a post on Tuesday by aviation analyst JonNYC, who quoted United’s modification notice describing the work. The 757-300 has been the most visible holdout in a program that has already transformed much of the airline’s narrowbody fleet.

The scope is broad. According to the notice, the aircraft will receive new Boeing Space Bins, Panasonic Audio Video On Demand, inflight entertainment at every seat, a full-cabin in-seat power system, new class dividers and cabin headers, and updated United branding, while all seats and monuments will be refreshed. United has not published a schedule, and travelers may continue to face the old cabin until modifications are completed.

Entertainment will be the most noticeable shift for passengers. The 757-300 currently relies on entertainment streamed to a passenger’s own device. That arrangement dates to an earlier reconfiguration, when DIRECTV seatback screens were removed in favor of streaming and power outlets were limited to rows 1 through 23. Installing screens and universal power therefore reverses a cost-saving decision, and one trade publication notes the plan reverses an earlier cabin approach that removed seatback screens from domestic aircraft.

Storage should improve as well. Existing bins are relatively small and often require passengers to place standard carry-on bags sideways. The replacement Space Bins are designed to hold more bags, although whether the 757-300 versions would match that capacity has not been confirmed. Cabin density is unlikely to change, since each aircraft is configured with 234 seats, a layout United adopted when it added 21 economy seats and kept 24 in first class under a plan reported in 2016.

Certification was the main obstacle. The larger bins were not previously certified for the 757, and United had to lead the certification effort because few carriers still fly the -300 model. Delta Air Lines is the only other US operator of the type. A small global fleet offers little incentive for a supplier to fund engineering work, which explains why the program reached the 757-300 only after the Airbus and 737 variants.

16.3 inches - 17.3 inches (41 cm - 44 cm)

Retrofit economics also shaped the timing. United’s broader United Next program dates to a June 2021 announcement that projected 99% completion by summer 2025. That target slipped, and the airline reported in March that 70% of its narrowbody retrofit plan was complete. Against that backdrop, a 21-aircraft subfleet needing bespoke certification naturally fell to the end of the queue.

United has reshaped its premium transcontinental plans as the MAX 10’s role pivots toward a higher density domestic workhorse.

Spending on cabin hardware generally implies an airline expects to keep an aircraft flying. Some members of the aviation community will interpret the work as a sign that United sees a continuing role for the 757-300 for many years. That view sits somewhat uneasily with earlier expectations. The A321neo and 737 MAX 10 are intended to replace the type, so the retrofit may serve as a bridge while those deliveries arrive, rather than a permanent commitment.

The routes involved are significant. The 757-300s have flown San Francisco to Chicago, Los Angeles to Washington Dulles, and Los Angeles to Chicago. All those routes are long, high-demand domestic markets where inconsistent product is most noticeable to premium customers. Standardizing the cabin also simplifies the airline’s marketing, since customers booking a United narrowbody will more reliably receive the same amenities.

It is important, though, to treat the details as reported rather than formally announced, as United has not confirmed the work yet. The primary source is JonNYC’s post, which reproduces what appears to be United’s internal modification language, and the airline has not issued a public release with dates, aircraft counts per quarter, or final bin specifications. Until it does, the scope is clear, but the timeline is not.

#6163. End Of An Era: Hong Kong’s Iconic “Symphony Of Lights” Show Ending

Hong Kong is one of my favorite cities in the world. When I think of Hong Kong, the beautiful waterfront and skyline on both sides of Victoria Harbour come to mind. Along those lines, a nightly staple of the waterfront is coming to an end, and I’m sad about it…

Since 2004, Hong Kong has had the “Symphony of Lights” show every single night at 8PM, lasting for around 10 minutes. It holds the Guinness World Record for being the world’s largest permanent light and sound show, as it involves dozens of buildings.

It’s one of the things that contributes to Hong Kong’s electric energy, as you have a sea of people lining up on the waterfront (typically on the Tsim Sha Tsui side, though sometimes also on the Central side) every night to watch it.

Well, after 22 years, the Symphony of Lights will be coming to an end. The last show is expected to take place on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. To mark the end of the era, the final show will feature special pyrotechnics and fireworks.

Why has Hong Kong decided to end the nightly Symphony of Lights show? Officially, it’s a strategic shift in the city’s tourism and event strategy, described as being driven by shifting visitor habits, diminishing appeal, high maintenance costs, and a pivot to seasonal attractions. We’re told that we can expect “something new” in the future, but it doesn’t sound like it’ll be a full replacement for the Symphony of Lights.

I must admit, I’m sad to see this change in Hong Kong. No matter how often I visited Hong Kong, I always made a point of watching the Symphony of Lights, and always found it to be so enjoyable. Hong Kong has one of the world’s most gorgeous skylines, and the nightly show just took that to the next level.

I am curious what the backstory here is. Was the cost of operating this really so high, in the scheme of things? While I can in theory appreciate the concept of diminishing appeal, the nightly show always had a crowd in the thousands waiting to enjoy it — that was true 20 years ago when I first visited Hong Kong, and it was also true when I visited earlier this year.

Hong Kongers will soon have to bid farewell to the Symphony of Lights, the iconic nightly show that has been lighting up the city’s skyline since 2004. Officially, this change is described as being due to shifting visitor habits, diminishing appeal, high maintenance costs, and a pivot to seasonal attractions.

I’ve enjoyed this show every time I visited Hong Kong, so I’m sad to see this development. The skyline is still incredible and leaves me in awe every time, but there’s no denying that the nightly show added just a little bit of extra sparkle.

What do you make of Hong Kong’s nightly Symphony of Lights ending?

#6162. American Airlines Plans To Bring Back First Class Mini-Meals On Shorter Flights—Starting With New York–Chicago

This is a very good change. A flight can take up much of your afternoon without crossing American’s 900-mile meal threshold, especially when you include getting to the airport, boarding, and a connection. A small meal makes first class more worthwhile.

JonNYC reports that American Airlines is bringing back light bites and mini-meals on 700–899-mile domestic first class flights, starting on NYC/ORD.

American used to have a service between a basket of packaged snacks and a full meal. Before the pandemic, shorter flights could get something plated that would tide you over.

In 2016 I reported plans for plated morning items, including yogurt and breakfast cake. And my 2018 menu coverage included Lite Bites cheeses with cracked black pepper cheddar, cave-aged cheddar, Appalachian Tomme, and smoked Gouda.

American’s mainline standard is a snack basket on 500–899-mile flights during meal times, with meals starting in the 900-mile range.

United actually raised its meal threshold from 800 to 900 miles in January 2024. American would be moving in the other direction, offering something more substantial on flights where Delta and United generally hand out snacks.

Alaska is still the standard to beat. They already feed passengers on shorter flights, and I’ve found their domestic first class food better than competitors’.

New York–Chicago is an obvious place to start. New York LaGuardia–O’Hare is about 730 miles, and New York JFK–O’Hare about 740. An expansion might include:

American also used to have meal “exception markets”: shorter routes that got meals for competitive reasons. My January 2020 service guide listed Chicago–Dallas, Chicago–Boston, Chicago–New York, Los Angeles–Denver, and LaGuardia–Atlanta, among others.

I like a broad 700–899-mile rule better than making customers depend on whether their particular city pair merits an exception, though the exception markets got real meals and some were even shorter like Chicago–Washington National at just 612 miles which still wouldn’ qualify for a lite bite under this distance band.

This does mean more work for flight attendants. Individual food service means preparation, distribution, and clearing, with less time to do it on a shorter flight. American is also adding first class seats to some of its aircraft.

The airline’s product turnaround has been surprising, and surprisingly fast. They’ve introduced new business class suites, improved regional cabins and internet, upgraded coffee, and put money into lounges. They’re also reversing years of bad product decisions, including plans to bring back seatback screens and add more extra legroom coach seats.

Their returning coach food reservation program, announced with an initial Dallas–Fort Worth–Los Angeles test, should help passengers get the item they actually want. Mostly, though, I like that American seems to be loading enough food that there’s still something left when the cart reaches my aisle.

American has now announced the return of lite bites, with options including:

There will be two options onboard a given flight, with choices rotating “throughout the year.”

#6161. Buy Wyndham Rewards Points With Best-Ever 100% Bonus (0.65 Cents Each): Worth It?

Wyndham Rewards has launched its latest promotion on purchased points, which is potentially in line with the best-ever offers that we’ve seen from the program. This could be a great value for unlocking discounted award stays, as the program is offering up to a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire points for 0.65 cents each.

Link: Buy Wyndham Rewards points with a bonus

Between 12:01AM ET on November 11 and 11:59PM on December 31, 2026, Wyndham Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. The best offer appears to be for up to a 100% bonus, though you’ll have to log into your account to see what you’re eligible for.

With this offer, you can unlock the highest bonus if you purchase at least 3,000 points in one transaction. If you purchase 1,000 or 2,000 points, you don’t receive any bonus. If you purchase points, they’ll post to your account within 72 hours, and purchases are non-refundable. Purchased points don’t count toward Wyndham Rewards elite status.

Ordinarily you can buy Wyndham Rewards points for 1.3 cents each, before any discounts or bonuses, and that includes all taxes and fees.

If you maxed out the promotion and were eligible for a 100% bonus, you could purchase 400,000 points (including 200,000 bonus points) for $2,600, which is a rate of 0.65 cents per point.

This is the best bonus offer I ever recall seeing from Wyndham Rewards, so if there has ever been a time to buy points, this is it.

Wyndham Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 100,000 points per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been doubled, to 200,000 points.

When Wyndham offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s most commonly an 80-100% bonus. So this 100% bonus is at the very top end of that scale. However, personally I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Wyndham Rewards on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Wyndham Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending.

I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

Generally speaking, I only recommend buying points when you have a specific, short-term use in mind. In the case of Wyndham Rewards points:

More generally, there are definitely some properties where there’s value in outright buying points for the purposes of a redemption. Let me actually give a direct example, as I recently purchased some Wyndham points for a hotel stay, rather than booking with cash. I needed to be in Colorado Springs, and I booked The Mining Exchange Hotel, part of Wyndham Registry Collection (the hotel even has a Michelin key!)

The cash rate for a base room at the hotel would’ve been $307.57, inclusive of taxes & fees.

Meanwhile the hotel was charging just 30,000 points. At a rate of 0.65 cents per point, that’s like paying $195 for the stay, inclusive of taxes & fees. Not bad, eh?

Well, it gets better than that. Wyndham Rewards often lets you book premium rooms at no extra cost when redeeming points, so I was able to book a club room for the same 30,000 points.

If paying cash, that would’ve cost $438.54, inclusive of taxes & fees.

Now, the club rooms absolutely aren’t worth it, since you just get access to a pantry with some packaged snacks. But hey, if the cost is the same, I’ll take it. 😉

Wyndham Rewards has a four tier award chart, so free night redemptions will cost one of the following amounts:

While I wouldn’t say there’s widespread appeal to buying Wyndham Rewards points for these kinds of redemptions, there are some situations where the numbers will work out. Perhaps the best value would come in situations where you just need to buy a few thousand points to have enough for an award stay.

Wyndham Rewards has more than 9,000 hotels across 20 brands in 80+ countries. Some of the most popular Wyndham Rewards brands include Registry Collection, Wyndham Grand, Dolce, Wyndham, La Quinta, Wingate, Wyndham Garden, Ramada, Days Inn, Super 8, Howard Johnson, and Travelodge.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Wyndham Rewards points to be worth 0.6 cents each. Admittedly that’s a very conservative valuation, and there should be opportunities to get way more value than that.

Wyndham Rewards has one of the most complicated points expiration policies of any hotel loyalty program:

Wyndham Rewards partners with a variety of transferable points currencies, including Bilt Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, and Citi ThankYou. The catch is that transfers are at a 1:1 ratio, so I wouldn’t at all consider that to be a good redemption value.

That’s because you could be getting way more value from your transferable points than moving them to a program where points can be purchased for well under a penny each.

Wyndham Rewards also has a portfolio of credit cards issued in the United States, which are potentially quite lucrative if you frequent the brand.

Wyndham Rewards is offering up to a 100% bonus on purchased points, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.65 cents each. While I most definitely wouldn’t speculatively buy Wyndham Rewards points at this cost, there are some situations where the math works out, so everyone should crunch the numbers for themselves.

To those who are Wyndham Rewards fans, are there any properties you can get outsized value at with this promotion?

#6160. Why Russia Is Targeting European Freezers

Rearmament isn’t just for the battlefield — civil defense matters, too.

A woman walks past partially empty shelves at a SuperValu store in Blanchardstown, Dublin, Ireland, November 2, 2026.

Twice in the space of a few weeks, Russian hackers have managed to seize control of supermarket refrigeration systems in Europe. It began with hundreds of French stores in mid-October, after which, in early November, hackers struck outlets in Sweden, Belgium, Ireland, the Netherlands, and elsewhere. The hackers remotely forced freezers and chillers into prolonged defrost mode, driving temperatures to more than 120 degrees Fahrenheit and spoiling large quantities of food. These attacks have revealed an underrated aspect of rearmament that has so far been almost completely overlooked: civil defense.

Hackers behind most ransomware attacks demand payment. These hackers simply disrupted Europe’s food supply and left without a message. Only a few days after the most recent (as of this writing) attacks, in early November, did a Russian group finally claim responsibility. European policymakers who may have wished that some random teenagers were behind the attacks instead had their fears confirmed: This was a Russian attack against Europe’s food supply.

#6159. United Airlines Plans Seatback Screens And Bigger Bins For Aging Boeing 757-300s—Retirement Can Wait

United Airlines is planning a major cabin upgrade for its 21 Boeing 757-300s, bringing seatback entertainment, larger overhead bins and refreshed interiors to planes that average roughly 24 years old. American Airlines retired its last 757s early in the pandemic. United apparently sees enough flying left in these stretched jets to spend money on them. #6158. 5 Things Passengers Never Realize About How Airlines Actually Decide Who Gets A Premium Economy Upgrade

For many travelers, an upgrade feels mysterious. One passenger gets moved to a better seat while another remains in economy, even though both have airline status, travel frequently, or arrive at the gate early. The result is a long list of myths about how airlines choose who gets upgraded, with many passengers convinced that a friendly conversation with a gate agent or a smart outfit can make the difference. But the algorithm behind the upgrade is much more complex.

The reality is usually far less personal and far more data-driven. Airlines use sophisticated ranking systems that weigh factors such as ticket type, loyalty status, upgrade instruments, spending habits, and even credit-card activity. While the exact formulas vary by carrier, major US airlines such as United Airlines and American Airlines have published enough details for frequent flyers to understand how the process really works. Here's a closer look at five things most passengers never realize about how airlines decide who gets a premium economy or even business-class upgrade and why.

Many travelers assume that upgrades are determined entirely by how often they fly. However, airlines increasingly reward customers based on total spending, whether that spending occurs in the air or on the ground. Sometimes it means that one expensive long-haul flight will beat many cheap short-haul hops in the final decision for an upgrade. American Airlines is one of the clearest examples of this trend.

Within American's elite-upgrade hierarchy, status remains important, but it is not the only factor. The carrier uses Loyalty Points as a major tiebreaker when comparing passengers within the same elite tier. According to American's published upgrade policies and industry analyses, passengers who have earned more Loyalty Points in the previous 12 months may receive higher priority than those with fewer points, even if both hold the same elite status level.

That means a customer who spends heavily on an AAdvantage co-branded credit card may outrank another traveler who flies more frequently but accumulates fewer Loyalty Points overall. In other words, airline loyalty programs increasingly measure customer value through total engagement rather than simply miles flown. American outlines these upgrade priorities on its official upgrades page, while analysis from NerdWallet and One Mile At A Time explains how Loyalty Points influence upgrade rankings.

While booking tickets with your friends, you might notice that sometimes the ticket price isn't the same for everyone, and various factors drive price differences for passengers booking the same flights and class. This is because airlines use dynamic pricing and revenue management systems, so two passengers can pay different amounts for the same fare class. Ticket prices constantly change based on demand, booking date, remaining seat inventory, route competition, and predicted sales. A passenger who books earlier, or during a fare sale, may pay significantly less than someone purchasing the same fare class later. All these hidden processes may affect your chances of an upgrade later. Airlines track those differences through fare classes that you’re assigned during booking, represented by letter codes that most travelers never notice during booking.

On United, fare class becomes a critical tiebreaker when travelers share the same elite status and upgrade category. According to published United upgrade guidance, economy upgrade priority generally follows the hierarchy of Y, B, M, E, U, H, Q, V, W, S, T, L, K, and finally G fares. A passenger booked in a higher fare class, therefore, receives priority over someone who purchased a more deeply discounted ticket.

United Airlines Economy Fare-Class Upgrade Priority

While many travelers celebrate finding the lowest fare available, that discount can become costly when upgrades are processed. A full-fare Y ticket may cost considerably more upfront, but it often enjoys substantially better upgrade priority than a deeply discounted fare.

But why do airlines reward higher fares? From the airline's perspective, prioritizing higher fares is logical. The carrier wants to reward passengers who generate more revenue on a particular flight. The result is that two travelers with identical status levels can experience very different outcomes simply because one purchased a more expensive fare. Upgrade algorithms are designed to recognize that difference automatically.

The lesson is clear, as in the old saying “buy nice or buy twice”: the cheapest ticket may save money during booking, but it can significantly reduce upgrade prospects later in the journey. Or you’ll simply have to pay from your pocket to get an upgrade.

Many travelers view premium economy as simply a more comfortable version of economy class. In reality, airlines often treat it as a distinct cabin with its own place in the upgrade hierarchy, sometimes closer to business class than to standard economy.

United Airlines' Premium Plus product provides a clear example. According to published upgrade guidance, passengers already seated in Premium Plus generally receive upgrade consideration before travelers booked in standard economy cabins. Premium Plus fare classes such as O, A, and R are seated ahead of economy passengers when upgrades to Polaris business class become available.

This means premium economy offers much more than just a better seat. It serves as a stepping stone to the next cabin. For frequent travelers chasing premium-cabin upgrades, purchasing premium economy can therefore be a calculated strategy. The higher initial fare may improve comfort immediately while also increasing the odds of moving up to business class later.

Airlines structure these priorities because premium economy customers have already demonstrated a willingness to pay more than standard economy passengers. As a result, they often receive preferential treatment when limited upgrade inventory becomes available.

Emergencies, holding patterns and more. Tap any flight to follow it on the tracker.

Elite status remains valuable, but many travelers overestimate its power. One of the most misunderstood realities of airline upgrades is that passengers using miles, upgrade certificates, or other paid upgrade instruments often receive priority ahead of travelers waiting for complimentary upgrades.

United Airlines provides a good illustration of this principle. According to The Points Guy and Upgraded Points, travelers redeeming PlusPoints or mileage upgrades generally receive priority before those relying solely on complimentary elite upgrades. This creates situations in which a mid-tier elite member can leapfrog a higher-status traveler simply because they used miles or PlusPoints to request an upgrade.

From the airline's perspective, this approach makes sense. The carrier receives additional value when a customer redeems miles, applies upgrade certificates, or otherwise commits resources toward an upgraded seat. For passengers, it means the following: status matters, but willingness to spend points or upgrade instruments can matter even more. Many flyers who assume they are near the top of the list discover that numerous paid upgrade requests are ahead of them.

Perhaps the biggest misconception in commercial aviation is the belief that gate agents personally choose who receives upgrades. While agents certainly manage last-minute seat assignments, most upgrade decisions are made by automated systems, including AI-driven programs, such as Sabre Upgrade IQ™, long before boarding begins.

Airline reservation systems continuously evaluate passengers based on status, fare class, upgrade type, spending history, and numerous additional factors. Those systems automatically process upgrades as seats become available and rank travelers according to established priority rules.

Industry analyses of United's upgrade process note that automated clearing typically handles most upgrades until relatively close to departure. Only in the final hours before a flight do gate agents begin managing the remaining list directly.

Many passengers, therefore, place far too much emphasis on charm, appearance, or personal interactions at the airport. A polite conversation is always appreciated, but it rarely changes an upgrade queue that was generated by sophisticated algorithms days or even weeks earlier, sometimes even during the booking process.

Major Factors Airlines Commonly Use When Ranking Upgrade Requests

Paid, mileage, or certificate upgrades often rank highest

Higher-priced tickets receive better priority

Premium economy may rank ahead of economy

The modern upgrade process is fundamentally a data exercise. Airlines increasingly use automated systems to determine which passengers provide the greatest value and should therefore receive the next available premium seat.

Airline upgrades are far less mysterious than many travelers think. Behind every upgrade list sits a carefully designed algorithm that evaluates revenue, loyalty, spending, fare type, and upgrade instruments. Although elite status still matters, it is only one piece of a much larger puzzle.

Passengers who understand these rules gain a significant advantage. Buying premium economy instead of standard economy, using upgrade certificates, purchasing higher fare classes, or building Loyalty Points through credit-card spending can all influence upgrade outcomes more than many travelers realize. The next time an upgrade clears, or doesn't, the answer probably isn't luck. It's mathematics, data, and a ranking system that began working long before anyone arrived at the airport.
