#6157. Buy IHG One Rewards Points With 100% Bonus (0.5 Cents Each): Worth It?

IHG One Rewards is currently offering a limited time 100% bonus on purchased points. With this, IHG One Rewards members can purchase points for as little as 0.5 cents each. Is this a good deal?

While I wouldn’t recommend buying points without a specific use in mind, there are absolutely ways to get outsized value, and this is in line with the best offers that we see from the program. With the right strategy, this could be an opportunity to get a significant discount on an IHG hotel stay, and I’ll show exactly how.

Link: Buy IHG One Rewards points with this promotion with a 100% bonus

Between 12:01AM ET on November 11 and 11:59PM ET on November 15, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a bonus on purchased points. Points can be purchased in increments of 1,000 points, and the bonus is structured as follows:

Note that the purchase of IHG points doesn’t count toward elite status, and purchased points will post within 72 hours of an eligible purchase (though usually much faster than that).

Ordinarily you can buy IHG One Rewards points for as little as one cent each (the pricing isn’t linear), before any discounts or bonuses, and that’s inclusive of all taxes and fees.

With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 200,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 400,000 points at a cost of $2,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

While The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 200,000 points, pre-bonus.

When IHG One Rewards does offer a promotion on purchased points, the 100% bonus or 50% discount is the most common offer. A 100% bonus and 50% discount give you the same price per point, so you’ll typically pay 0.5 cents per point during a promotion.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

However, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through November 15, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

Do you plan on buying IHG points with a bonus?

#6156. Bank Of America’s No Annual Fee Card Pays 6% In Year One — Here’s The Best Way To Use It

The Bank of America® Customized Cash Rewards credit card pays 6% back in a category you choose during your first year, with no annual fee. That can include online shopping, phone and internet bills, or home repairs. Bank of America® Customized Cash Rewards‘ initial bonus offer is a $200 online cash rewards bonus after you make at least $1,000 in purchases in the first 90 days of account opening. I like finding worthwhile cards outside the familiar bank discussions. More competition is good, and a card can deserve some of your spending without replacing everything else in your wallet. What The Card Currently Offers The standard consumer card has: No annual fee. A $200 initial bonus after $1,000 in purchases within 90 days of account opening. 6% in your selected category during the first year: the normal 3% plus a temporary extra 3%. 2% at grocery stores and wholesale clubs. 1% on other purchases. The higher rates all share a $2,500 quarterly spending allowance; once you’ve used it, those purchases earn 1% too. Banking relationship bonuses can increase earning. For the choice earning category, you can select among gas and electric vehicle charging; online shopping, including cable, internet, phone plans and streaming; dining; travel; drug stores and pharmacies; or home improvement and furnishings. You can change your category once each calendar month for future purchases. Leave it alone and your selection carries forward. It starts out as gas and charging, so someone getting the card for online shopping needs to change that setting. Earning scales withBofA RewardsTM based on qualifying funds with the bank: Relationship Tier And Qualifying Balance Choice Category, First Year Choice Category, Afterward Groceries And Wholesale Clubs Other Spending / After Cap Not enrolled 6% 3% 2% 1% Member: no minimum balance 6.3% 3.3% 2.2% 1.1% Preferred Plus: $30,000+ 6.75% 3.75% 2.5% 1.25% Preferred Honors: $100,000+ 7.5% 4.5% 3% 1.5% Premier: $1 million+ 8.25% 5.25% 3.5% 1.75% The first three rewards columns remain subject to the shared quarterly spending limit. The banking program requires enrollment and an eligible personal checking account. Higher tiers generally use your combined qualifying average balances over three months. The relationship bonuses are 10%, 25%, 50% and 75%. They apply to the normal earnings, while the extra 3% first-year bonus isn’t multiplied. (At the highest tier the calculation is 3% × 1.75 + 3% = 8.25%, not 10.5%). Qualifying Merrill investments, including eligible retirement accounts, count toward the balance requirement. You don’t have to leave $100,000 sitting in a checking account. Online Shopping And Home Improvement Are My Preferred Categories For someone who already has good travel cards, I’d look first at purchases those cards don’t bonus. Online shopping would be my default selection. Bank of America’s category definitions include purchases through websites and apps, plus cable, internet, phone plans and streaming. Merchant examples include Amazon, Walmart, Etsy and Ticketmaster. That covers purchases across different merchants with one selection, and you can combine eligible shopping portal rewards with the cash back from paying by card. Online shopping has exclusions: taxes, insurance, medical bills, tuition, utilities and various non-retail services don’t become bonus purchases by paying on the website. Home improvement and furnishings. The bank includes qualifying contractors such as plumbers and electricians, alongside furniture and hardware stores. I’d keep online shopping selected most of the time and switch before paying for a repair or furniture purchase. Travel is useful, especially in the first year. The bank includes airlines and hotels, but also cruises, vacation rentals, attractions, transit and parking. You can book directly rather than going through a bank’s travel portal. That makes it worth considering for a domestic vacation rental or cruise payment. I earn well with other cards on airfare and hotels, but bonusing short-term rentals and cruises can fill a gap. How I’d Fit It Into A Travel Rewards Wallet I’d rate this 4 out of 5 as a spending category specialist for someone who can use the first-year offer or who qualifies for elevated banking rewards. It’s best for someone with online purchases or home improvement bills that otherwise earn an ordinary return. The standard card charges a 3% foreign transaction fee. This is for domestic purchases. And even the highest relationship tier pays just 1.75% on ordinary spending and after the cap, less than a straightforward 2% card. You can redeem cash back for statement credits without a minimum, or deposit it into eligible Bank of America or Merrill accounts. Checks, qualifying Merrill 529 contributions and automatic redemptions have $25 minimums. Rewards don’t expire while the account remains open. I’d take the cash. It can pay award ticket taxes, a hotel outside a chain, or anything else. #6155. Trump’s Amnesty Talk

President Donald Trump looks on as White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller speaks about birthright citizenship in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., August 6, 2026.

Vice President JD Vance warned in his famous post-midterm X post that Republicans would begin advocating for amnesty in the aftermath of the election. He was right, although he didn’t mention that the president of the United States would be one of them.

In a 60 Minutes interview over the weekend, Trump said he’d like to find a deal with Democrats to regularize the legal status of good, hardworking illegal immigrants. Whenever Trump has talked in these terms in the past, or mused about increasing levels of legal immigration, his restrictionist aides have — rightly — pulled him back.

This will probably happen again, given that the president has just made the ur-immigration hawk Stephen Miller his chief of staff. Even if Trump persists, it’s hard to see how there’d be any deal in the offing with Democrats who think they won, in part, on the excesses of the president’s immigration enforcement and have a chance for a trifecta in 2028 that could roll back his immigration agenda entirely. Are they really going to make concessions on enforcement or legal immigration numbers?

There’s no doubt that the administration’s immigration regime hurt among Hispanics voters and the general electorate as well, although not nearly as much as corruption, prices, and the Iran war. With a vast illegal immigrant population in the United States and limited enforcement resources, the administration has understandably looked to self-deportation as a force multiplier. If there are high-profile apprehensions and deportations, illegal immigrants see that and decide to go home on their own. This dynamic has clearly contributed to a notable diminishment in the foreign-born population in Trump’s second term.

The political problem is that everyone else sees those apprehensions and detentions and may not like them, especially if they are needlessly combative for the sake of cable-news coverage and internet clicks. This was the approach of former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, whose subtraction from the administration was a net addition. Border czar Tom Homan took over the immigration portfolio and has tried to avoid headlines, but enforcement has still been overwhelming based on apprehensions in public places.

What’s been missing is an emphasis on what our friends at the Center for Immigration Studies call bureaucratic or briefcase enforcement, the nuts-and-bolts work to track down, warn, and punish as necessary employers who hire illegal workers. Ideally, we’d have a national E-Verify system to instantaneously flag such workers. Still, there’s much that can be done with currently existing tools, and Homan himself favors deploying them.

If we squeeze illegal workers out of the labor market, it creates an incentive for them to leave, since so many came here looking for a job. At the same time, such largely invisible enforcement doesn’t generate occasions for demonstrations and turmoil in the streets.

Yet the president is an obstacle to adopting this tactic. He has sympathy for employers desperate for immigrant labor — since he was one himself — and influential business constituencies will balk at intense workplace enforcement. So, we have the president wildly swinging from supporting splashy actions targeting specific cities to talking about throwing in the towel.

At some point, when the illegal population is down substantially and there’s an enforcement system in place that can’t be ignored or gamed, there will be a case for amnesty for specific categories of illegal immigrants. We aren’t there yet, and we shouldn’t be thinking of giving up after one election loss. Vance implied that it was GOP quislings who would immediately turn to amnesty after the midterm drubbing, but, alas, the call is coming from inside the house.

#6154. Etihad Slashes Flights, Pulls Airbus A380 Off Two Routes (Including Toronto)

Etihad Airways has just filed a major schedule update for early 2027, impacting a couple of dozen routes. In isolation, you might not think much of this, as the first several weeks of the year have weaker demand in many markets. However, in light of what’s going on in Etihad’s commercial division, I can’t help but be curious if there’s a bit more to this, and wonder how things will evolve.

AeroRoutes reports on how Abu Dhabi-based Etihad has filed a schedule change for the first quarter of 2027, with most of the changes taking place for flights as of January 11, 2027. For the most part, the reductions are for around a couple of months, through March 2027. There are two ways to look at this:

The frequency reductions we’re seeing are pretty significant. Just to look at service to North America:

Specific to the A380, it seems that Etihad is taking the jet off the Toronto and Singapore (SIN) routes over that period, and it doesn’t seem like the super jumbo will be flying any other routes in place of that, at least based on current schedule filings. During that period, Etihad will only be flying the A380 to four destinations — Bangkok (BKK), London (LHR), Paris (CDG), and Tokyo Narita (NRT).

It’s a fascinating time for Etihad. Obviously Gulf carriers are having a rather difficult time with everything going on in the region at the moment, and it comes at a unique time for Etihad, as the carrier has been going through a massive expansion.

Now, I’ve been a bit skeptical about the claimed economics of this expansion, but Etihad management has insisted everything couldn’t be better… until Etihad Chief Commercial Officer Arik De recently “departed” the airline.

The can of worms that this departure opened is truly unlike anything I’ve seen at any airline before… and I’ve been following this industry for a long time. Seriously, check out the 520+ comments on my post about his departure, because employees have a lot to say. It’s so salacious that it has gotten OMAAT blocked in the UAE.

The point is, if even a quarter of the things are to be believed — and I’ve had some very interesting conversations with some formerly very high up people at the airline — then the carrier’s entire commercial strategy has been a bit questionable, to put it politely, and more about serving a certain someone’s LinkedIn profile ego, rather than actually developing a commercial strategy.

So with him no longer there, I’m curious to see how this all evolves. Let me emphasize that this is of course in no way a knock on all the hardworking employees at Etihad who have had to endure this “leadership” for too long. It seems like they now have quite the web to untangle, especially given the toxic people who are reportedly still there.

Etihad Airways has just filed a pretty big schedule change for early 2027, whereby a couple of dozen routes are seeing significant capacity reductions. Most notably, the Airbus A380 is being taken off of both the Toronto and Singapore routes.

In isolation, you might not think much of this, as demand is often a little lighter earlier in the year. But what I find interesting is that this follows a period of very rapid expansion, along with the carrier’s head of commercial strategy getting the boot.

Based on what I’ve heard from a countless number of current and former Etihad management employees, the strategy of the past couple of years hasn’t been as sound as a certain someone has tried to make it appear. We’ll see how this all unravels.

What do you make of this Etihad schedule change, and how do you see things playing out?

#6153. “Light Bites”: American Airlines To Reinstate First Class Meals On Flights Between 700-899 Miles

American Airlines is bringing fresh food back to First Class on selected shorter domestic flights, introducing a new menu of "light bites" on services between Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD) and John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) or LaGuardia Airport (LGA) in New York. The offerings include smoked salmon, whipped burrata, and poached shrimp, providing passengers with something more substantial than the packaged snacks traditionally available on these routes.

The change introduces a new, intermediate level of catering between snack-only flights and the full meals generally provided on services of 900 miles (1,450 km) or more. It also restores an element of American's pre-pandemic First Class experience, as US airlines compete to attract premium passengers through better seats, lounges, and onboard dining.

According to the airline's November 11 announcement, the 'light bites' will debut this month on flights linking the airline's Chicago hub with JFK and LGA. Passengers will be able to choose between two fresh options, with selections rotating throughout the year. Unlike American's standard First Class meals, the new dishes cannot be preordered, and the selections will only be available to choose from onboard.

The menu includes six potential breakfast dishes and eight lunch or dinner selections. Choices range from familiar sandwiches and fruit plates to more distinctive offerings, including tropical chia overnight oats for breakfast, and blackened chicken later in the day. The complete list of announced dishes is shown below, although only two options will be offered on any particular flight.

The initiative follows other catering improvements, including expanded Pecan Lodge barbecue offerings on eligible Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) departures, refreshed Main Cabin snacks, and enhanced Flagship Dining facilities at Los Angeles. American's Vice President of Culinary Strategy and Operations, Raphael Girardoni, described the new offering as an elevated experience on a popular route:

"We want to exceed the expectations of even our most discerning customers, and this new, more substantial menu offering is designed to do just that."

American's latest announcement marks a return to a service that first began more than a decade ago. In April 2015, the airline announced improved domestic First Class catering, replacing snack baskets with plated selections on flights of 700–899 miles (1,130–1,450 km). These included charcuterie, hummus with pita bread, and fruits and cheese, accompanied by warm nuts.

By 2019, American maintained a three-tier First Class catering structure for all domestic routes. This meant packaged snacks on the shortest flights, plated snacks on intermediate services, and full meals from approximately 900 miles (1,450 km). Longer flights received more elaborate service, while selected shorter routes qualified for full meals because of competitive considerations. The historical First Class catering arrangements illustrate how much the offering varied by distance.

Plated snacks introduced on 700–899-mile flights

Three-tier service retained, with exceptions for certain shorter routes

Pandemic-era reductions; packaged snacks became standard on shorter flights

Fresh Light Bites return on selected Chicago–New York flights

The pandemic brought substantial reductions to onboard catering, and the plated snacks previously available on shorter services largely disappeared. American's decision to restore them fits its wider premium investment strategy, as the airline seeks to improve the passenger experience beyond the seat itself.

DFW to LAX travelers get a reserved buy on board trial with wraps, snack boxes and fruit plates landing in October.

American's light bites offering will create a new distinction from Delta Air Lines and United Airlines. They typically reserve full First Class meals for flights of at least 900 miles (1,450 km), with packaged snacks provided on routes below that threshold. Some routes and departure times are exceptions.

Light Bites on select routes; snacks elsewhere

Alaska Airlines stands out by offering freshly prepared First Class meals on flights as short as 670 miles (1,080 km). Its Pacific Northwest-inspired menus include strawberry burrata salad and lemon pesto gnocchi, with up to five dishes available for preorder. Unlike American's new Light Bites, Alaska passengers can reserve their preferred food before departure, giving the airline an additional competitive advantage.

American could eventually extend Light Bites to other high-volume routes in the 700-899 mile range, such as Chicago–Dallas, Philadelphia–Orlando, or Miami–Nashville. For passengers spending several hours traveling, fresh food could make a meaningful difference to the premium experience. The question is whether American will restore this benefit across its full network, or keep it confined to selected competitive markets.

#6152. United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby Bans AI Agents From Booking Tickets, Doesn’t Want “Another Middleman”

“To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman.”

I get that they want to negotiate the terms before a new company gets between United and its customers. But United can’t just decide that customers will have to do the work themselves and expect that all customers will go ahead and do the work to buy tickets from United when it becomes easier just to buy from someone else. And writing a ban into a contract doesn’t mean United can actually identify an AI booking that comes through Expedia.

United’s November 11 contract of carriage revision adds AI agents to its prohibited ticketing practices. Rule 6.J.6 bans: The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product. The definition includes assistants accessing United through a travel agency or another intermediary. Human supervision or approval doesn’t circumvent that. And its Rule 5.H gives United the right to cancel reservations made, modified or serviced by these agents. The Wall Street Journal says agents can still present United flights and prices. AI research, followed by the customer making a purchase on their own, doesn’t run afoul of United’s rules. United Wouldn’t Know If An AI Agent Bought Through Expedia? Expedia already has a ChatGPT integration. It returns flight and hotel options with prices and availability. Expedia’s current instructions then send the customer to Expedia to complete the purchase. It’s not an autonomous purchase inside ChatGPT, but if an agent completes the purchase on Expedia United just sees an Expedia booking not how the booking was made. United says its systems can identify booking sources. Sure, but that is a non-sequitur. A contractual ban isn’t a technical one. United may push intermediaries to enforce the restriction, but there are lots of intermediaries out there. But we’ve seen airlines go to war with online travel agencies before, cutting off their own sales. The Strongest Case For United Is About Bargaining Power United may want to limit access to its sysems: The next middleman could become expensive. An assistant that decides which flights customers see can eventually demand referral fees, sell placement or favor suppliers that agree to its terms. Sam Altman says that if an AI does this, no one will trust it, and the stakes are too high to compromise trust for a travel commission. Someone has to own the mistakes. An agent can buy the wrong dates, misunderstand a fare restriction or cancel a ticket the customer wanted to keep. Agencies have commercial arrangements for ticketing and servicing. An AI assistant operating a browser may not bring the same accountability. And the law is evolving here. I’ve covered Delta’s own AI canceling a return flight it said it would preserve. Delta acknowledged a bug and restored the itinerary. Shopping consumes resources even when nobody buys. An agent can compare far more combinations than a human. The International Air Transport Association has examined the cost of growing search volumes. But United isn’t banning search, just completing the transaction. United can do this now, but it won’t last. The airline says agent bookings are still rare. That makes this a relatively inexpensive time to withhold permission. Every customer who gets used to buying another airline through an assistant becomes harder to win back. And the same customers most likely to use an AI assistant are the ones most likely to come over to United for Starlink. United has a hub in San Francisco. It’s ultimately not going to work for Scott Kirby to stand athwart history yelling “stop!” Customers Have A Reason To Hire The Bot United’s safety argument is weak. The federal hazardous-materials rule requires passenger notices, including at ticket purchase where practical and at check-in, and passenger acknowledgment in self-service transactions. It doesn’t require the customer to manually complete every other step of a booking. An assistant can stop and ask the passenger to review a disclosure or give a required confirmation. United’s definition still covers an agent whose actions the customer supervises and approves. Nor does accepting an agent have to mean giving unfamiliar software unrestricted use of a MileagePlus password. Visa is developing ways for merchants to recognize approved agents and connect their actions with customer and payment information. The customer’s time is part of the cost of buying a flight. If I can tell an assistant my dates, preferred airports, seat requirements and budget, there’s value in having it compare the choices and handle the purchase. Sometimes United’s schedule will be good enough that consumers will do the extra work. Sometimes another airline will offer a comparable trip and let an assistant finish it. We’ve already seen an airline overestimate its ability to make customers use its preferred distribution channels. American backed away from its plan to deny mileage earning on certain travel agency bookings. Customers didn’t all abandon the agencies and processes they preferred just because American wanted them to. There’s also an obvious reason airlines might dislike an assistant that works well for the passenger. It can compare the total price, recognize benefits the customer already gets from status or a credit card, and decline add-ons that aren’t worth buying. United has the worst value prop of any U.S. airline for basic economy! I’ve made the same argument about rewards credit cards: companies are excited about using AI to sell more, but customers get better tools too. It can compare the total price, recognize benefits the customer already gets from status or a credit card, and decline add-ons that aren’t worth buying. United has the worst value prop of any U.S. airline for basic economy! I’ve made the same argument about rewards credit cards: companies are excited about using AI to sell more, but customers get better tools too.

#6151. Cathay Pacific Orders 41 Airbus A330-900neos, As New Regional Workhorse

In August 2024, Cathay Pacific placed an order for 30 Airbus A330neos. There’s now an update, as the airline has just bumped this order by 11 more planes, meaning that there are now a total of 41 of these aircraft on order. Let’s take a look at all the details, and discuss what this means for fleet modernization at the Hong Kong based oneworld carrier.

Cathay Pacific now has a firm order for 41 Airbus A330-900neo aircraft, which are expected to be delivered between 2028 and 2035.

This follows an evaluation of the carrier’s mid-size wide body fleet renewal program, and it will enable Cathay Pacific to modernize its earlier generation A330-300 fleet, and expand its operations on high capacity regional routes. However, the airline is leaving plans for this plane open, and also emphasizes how the jet offers the flexibility to serve longer range destinations.

For those not familiar, the A330neo is the updated version of the A330, featuring improved range and fuel efficiency. The A330-900neo is the larger of the two new variants (with the other being the A330-800neo). The plane has a range of 7,200 nautical miles, plus a capacity for 287 passengers in a standard three cabin configuration.

I think it’s safe to assume that at least most of these A330neos will be equipped with the new Aria Studio business class product, which is expected to be retrofitted on select existing A330s in the coming months. This will finally see the carrier introduce a dedicated regional product with flat beds, which is exciting, though it’s not quite to the level of the long haul Aria Suite business class.

Here’s how Cathay Pacific CEO Ronald Lam described how the A330neo fits into the carrier’s fleet, back when the first 30 frames were ordered:

“The A330 is an aircraft type that has been serving Cathay Pacific well for nearly 30 years. These new aircraft will principally serve our regional destinations in Asia, while also providing the flexibility to serve longer-haul destinations as required. The improved fuel efficiency of these A330neos, together with their high standards of comfort, will enable us to further elevate the experience we provide for our customers while also contributing towards our goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.”

Cathay Pacific refreshing its short and medium haul fleet with the Airbus A330-900neo makes perfect sense, and is just about the safest, most expected aircraft order that Cathay Pacific could place. For context on Cathay Pacific’s fleet, the airline has:

Now Cathay Pacific’s fleet renewal plans are becoming a bit clearer, as the airline has:

So a decade down the road, you can expect that Cathay Pacific will primarily be flying A321neos, A330-900neos, A350s (-900s and -1000s), and 777-9s. That seems like a pretty logical fleet development plan to me.

Cathay Pacific now has an order for 41 Airbus A330-900neos, which the airline will primarily use to modernize and grow its regional fleet. The carrier already flies A330-300s, some of which are nearly 25 years old, so it’s logical that the airline would slowly be looking to replace these jets.

Cathay Pacific now has a pretty impressive (but not overly ambitious) order book, with A321neos, A330-900neos, and 777-9s, used for fleet renewal.

What do you make of Cathay Pacific’s Airbus A330-900neo order?

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

It's a question we've been diving deep into at The Points Guy this month (and something we've been debating for years now). Not only has it been harder to get upgrades and more expensive to earn status, but redemptions have gotten more expensive and watered-down benefits have made pursuing status less appealing for many of us at The Points Guy.

But not me. Despite my complaints, I'm still a fan of top-tier status and can't quit the hamster wheel, though I'm not trying for quite so many these days.

I've already requalified for World of Hyatt Globalist status this year, and I'll be able to requalify for top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage status. But I will also hold lower-tier status with United MileagePlus, Alaska Airlines' Atmos Rewards program and Delta SkyMiles.

In 2027, I'll continue to hold Platinum Elite status in IHG One Rewards and Marriott Bonvoy, as well as Hilton Honors Diamond status and Air Canada Aeroplan 25K status, just for carrying credit cards.

I even have top-tier status with Starbucks Rewards.

Here's the full breakdown of my elite-status plans for 2027, the credit cards I use to fast-track them, plus some tips to help you achieve your own status goals before the end of the year.

I've held top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage Executive Platinum status on and off for years now. I'm already getting closer to requalifying for 2027, and since the qualification year runs through Feb. 28, I have a few more months to work toward my goal.

So far, I've earned 148,538 Loyalty Points — the metric that AAdvantage members must accrue to earn elite status — toward the 200,000 Loyalty Points required to qualify for the Executive Platinum tier. Once I hit that threshold, I'll requalify for perks like a 120% mileage bonus, Group 1 boarding, complimentary food and drinks when traveling in the main cabin and more.

Related: 5 ways to earn more American Airlines Loyalty Points before February ends

Thanks to the airline's Loyalty Point Rewards milestones, I can also hit a few more reward tiers along the way to Executive Platinum status. For example, once I hit 175,000 Loyalty Points, I can choose from a menu of valuable benefits, including two systemwide upgrade certificates.

I'm likely to choose systemwide upgrades again, but the 25,000 bonus miles and the trip credits are probably the best alternate options.

I've already used two systemwide upgrades from coach to business class on AA's transcontinental flight from San Francisco to New York and back. I also just confirmed two more upgrades for upcoming international trips, including a flight to Paris from New York and another from London back to New York.

Holding the (see rates and fees) makes it easier to rack up Loyalty Points. This card helps me reach my status goal by netting me up to 40,000 additional Loyalty Points per elite status qualification year (10,000 bonus Loyalty Points after reaching 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points).

Related: How I booked Japan Airlines first class for just 80K American Airlines AAdvantage miles

Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards is now the only major U.S. airline loyalty program that lets you earn elite status from actual flight miles. That means you don't have to spend an outrageous amount of money to earn top-tier status (though you can choose to earn status via spending). Alaska Atmos Rewards members can now also earn points on award redemptions, which has driven my status earnings this year.

I've spent my Atmos Rewards points on award tickets flying Cathay Pacific within Asia and a flight from Seattle to Hong Kong in business class, a Hawaiian Airlines first-class flight from Honolulu to New York and an American Airlines flight from New York to Prague.

So far, I've earned the 40,000 status points required for Gold status this year through a combination of reward flights and spending on my . In addition to earning 1 status point for every $2 spent, with no spending cap, I also earn 10,000 status points each year on my account anniversary and 3 points per $1 on all foreign transactions with this card. This makes it worth the $395 annual fee, to me.

(Cardholders with the $95 annual fee earn 1 status point per $3 spent, also with no spending cap.)

While Alaska's partnership with American Airlines means I can fly Alaska flights with my top-tier American Airlines AAdvantage status, I'm considering pursuing an even higher Alaska status in 2027. One of the main reasons is that Alaska upgrades its top-tier Titanium members (and a companion) to business class on international flights on the day of departure. Those with status are also now eligible for complimentary upgrades on Hawaiian Airlines flights. I've gotten upgraded on Hawaiian a few times with my status.

I'm also putting a ton of spending on my Summit card now, since Atmos Rewards has a partnership with Bilt that gets you 3 Atmos Rewards points for every dollar of rent you put on the card.

All that spending could help get me a good chunk of the way toward top-tier Titanium status, which requires 135,000 status points. I need to make a decision soon about my 2027 focus, but I haven't been able to cut the cord with American Airlines and fully commit to Alaska... at least not yet.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Alaska Atmos Rewards elite status

Over the past few years, my status with Delta has been on a steep decline. I enjoyed several years as a Delta Diamond, but it's just become too expensive (28,000 Medallion Qualification Dollars, to be exact) to earn top-tier status.

I only qualified for entry-level Silver last year, which requires 5,000 MQDs. A friend threw me a bone and gifted me second-tier Gold status, which typically requires 10,000 MQDs, but I'm not on track to re-earn it for 2027.

So far, my total spending this year is just 7,338 MQDs. This includes 5,000 MQDs just for holding the and the .

The $650 annual fee (see rates and fees) for the Delta Reserve is steep, but it's often worth it for those chasing status. It's just not enough of a boost to get me even to Gold status.

The Reserve card does give 1 MQD for every $10 you spend on the card. Technically, you could spend your way to status, but there's no way I can put that much spending on my Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card. While I still like the card for all its perks, I'm no longer putting much spending on it.

While I am likely to drop down to Silver for 2027, I'll still fly Delta occasionally.

I've made great use of SkyMiles over the years. Last year, I lucked out with an award from Mexico City International Airport (MEX) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and then to Brisbane Airport (BNE) in Delta One. There was a brief moment when the flight was available for just 73,000 SkyMiles one-way. I jumped at the opportunity to fly in Delta One on the more-than-14-hour flight to Australia.

Despite being what I'd consider the least valuable airline currency, SkyMiles remain appealing, and I'll keep my Reserve and Platinum cards for the long term. I've gotten a lot of use out of the statement credits that come with holding the cards.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Delta Medallion elite status

I added another airline elite status to my collection in 2026: Air Canada Aeroplan 25K status, which I received simply for signing up for the (see rates and fees) and carrying the card. This would typically require earning 25,000 Status Qualifying Credits through the airline.

Unfortunately, I haven't had many opportunities to actually fly with Air Canada, and I've even let some of my valuable eUpgrade credits expire unused.

Still, I've become increasingly interested in the Air Canada Aeroplan program, especially because of its extensive network of airline partners and the ability to book some excellent business-class award flights through them.

One of my favorite redemptions using my welcome bonus on that card was booking a business-class flight on Emirates from Rio de Janeiro to Buenos Aires for just 56,000 Aeroplan points. It's a fascinating fifth-freedom route, and I was especially excited about the opportunity to finally experience Emirates.

I was also able to book Swiss Airlines business class from Cairo to Zurich and then on to New York for just 85,000 Aeroplan points.

Looking ahead, I'm particularly intrigued by Aeroplan's generous stopover rules. The program allows travelers to add a stopover of more than 24 hours on eligible international one-way award itineraries for just 5,000 additional points. That's an incredible opportunity to visit two destinations on a single award ticket.

Even though I haven't gotten much use out of my Air Canada elite status, Aeroplan remains one of the most interesting airline loyalty programs in my points-and-miles arsenal. I'm hoping to put more of those points — and perhaps some of those elite benefits — to work in the year ahead.

Related: How to redeem Aeroplan points for maximum value

Another new status for me is United Airlines MileagePlus Premier Silver. I actually did a status challenge with United late last year, and enjoyed a few months of top-tier United Premier 1K status, but I wasn't able to complete the challenge to unlock it for a full year.

Still, I've really enjoyed flying United more. It's easier to get to their hub at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) from my New York City apartment, and I ended up flying and earning enough this year to earn the entry-level United Silver status, which requires at least 6,000 Premier qualifying points or 15 Premier Qualifying Flights and 5,000 PQPs. (In 2027, United is ditching PQFs, making status eligible only through PQPs.)

Silver status allows me to get priority boarding, extra-legroom seats at check-in 24 hours before flying and standby for earlier flights.

During the brief window I had 1K status, I really enjoyed boarding ahead of Group 1.

Related: 5 last-minute ways to earn United elite status this year

More importantly, during my challenge I signed up for the (see rates and fees), which got me a good stash of United miles that I've used effectively.

I was able to spend just 85,000 United miles for a one-way business-class flight from Tokyo to Chicago and then on to Newark this year, and I've just booked another business-class flight from Sydney, Australia, back to New York for 85,000 United miles.

I've earned a total of 8,640 PQPs toward status this year, but I'm unlikely to earn the more than 3,000 more I'd need for Premier Gold before the end of the year. I think Silver status is just fine for me for now.

I've loved having top-tier World of Hyatt Globalist status again this year. I've been able to use suite upgrades at several stand-out properties this year, including the Grand Hyatt Kauai Resort & Spa in Hawaii, the Grand Hyatt Rio de Janeiro in Brazil and the Hyatt Regency Cairo West in Egypt.

Globalist benefits include guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, free breakfast and better upgrade odds.

This year, I've earned top-tier status organically with stays all over the world. I especially loved finally getting to check out the newly renovated Park Hyatt Tokyo and to stay at the Park Hyatts in Shanghai and Beijing.

While earning Globalist status requires 60 nights at Hyatt hotels per year, I've already stayed 79 nights this year. I may try to hit 90 nights in 2026, so I can earn another Milestone Rewards choice.

I also plan on keeping both my (see rates and fees) and my (see rates and fees) to help me get more elite nights toward status each year.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Hyatt stays?

I've also been putting Hyatt stays on my World of Hyatt Credit Card to earn 4 points per dollar spent at Hyatt hotels and resorts. You also earn two elite nights for every $5,000 you put on the personal card.

To me, World of Hyatt is the most valuable hotel loyalty program because I often get upgraded and never have to fight for late checkout. Hyatt points also stretch very far, especially compared with Hilton and Marriott. I already have trips on the books next year for Alila Villas Uluwatu in Indonesia, Park Hyatt Milan and Hyatt Paris Madeleine.

Related: How to redeem Hyatt points for free nights and more

Hilton Honors elite status is one of the easiest achievements to reach. Although I stayed at a Hilton hotel only a few times this year, I maintained Diamond status. How did I manage that? It's a perk of holding .

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning Hilton Honors elite status

The card comes with Hilton Diamond status for as long as you hold it. Despite a $550 annual card fee (see rates and fees), the card is still worth keeping.

There are other valuable inclusions, such as up to $400 to spend at Hilton resorts every year (up to $200 in statement credits from January to June and another up to $200 in statement credits from July to December), up to $200 in statement credits for eligible flight purchases (up to $50 per quarter) and a free night when you open the account and reach your annual card anniversary.

Last year, I used my free night at the chic Conrad Tokyo on a room that would have been more than $1,100. This year, I used it at the Hilton Tokyo in a room that went for more than $650 a night.

I used one of my $200 stay statement credits last year at the Hilton Tangier Al Houara Resort & Spa in Morocco, and the other at Resorts World Las Vegas. In past years, I've also used it at Hilton Cancun Mar Caribe All-Inclusive Resort and Hilton Hawaiian Village Waikiki Beach Resort in Hawaii.

I also use the airline fee credits regularly. When using the Aspire card to pay, you get up to $50 in statement credits for eligible airline purchases each quarter.

Thanks to this card, I've had Hilton Diamond status since 2020.

Related: No suite upgrade but charm aplenty: What it's like staying at one of Hilton's SLH properties as a top-tier elite

While I have had some nice stays at Hilton properties — including the stunning Conrad Bora Bora Nui — over the years, I've rarely been upgraded despite my Diamond status. Still, the statement credits alone justify keeping the Aspire card and my Diamond status for 2027, even if I don't have as much luck getting upgrades with Hilton as I do with Hyatt.

I will earn Platinum Elite status with Marriott again this year just for holding a credit card.

In the past, I've been content with the Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status I receive courtesy of the ; it gives status in several hotel programs, including Marriott Bonvoy (enrollment required).

Related: Guide to Marriott and Hilton elite status with the Amex Platinum and Business Platinum

Then in 2022, American Express surprised everyone by announcing that holders of the would get Platinum Elite status for as long as they hold the card. I jumped at the chance to apply for it. As a result, I've held Platinum Elite status since then.

I've spent more than two dozen nights at Marriott properties this year and having Platinum Elite status certainly enhanced my trips with benefits like guaranteed late checkout, lounge access and complimentary breakfast. I even got an upgrade at the Ritz-Carlton in Hong Kong.

I used the annual free night that comes with the Brilliant card two years in a row at the lakefront Hotel President Wilson in Geneva, Switzerland. Last year, I used it for London's Bankside Hotel.

Related: 30 best Marriott hotels in the world that you can book with points

So far, I've booked 46 Marriott nights this year. I won't try to get the higher Titanium status — which requires 75 nights — though the idea of opening the is intriguing. Each year you hold the card, you receive 15 elite night credits toward the next level of Marriott Bonvoy elite status.

At least for now, though, I'll keep the personal Brilliant card open and enjoy Platinum Elite status without worrying about how many nights I need to stay.

Related: Last-minute strategies to earn Marriott Bonvoy elite status

Like my other hotel statuses, I have Platinum Elite status with IHG One Rewards by virtue of holding its hotel-branded card.

Last year, I stayed at several memorable IHG properties, including the Kimpton Fitzroy in London, the InterContinental Porto in Portugal, the Kimpton Overland Hotel in Atlanta and the InterContinental Ljubljana in Slovenia. This year, I've checked into the Hotel InterContinental Bordeaux Le Grand and WM Hotel in Sai Kung (a Vignette property) near Hong Kong.

Despite staying only seven nights at IHG hotels in 2026, I will maintain IHG Platinum Elite status simply by holding the IHG One Rewards Select Credit Card (no longer open to new applicants). In addition to elite status, my favorite perk of this card is its free night award worth up to 40,000 points, which I've used at the Kimpton Armory Hotel in Bozeman, Montana, and the aforementioned InterContinental in Portugal.

The information for the IHG One Rewards Select card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The new version of the card is the (see rates and fees), which also provides Platinum Elite status. It also comes with a fourth night free on award stays and the ability to add points to your 60,000-point anniversary free night certificate (these perks aren't available on the Select card). The annual fee is $350.

I'll keep my IHG card for status (and a free night) again next year. I'm also sitting on a nice stash of points, so odds are I'll enjoy some great redemptions in the not-too-distant future — though I don't have any IHG stays planned so far in 2027.

Related: Last-minute strategies for earning IHG One Rewards elite status

The last status I'll mention is with Starbucks, since I'm a regular at the cafe near my apartment.

That regularity earned me top-tier Reserve status in the Starbucks Rewards program, which was overhauled earlier this year.

Reserve status earns 0.7 Stars more per dollar spent than entry-level Green status (for a total of 1.7 Stars per dollar) and requires earning an eye-watering 2,500 Stars over a rolling 12-month period to reach. That's 2,000 more Stars than necessary for the next-lowest tier, Gold.

It may not be the most rewarding program in the world — especially if you have a lower status tier — but the savings I get through the program add up and have me just as hooked on it as I am on my preferred hotel and airline programs.

Related: Why I got top-tier status with Starbucks and enjoy it — despite the reduced earnings for some

I've thought about going fully free agent and stopping my pursuit of status. But the truth is, I have fun on the hamster wheel, and the perks really make the game worth playing.

I'll have top-tier status with American, Hyatt and Hilton again next year. I'm excited to use more of my perks in 2027, and I will report back on my 2028 plans next year.

If you're considering going for status, you should really do the math to see if the extra costs are worth the benefits you get. It's harder to earn status these days, and the benefits keep getting whittled down. Don't do it unless you know you will use the perks and that you can do it without spending a small fortune.

It can be more cost-effective to get a credit card that automatically gives you some status perks, like free checked bags and priority boarding.

At least think about it. I'm not sure I'm the best at following my own advice.

#6149. ICE Checked 7 White Men’s IDs At The Airport—Then Arrested A State Trooper

Two ICE agents spent nearly an hour at the Madison, Wisconsin airport looking for a state trooper. Before finding him, they approached at least seven other white men and checked their IDs. Then they handcuffed the 21-year old officer, who had federal permission to work through 2030 and was flying to visit his parents. Newly released surveillance footage shows how the November 5 arrest unfolded. Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe was released the following evening after a Republican congressman contacted the Homeland Security secretary. He still faces immigration proceedings. They Went Looking For White People! In Wisconson! The two immigration agents wore baseball caps and hoodies, with no obvious identification on their clothing. They carried manila folders and consulted papers while looking for someone matching Van Der Merwe’s description. The agents approached seven white men visible in the recording, plus another person outside the camera’s view. The men generally looked young, wore everything from sweatpants to business casual, and mostly carried backpacks. They produced ID and were allowed to continue. Two uniformed deputies waited with the agents. Once their target arrived, he handed over identification, spoke with the agents and walked with them to the airport’s entrance doors. An agent handcuffed him there. Van Der Merwe explained that he had a work permit and a pending asylum application, and the agents said they “did not care.” The Government Had Authorized Him To Work Van Der Merwe’s parents brought him from South Africa in March 2019, when he was 14. His original admission permitted a six month stay. His attorney says the family applied for asylum and has spent seven years waiting for an interview. He’s included in his father’s application and holds federal employment authorization through 2030. According to his attorney, he wanted to join the military but couldn’t because of his immigration status. He earned a criminal justice degree at New Mexico Military Institute and went into law enforcement instead. He’s been with the Wisconsin State Patrol since July 13, 2025 He was work-authorized by the federal government but that’s also consistent with a visa overstay, as I explained when ICE arrested Southwest Airlines flight attendant Lorenzo Thompson at Nashville airport. A person can have an unresolved asylum claim, hold a valid employment authorization document, and still face removal proceedings. That’s a pretty upside down world, since the government said he could work here and should allow him to stay pending resolution of asylum – which he’s been waiting for the government to address for years. Homeland Security says Van Der Merwe overstayed his original admission. His lawyer says he’s followed the legal process and has been waiting for the government to decide his case. Federal law allows detention while a removal case is pending. Prior to the Trump administration, a work-authorized individual with a pending asylum claim was essentially considered to be in valid status, and ICE hasn’t alleged any separate crime. The government knows where he lives and works, in a role promoting public safety, so it’s not clear what benefit there is to taking him off a family trip and putting him in jail while his asylum claim remains unresolved. The President now says his approach to immigration has been too harsh. Q: You think your deportation policy went too far? Trump: I think it might be too tough. https://t.co/NKhFjZKxnd — Clash Report (@clashreport) November 8, 2026 Airports Make People Easy To Find TSA likely alerted ICE when he bought his ticket. A May 2025 agreement obtained by American Oversight formalized information sharing between TSA and ICE, including storage of information by ICE. As I wrote in July, passenger information collected for aviation security is being used to locate immigration targets. Homeland Security says it considers people unlawfully present “can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.” An airline reservation tells the government where someone plans to be and when. That makes an airport a convenient place to arrest them. But using TSA this way becomes a distraction from its security focus. We’ve already seen a U.S. citizen handcuffed while boarding Delta after being mistaken for a British man, and plainclothes agents abandon an attempted arrest at Las Vegas airport, leaving a traveler with a handcuff attached. Van Der Merwe went to jail and was released November 6 without posting bond after Representative Derrick Van Orden contacted Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Newly released surveillance footage shows how the November 5 arrest unfolded. Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe was released the following evening after a Republican congressman contacted the Homeland Security secretary. He still faces immigration proceedings.

In Wisconson! The two immigration agents wore baseball caps and hoodies, with no obvious identification on their clothing. They carried manila folders and consulted papers while looking for someone matching Van Der Merwe’s description. The agents approached seven white men visible in the recording, plus another person outside the camera’s view. The men generally looked young, wore everything from sweatpants to business casual, and mostly carried backpacks. They produced ID and were allowed to continue. Two uniformed deputies waited with the agents. Once their target arrived, he handed over identification, spoke with the agents and walked with them to the airport’s entrance doors. An agent handcuffed him there. Translation: I got my arse handed to me on Tuesday so we will take revenge but if caught: “the agents are at fault”.

And this is a surprise? Make a quota, get to stay a masked armed agent who can drag people off the street. And of course they didn’t care! “The New Yorker” just had an article about border agents who couldn’t take it anymore. Those who stayed just shut down and did what they were told. Maybe most governments run like that, but they do better having systems with some kind of sense and humanity.

There is no place for a secret police force in a so-called free country. Conservatives and libertarians once believed in limited government and personal freedom. That seems to be all forgotten in the race to see who can hate immigrants more.

The whole administration approach with quotas is just wrong.

Every administration has kicked the immigration law revisions can down the road.

The US is long overdue for a comprehensive and integrated immigration policy review and update.

Just another episode in the idiotic, nonsensical world of Trump. How about deporting Elon instead? He’s a far greater threat to this country than a state trooper risking his life to keep citizens safe.

@drrichard — “But, but… the leopards won’t eat MY face…” — That state trooper, probably.

Our immigration enforcement is out of control. Masked storm troopers roaming the streets and airports demanding “show me your papers” because they think you look like someone? It’s like out of some Cold War spy movie, except those goons aren’t masked.

And don’t claim that you have a big concern about “following the rules” especially if you think a man who sexually assaulted a woman in a department store dressing room and has 34 felony convictions should be President of the United States. Or if you hire gardeners, maids and other domestic workers without verifying their immigration status.

The money and effort expended in this indiscriminate, xenophobic hysteria makes no sense. Reform immigration and immigration enforcement.

And this is why I left some blood in Vietnam? “WHAT A COUNTRY”.

#6148. Delta Platinum Amex Card Review: Big Benefits & Strong Welcome Offer

The Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card is the second most premium personal credit card in the Delta SkyMiles and Amex co-brand card portfolio.

If you fly Delta several times a year and want perks like a companion certificate and the ability to spend toward elite status qualification, the Delta Platinum Amex is worth a look, and can easily be worth more than the fee. This post is my in-depth Delta Platinum Card review, so let’s get into all the details.

Link: Learn more about the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card

Before we get too deep into my Delta Platinum Amex review, let me give a quick overview of the card’s main features and fees:

I also put together my top pros and cons for the Delta Platinum SkyMiles Card:

Let’s cover the welcome bonus, eligibility details, and fees, of the Delta Platinum Card. After all, these are major factors that people consider when applying for cards.

The Delta Platinum Card currently has the following welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 90,000 Bonus Miles after you spend $3,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Card Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, SkyMiles are worth 1.1 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus is worth up to $990. While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have quite a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles.

The welcome offer on the Delta Platinum Card is “once in a lifetime,” so it’s not available if you currently have the card, or if you’ve had the card in the past. You’re also not eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had the personal version of the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more). However, you are eligible for this card if you’ve had any version of the business Delta Amex cards before.

One thing worth emphasizing is that if you’re going to apply for multiple personal Delta Amex cards, you’ll want to pick up the less premium cards first, and then work your way up. That way you’re potentially eligible for the welcome offers on each of the cards. Meanwhile if you start with the most premium card, you wouldn’t be eligible for the offers on the less premium cards.

You can read more about Amex’s general application restrictions here.

The Platinum Delta Amex has a $350 annual fee (Rates & Fees). You can add additional users to the card at no extra cost (Rates & Fees). As mentioned above, this is the second highest annual fee personal card in the Delta and Amex portfolio.

If you are going to put spending on the Delta Platinum Amex, the good news is that there are no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use the card abroad without paying high fees.

When applying for a credit card, the rewards structure is obviously a major consideration for people. With airline credit cards, the question typically comes down to both the miles offered on spending, as well as the ability to qualify for elite status with spending. How does the Delta Platinum Card do on that front? Well, among airline cards, I’d say it’s pretty competitive, so let’s cover those details.

The Delta Platinum Amex offers the following miles earning opportunities for spending:

Since I value Delta miles at 1.1 cents, I think this card offers a 3.3% return on its 3x miles categories (purchases made directly with Delta and directly with hotels), a 2.2% return on its 2x miles categories (restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets), and a 1.1% return on non-bonus spending.

The card has solid bonus categories for a co-branded airline card, but purely in terms of rewards for spending, I think there are still better cards out there for airfare purchases, hotel purchases, restaurant purchases, and grocery store purchases.

Nowadays, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status is earned exclusively based on how many Medallion Qualification Dollars (MQDs) you rack up. When it comes to earning MQDs through credit card spending, the Delta Platinum Amex can help you earn status:

For context, Delta SkyMiles Medallion elite status has the following annual MQD requirements:

If you’re serious about earning elite status with credit card spending, you’ll want to consider the more premium Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more) instead, since it earns MQDs twice as fast — you earn $1 MQD per $10 of eligible purchases, rather than $1 MQD per $20 of eligible purchases.

While Delta SkyMiles is far from my favorite mileage currency, it does have a high floor value, so there are good ways to redeem Delta SkyMiles. You can redeem SkyMiles for flights on Delta or SkyTeam partners, like Air France, China Airlines, and Korean Air. You can also redeem SkyMiles on airlines like LATAM and WestJet, which aren’t part of SkyTeam.

Partner award flights can be an especially good option if you focus on flights that don’t touch the United States, since flights that do are more expensive and get you less value for your miles. I’ve also seen some good award prices for Delta One (business class) awards, specifically for booking roundtrip rather than one way.

The Platinum Delta Credit Card has a nice welcome offer. In general, I’d say it could be worth putting spending on the card if you’re trying to earn Medallion elite status with Delta SkyMiles. For most people, the reason you’ll want to keep this card long term is because of the perks and benefits that it offers, which for many people will more than offset the annual fee. Let’s go over some of those benefits.

Every year upon renewal of your Delta Platinum Card, you can receive a Delta Main roundtrip companion certificate. You just have to pay the government-imposed taxes and fees for the companion. This is a great deal that can be worth significantly more than the annual fee in and of itself.

If redeeming the certificate there are some things to be aware of:

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you can receive up to $150 in Delta Stays credit annually. The way this works, you can receive $150 in statement credits per calendar year when you use your card to pay for a new Delta Stays prepaid hotel or vacation rental booking on the Delta Stays platform.

While I’m not usually a fan of using airline portals to book hotel stays and vacation rentals, this could prove worthwhile, as you can use it for a hotel stay costing right around $150, if you wanted to. If used right, there’s real value here.

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you receive up to $120 in rideshare credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on U.S. rideshare purchases with select providers. This is super easy to unlock, though admittedly the increments as such are quite small.

Just for having the Delta Platinum Card, you receive up to $120 in Resy credits annually (Enrollment required). The way this works, you can receive up to $10 in statement credits each month after using your card on eligible purchases with U.S. Resy restaurants.

Just for having the Platinum Delta Card you get a first checked bag free. With the ever-increasing cost of a checked bag with Delta, this can really add up.

Depending on how many bags you’re checking, a single trip could pay for the card’s annual fee.

You receive priority boarding just for having the Delta Platinum Amex. This helps maximize your odds of finding space for your carry-on and getting to your seat sooner. To receive this benefit, you’ll need to ensure the primary cardmember’s SkyMiles number is linked to the reservation (though there’s no need to actually pay for the flight with the card).

This benefit is valid for a total of up to nine people traveling on the same reservation with the primary cardmember.

If you have the Delta Platinum Card, then you can save 20% in the form of a statement credit for eligible pre-purchased meals, and in-flight purchases of food, alcoholic beverages, and audio headsets, on Delta flights. Allow 8-12 weeks for the statement credit to post.

The Platinum Delta Amex offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit. This benefit applies once every four years for the application fee for TSA PreCheck or Global Entry. This can save you time both at security and immigration, and is something I highly recommend signing up for if eligible. (Enrollment required)

Delta has a Pay With Miles feature, where if you have a Delta co-branded credit card, you can redeem miles for one cent each toward a Delta flight purchase (in increments of 5,000 miles per $50). That’s not the best deal in the world, though this is a feature that’s exclusively available to those with an eligible Delta Amex card.

Some people find this to be useful since they can redeem their miles toward flights, and then they still earn miles and MQDs on the portion of the fare they pay in cash.

With the TakeOff 15 perk (exclusively for those with select Delta Amex cards), you can save 15% on the cost of a SkyMiles award ticket when traveling exclusively on Delta (the discount doesn’t apply to taxes and fees). Delta SkyMiles award pricing is dynamic, and generally you’ll find that each mile gets you a bit over a cent toward the cost of a ticket.

Saving 15% on these awards is valuable, and means that you’ll generally get somewhere around 1.2-1.3 cents of value per mile (or sometimes even more). In many cases this will end up being a better value than using the Pay With Miles option, so it’s a real perk of the card.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards.

Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year. You can access these offers by logging into your account and scrolling down to the bottom of your account summary page. (Enrollment required)

The Delta Platinum Card gets you complimentary Hertz Five Star status. Enrollment is required, and you receive the following benefits with the rental car company:

The Delta Platinum Amex comes with a handful of coverage benefits that can protect you and your belongings both at home and on the road, including:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc. Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

The Delta Platinum Credit Card isn’t necessarily the best card for the casual Delta flyer, and it’s also not a card I’d recommend putting much spending on, unless you value the MQDs that you can earn with the card. Even if you value MQDs, you’re better off with the more premium card, since you can earn them twice as fast.

However, this card has solid perks, ranging from a companion certificate, to free checked bags, to priority boarding, to savings on award flights, to access to exclusive award redemption opportunities, to valuable statement credits, and more.

Bigger picture, is the Delta Platinum Card worth it, though? There are a few things to consider.

If the Delta Platinum Amex sounds interesting to you but you are instead looking for a card for your small business, consider the Delta SkyMiles® Platinum Business American Express Card.

Most of the benefits of the card are the same. The main earning difference is that the business card earns 1.5x miles on transit, at U.S. shipping providers, and on single eligible purchases of $5,000 or more (on up to $100,000 of combined eligible purchases per year), while the personal card offers 2x miles at restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets (both cards offer 3x miles on Delta purchases and hotel purchases).

The business version of the card also offers an annual Delta Stays credit of up to $200, rather than one of up to $150, so it’s arguably more lucrative.

The Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (learn more) is a good card for occasional Delta flyers who want basic airline perks. It has a $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150. (Rates & Fees) and a smaller list of perks, including:

The Delta Gold Card offers the same discounts you get with the Delta Platinum Card, as well as the rideshare credit, but in this case it only kicks in after your first renewal. The Delta Gold Card doesn’t earn MQDs toward status, so that’s another potential downside to keep in mind.

For the very frequent Delta flyer, there’s the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (learn more), which has a $650 annual fee (Rates & Fees). What differentiates this card?

If you are looking to earn Delta SkyMiles through credit card spending then consider using a card earning Amex Membership Rewards points. These points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles at a 1:1 ratio, and you can in many cases earn points at a much faster rate.

For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50K per calendar year, and then 1x) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25K per calendar year, and then 1x), and 3x points on flights booked directly with airlines or at amextravel.com

Furthermore, earning Amex points gives you more flexibility to redeem in other ways, given all the great uses of Membership Rewards points.

The information and associated card details on this page for the American Express Green Card have been collected independently by OMAAT and have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The information and associated card details on this page for the American Express Green Card have been collected independently by OMAAT and have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The Delta Platinum Amex offers solid perks for those who fly Delta frequently, especially Medallion members. For many, the annual companion certificate will more than justify the annual fee in and of itself, without even accounting for all of the other perks. Some will also get value from the 2,500 MQDs that are offered annually just for having the card.

The annual fee on this card is potentially quite easy to justify, thanks to all the credits you can earn with rideshares, Resy, and even Delta Stays.

If you want to learn more about the Delta Platinum Amex Card, follow this link.

The following links will direct you to the rates and fees for mentioned American Express Cards. These include: Delta SkyMiles® Gold American Express Card (Rates & Fees), Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card (Rates & Fees), and Delta SkyMiles® Platinum American Express Card (Rates & Fees).
